questions.stem: At San Pedro Tutoring Centre, a teacher's algorithm must input a mark and work out a grade for each of the 25 students in her class, carrying out the same steps every time. Which control structure is needed to handle all 25 students?
questions.explain: Doing the same steps for each of a known number of students is repetition (a FOR loop). Selection is tempting because grading involves decisions, but processing all 25 students is what needs the loop; nothing is chosen between paths at that level.

questions.stem: A clerk at the Young Street Duty-Free shop uses an algorithm that keeps a running total of the value of every item a cruise passenger buys. Which statement in the algorithm acts as the accumulator?
questions.explain: An accumulator adds a varying value (each price) to a running total. count ← count + 1 is the tempting distractor, but adding a fixed 1 makes it a counter, which counts the items rather than totalling their value.

questions.stem: A St. John’s radio station uses this algorithm to count down before the morning news: FOR n ← 9 DOWNTO 4 DO OUTPUT n ENDFOR. How many times is the body of the loop executed?
questions.explain: n takes 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4: six values (9 − 4 + 1). 5 is tempting if you subtract without adding 1; 0 is tempting if you think a loop cannot run from a larger to a smaller number, but DOWNTO counts down.

questions.stem: A student programmer at the Saba Dive Centre has defined and analysed the dive-booking problem and wants to start typing Python code straight away. According to the stages of program development, which stage should come immediately BEFORE coding?
questions.explain: The algorithm is designed and desk-checked before it is coded: it is the precursor of the program. Testing and debugging is tempting but can only happen once code exists.

questions.stem: A programmer at the Roseau Freight Company is rewriting the company's parcel-tracking program in C++, and the manager asks what kind of language C++ is. C++ is BEST classified as which type of programming language?
questions.explain: C++ extends C with classes and objects, so it is classified as object-oriented. It can be used procedurally, but none of the other options fit: logic is Prolog, functional is Haskell, and markup languages such as HTML are not programming languages.

questions.stem:
IT captures, stores, processes, retrieves, transmits and presents data. Watch IT at work across the Caribbean and decide which job it is doing at that moment.

Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

A utility meter reader's handheld device records the reading from a meter in English Harbour.
questions.explain: Recording the reading brings data into the system: capture.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

A check-in kiosk at Piarco Airport scans a passenger's passport.
questions.explain: Scanning the passport captures data as input.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

The electricity company's billing software multiplies each customer's units used by the tariff to work out the bill.
questions.explain: Calculating turns raw readings into a bill: processing.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

The Bay Street Jewellers' till adds up a cruise passenger's purchases and applies a duty-free discount.
questions.explain: Adding and applying a discount is processing.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

The Gros Islet clinic keeps patient records on its server and calls one up when the patient returns.
questions.explain: Keeping records and opening them again later is storing and retrieving.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

Seagrape Bay Secondary School keeps last term's assignments in Google Classroom so students can open them for revision.
questions.explain: The work is stored and retrieved when needed.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

A card terminal in a St. John’s shop sends a payment request to the bank's server.
questions.explain: Sending data from one place to another is transmission.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

The San Fernando clinic emails an X-ray image to a specialist in Curaçao.
questions.explain: Sending the image across the network is transmission.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

The Island Courier's website displays the morning headlines on readers' phones.
questions.explain: Showing information to the reader is presenting output.

questions.stem:
Which information-handling job is IT doing here?

Flight information screens at Nassau's airport show departure times and gate numbers.
questions.explain: Displaying information to passengers is presenting output.

questions.stem:
IT is used in every sector, and inside each organisation IT work covers infrastructure, software, data and information management, user support and security. Read each situation and choose the BEST answer.

At the Bayside Insurance office in Bridgetown, Kerwin runs new network cables and replaces a faulty router. Which area of IT work is this?
questions.explain: Networks, cables, routers and servers are infrastructure.

questions.stem: At the Sunset Supermarket in Frigate Bay, the IT officer installs and configures the new version of the accounting package on every office computer. Which area of IT work is this?
questions.explain: Installing and configuring applications is the software part of IT work.

questions.stem: A new receptionist at the Gros Islet Resort cannot print guest invoices, so the IT technician shows her step by step and writes a short guide. Which area of IT work is this?
questions.explain: Helping and training users is user support (help desk and training).

questions.stem: At a law firm on Frederick Street in Port of Spain, the IT team sets up a firewall, enforces strong passwords and encrypts laptops in case they are stolen. Which area of IT work is this?
questions.explain: Protecting systems and data from unauthorised access is security.

questions.stem: At the Seaside Pharmacy in Portsmouth, the IT officer removes duplicate customer records and checks that the stock database is backed up every night. Which area of IT work is this?
questions.explain: Keeping data accurate, organised and backed up is data and information management.

questions.stem: Customers in Barbados use a mobile app to transfer money at midnight without visiting a branch. In which sector is IT being used?
questions.explain: Mobile and online banking is IT usage in banking and finance.

questions.stem: After Hurricane Irma in 2017, relief agencies used satellite phones and social media to locate families in Barbuda. In which sector is IT being used?
questions.explain: Emergency communication and coordination is IT usage in disaster management.

questions.stem: At a Sea-Almond Secondary School careers talk, an electricity company officer explains that her department keeps the meters, billing software, servers and network running so that customer data becomes accurate bills and online account information. A student asks what "the field of IT" means. Which statement BEST describes it?
options: Any use of a computer for entertainment such as gaming or streaming.
The use and management of computers, software, networks and telecommunications to capture, process, store, transmit and present information for people and organisations.
The scientific study of algorithms and the theory of computation.
The design of the electronic circuits and processors inside computers.

questions.stem:
A Grade 12 group is preparing a "Let's Talk IT" discussion on the scope of IT in Barbados. Sort each statement.

Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

Passengers check in for flights at self-service kiosks at GAIA.
questions.explain: A usage in tourism and transport.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

A wrongly typed meter reading produces an incorrect electricity bill.
questions.explain: Garbage in, garbage out: the computer cannot judge whether input is correct.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

Students submit assignments through Microsoft Teams.
questions.explain: A usage in education.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

Card machines stop working during a long island-wide power cut.
questions.explain: Dependence on power and connectivity is a limitation.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

A clinic shares an X-ray image with a specialist in Curaçao.
questions.explain: A usage in health (telemedicine).

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

A laptop bought five years ago can no longer run the latest software.
questions.explain: Rapid obsolescence is a limitation.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

A program cannot decide whether an unusual refund request is fair.
questions.explain: IT lacks human judgement for situations its rules do not cover.

questions.stem:
Is this a usage of IT or a limitation of IT?

Satellite phones and social media help relief agencies coordinate after a hurricane.
questions.explain: A usage in disaster management.

questions.stem:
Read each job task and choose the discipline it BEST represents.

Designing the circuit board and firmware for a new smart water meter.
questions.explain: Designing hardware and firmware is Computer Engineering.

questions.stem: Proving that a new search algorithm is faster than existing ones.
questions.explain: Analysing algorithms is Computer Science.

questions.stem: Leading a team that builds, tests and maintains a national tax-filing system over three years.
questions.explain: A disciplined, large-scale development process is Software Engineering.

questions.stem: Studying how a hotel handles bookings and recommending a system that gives managers better reports.
questions.explain: Analysing business processes and information needs is Information Systems.

questions.stem: Setting up the Wi-Fi network, user accounts and backups for a school and helping teachers when devices fail.
questions.explain: Deploying, administering and supporting infrastructure for users is IT.

questions.stem: Deciding whether an airline should invest in a new reservation system to support its expansion strategy.
questions.explain: Aligning technology investment with business strategy is Information Systems.

questions.stem: The Holetown Marina wants to know which services earn the most profit so the owners can plan expansion. A consultant studies how bookings, fuel sales and berth fees are recorded and designs a reporting system for management. This work BEST belongs to which discipline?
options: Computer Science, because data is being analysed.
Computer Engineering, because a new system is being designed.
Information Technology, because it involves a computer system.
Information Systems, because it focuses on the organisation's processes and information needs for decision-making.

questions.stem:
Professional organisations do much more than collect membership fees. Read each situation and decide what the professional body is doing.

A new router sold in Belmopan works with every brand of phone and laptop because the makers all follow IEEE 802.11.
questions.explain: IEEE develops technical standards so products from different makers work together.

questions.stem: A software developer in Barbados refuses to hide a known security flaw from a client, pointing to the rules her professional body expects members to follow.
options: Publishing a code of ethics or conduct
questions.explain: Codes of ethics and conduct (ACM, IEEE, BCS) guide members' professional behaviour.

questions.stem: BCS examines a university's computing degree and confirms that it meets professional standards.
questions.explain: Accrediting degrees is how professional bodies guide and assure the quality of education.

questions.stem: An IT manager in Trinidad and Tobago is awarded Chartered IT Professional (CITP) status after showing her experience and competence.
questions.explain: BCS recognises qualified professionals through chartered status.

questions.stem: A Coralstone College lecturer in Belize reads recent studies on hotel booking systems in the AIS eLibrary and presents her own paper at AMCIS.
questions.explain: AIS publishes Information Systems research and runs conferences such as AMCIS and ICIS.

questions.stem: Computing students at a regional university join an IEEE student branch, enter a robotics competition and meet engineers who later offer internships.
questions.explain: Student branches and chapters support members' careers through networking, competitions and mentoring.

questions.stem: ACM presents the A.M. Turing Award to a computer scientist whose work changed computing.
questions.explain: ACM's Turing Award, often called the "Nobel Prize of computing", recognises outstanding contributions.

questions.stem: A tourist's laptop bought in Canada connects without trouble to the Wi-Fi in a Belize City café whose router was made by a different company in Asia. Which professional organisation's work BEST explains this?
options: BCS, because it accredits computing degrees.
AIS, because it studies how organisations use information systems.
ACM, because it publishes the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct.
IEEE, because its 802.11 standard defines how Wi-Fi devices communicate.

questions.stem:
A careers fair at Sea-Almond Secondary School in St. Lucia lists these job adverts. Sort each job by the discipline that BEST prepares a candidate for it.

Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Embedded systems engineer to design control boards for desalination plant pumps.
questions.explain: Designing control hardware is Computer Engineering.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Mobile app developer to build and maintain a ferry-booking app for the Castries to Martinique route.
questions.explain: Building and maintaining software is Software Engineering.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Network administrator for a hotel chain in Rodney Bay.
questions.explain: Running network infrastructure is IT.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Business analyst to redesign the claims process at an insurance company in Barbados.
questions.explain: Analysing business processes is Information Systems.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Help desk technician supporting staff at a ministry in Castries.
questions.explain: User support is a core IT role.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Hardware engineer to design a sensor that measures water levels in English Harbour.
questions.explain: Designing physical devices is Computer Engineering.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

IT manager to align technology spending with a bank's five-year strategy.
questions.explain: Aligning technology with organisational strategy is Information Systems.

questions.stem:
Which discipline does this career draw on most?

Quality assurance tester for a large accounting software product.
questions.explain: Testing within a disciplined development process is Software Engineering.

questions.stem:
You are a peer mentor at Sea-Almond Secondary School. Jaden, a CAPE student, wants a career in computing but is not sure which path to take. Give him the best advice.

Jaden says: "I like fixing the school's Wi-Fi and helping teachers with their laptops, but I am not interested in maths proofs or designing chips." What do you suggest first?
options: His interests match Information Technology: infrastructure and supporting users. Suggest he explore IT roles such as network or systems administration.
Tell him Computer Engineering is the best path because all computing jobs are the same.

questions.stem: Jaden asks how he can find out more about real IT jobs in the region. What do you recommend?
options: Research adverts, interview the school's IT officer as a resource person and read the BCS and IEEE websites about the profession.
Just watch one video online and decide from that.

questions.stem: Jaden worries: "If I go into IT, will a computer just do my job? Computers can do everything now." How do you respond?
options: Explain IT's limitations: systems need people to check data, make judgements, maintain equipment and keep services running during power or network failures, as after Hurricane Irma.
Agree that IT has no limitations, so he should choose another career.

questions.stem: Keisha, a CAPE student at Mahoe Grove High School, is practising a Paper 02-style question: "Describe ONE limitation of Information Technology." (2 marks) Her study group writes four answers. Which answer would earn BOTH marks?
options: IT is used in banking, tourism and education.
IT depends on a reliable power supply, so when electricity fails, for example after a hurricane, businesses cannot process card payments or access their records.

questions.stem:
A Lower Sixth class at Sea-Almond Secondary School is drafting answers to "Outline the history of computer hardware." Judge each point a student wrote as an examiner would.

Kayla writes: "Then came transistors."
questions.explain: Not wrong, but thin. Kayla needs a period (late 1950s to mid-1960s) and an effect (smaller, cooler, more reliable).

questions.stem: Jaden writes: "About 1971, the microprocessor put a whole CPU on one chip, which led to cheap personal computers."
questions.explain: Date, defining technology and effect in one sentence: a full outline point.

questions.stem: Amara writes: "The Internet was invented and everybody started using it."
questions.explain: No date, no technology (ARPANET, packet switching, TCP/IP) and a vague effect. It earns little.

questions.stem: Shanice writes: "The 1990s: the microprocessor was invented."
questions.explain: The date is wrong. The first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, came in 1971.

questions.stem: Devon writes: "First-generation computers (1940s to mid-1950s) used vacuum tubes, so they filled rooms, used huge power and overheated."
questions.explain: Period, component and effects linked by "so": strong.

questions.stem: Luis writes: "The World Wide Web came first, and then ARPANET joined the networks together."
questions.explain: The order is reversed. ARPANET (1969) came about twenty years before the Web (1989 to 1991).

questions.stem: At the Montego Bay Computer Museum in Kingston, a guide stands between a 1940s vacuum-tube computer and a 1960 transistor computer. She tells visitors the newer machine broke down far less often and was cheaper to run. Which statement BEST explains why?
options: The stored-program concept meant computers no longer needed electricity to hold data.
High-level languages such as FORTRAN made the hardware more reliable.
Transistors replaced vacuum tubes, so the machines used less power, produced less heat and had far fewer component failures.
Integrated circuits placed thousands of transistors on one chip, so there were fewer connections to fail.

questions.stem:
The Frigate Bay Computer Museum in Basseterre has mixed up its display cards. Sort each card into the generation it describes.

Which generation?

A room-sized machine needs its own air-conditioned hall because thousands of glowing tubes keep overheating and burning out
questions.explain: Heat and frequent failures are the classic effects of vacuum tubes.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

Programmers key in binary machine-language codes that work only on that one machine
questions.explain: Machine language was the only option for first-generation computers.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

A large firm's payroll machine stores data in magnetic core memory and runs programs written in COBOL
questions.explain: Core memory and early high-level languages arrived with transistors.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

Individual solid-state switches, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, are wired one by one onto circuit boards
questions.explain: Discrete (separate) transistors define the second generation.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

A university department buys its own cabinet-sized PDP-8 and staff share it from terminals by time-sharing
questions.explain: ICs made minicomputers and time-sharing operating systems possible.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

A bank upgrades to a bigger model in a compatible family of computers without rewriting its programs
questions.explain: The IBM System/360 family (1964) was built with integrated circuits.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

The Sunset Reef Hotel in Gros Islet runs its front desk on a small PC with a graphical user interface
questions.explain: Cheap desktop PCs with GUIs are fourth-generation machines.

questions.stem:
Which generation?

A whole CPU fits on one chip, so a student carries a laptop to Flamboyant Heights College
questions.explain: A CPU on one chip is the microprocessor: fourth generation.

questions.stem:
Sort each system into the category of computer that BEST fits it.

Which category is this?

Runs a hurricane-track model with billions of calculations for a regional weather service
questions.explain: One enormous calculation needing maximum speed: a supercomputer.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

Processes thousands of card payments every second for a large regional bank
questions.explain: High transaction volume, many users and high reliability: a mainframe.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

A 1960s cabinet-sized DEC PDP-8 shared by one university laboratory
questions.explain: Cheaper than a mainframe and serving one department: a minicomputer.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

A laptop a Sixth Form student uses to type a research report
questions.explain: A single-user machine built around a microprocessor: a microcomputer.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

The chip that controls the wash cycle in a washing machine
questions.explain: A computer built into a product for one task: embedded.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

A smartphone used to pay for a taxi at Piarco Airport
questions.explain: Handheld, battery-powered: mobile.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

Central airline reservation system handling bookings worldwide
questions.explain: Huge numbers of simultaneous transactions: a mainframe.

questions.stem:
Which category is this?

A desktop PC in the Seaside Pharmacy in San Pedro
questions.explain: A desktop for one user at a time: a microcomputer.

questions.stem: Leeward Islands Bank, with branches in Barbados, St. Vincent and St. Kitts, must process millions of account transactions a day, with almost no downtime and thousands of users connected at once. Which category of computer BEST suits this requirement?
options: A group of microcomputers, because each teller could keep their own records.
A minicomputer, because it is cheaper and serves a single department.
A mainframe, because it is designed for very high volumes of transactions, many simultaneous users and high reliability.
A supercomputer, because it is the fastest type of computer available.

questions.stem:
A business consultant in Roseau is showing clients how software has changed over the decades. Decide which stage of software history each situation shows.

In 1975 the Caribbean Mutual Insurance in Trinidad pays a team of programmers to write its own billing program for a leased mainframe.
questions.explain: Written specially for one organisation: custom software, typical of the 1950s to 1970s.

questions.stem: In 1995 the Regent Street jeweller buys a spreadsheet package and keeps stock records on one PC without hiring a programmer.
questions.explain: Bought ready-made for many users: packaged software, which spread with microcomputers.

questions.stem: Today Exuma Island Tours takes bookings through an online service it opens in a phone browser and pays for monthly.
questions.explain: Delivered over the Internet as a service: cloud software.

questions.stem: In 1985 a clerk at the Kralendijk Shipping Agency types text commands at a prompt to list and copy files in MS-DOS.
questions.explain: Typed commands with no icons: a command-line interface.

questions.stem: In 1998 a receptionist at the Montego Bay Clinic clicks icons and menus with a mouse in Windows 95.
questions.explain: Windows, icons, menus and a pointer: a GUI.

questions.stem: Today a waiter at the English Harbour Grill taps orders into an Android tablet.
questions.explain: Tapping the screen with a finger: a touch interface on a mobile operating system.

questions.stem: A school computer lab in Dominica installs Linux and the Firefox browser free of charge because their source code is publicly available.
options: Packaged software sold in a box
questions.explain: Freely available source code: open-source software.

questions.stem:
Classify each software milestone.

FORTRAN (1957), used to write scientific calculations
questions.explain: FORTRAN is a high-level programming language.

questions.stem: UNIX (1969 onward), a multi-user system that manages the computer's resources
questions.explain: UNIX manages hardware, files and users: an operating system.

questions.stem: VisiCalc (1979), the first electronic spreadsheet
questions.explain: A spreadsheet is application software for end users.

questions.stem: MS-DOS (1981), shipped with the IBM PC
questions.explain: DOS stands for Disk Operating System.

questions.stem: COBOL (1959), designed for business record-keeping
questions.explain: COBOL is a programming language, even though its purpose is business.

questions.stem: Android (2008), which runs most of the smartphones sold in the Caribbean today
questions.explain: Android is a mobile operating system.

questions.stem: In a Coralstone College lecture, students learn that before the early 1980s a US research network and several other computer networks existed but could not easily exchange data with each other. Which development MOST directly allowed them to interconnect as one Internet?
options: Email, because it let users on different computers send messages.
The World Wide Web, because it linked pages with hyperlinks.
The Mosaic browser, because it displayed images.
The TCP/IP protocol suite, adopted by ARPANET in 1983, which gave all networks common rules for addressing and transmitting packets.

questions.stem:
You are advising the owners of the Pelican Key Guesthouse in Frigate Bay, who have questions about how the island stays connected. Choose the best answer each time.

The owner asks why guests' video calls to Europe travel mainly by undersea cable rather than by satellite.
options: Cables can never be damaged by storms
Fibre gives higher bandwidth and lower latency
questions.explain: Fibre carries far more data with much less delay. Satellites can reach islands, and cables can be damaged.

questions.stem: A guest from Jamaica remembers mobile phones and calls becoming much cheaper in the early 2000s. What MOST caused this?
options: Liberalisation ended single-provider markets and new operators such as Digicel competed
questions.explain: Opening markets to competition from around 2000 drove prices down and spread mobile phones.

questions.stem: After Hurricane Irma (2017), the owner reads that rebuilding focused on "resilience". What does that mean here?
options: Stronger towers, more underground fibre and back-up power so services survive storms
questions.explain: Resilience means the network keeps working, or recovers quickly, when disaster strikes.

questions.stem: Most of the guesthouse staff go online with smartphones rather than PCs. Which development made this common across the Caribbean?
questions.explain: Mobile data made the smartphone the main Internet device for many households.

questions.stem: The owner asks what first linked Caribbean islands to Europe and North America for fast messages in the late nineteenth century.
questions.explain: Telegraph cables on the seabed came first; fibre arrived a century later.

questions.stem: The owner asks why satellite links are still kept if cables carry most international traffic.
options: Because cables only carry voice calls
As a back-up and for remote areas if a cable is cut
Because satellites have lower latency than fibre
questions.explain: Satellites give an alternative route. Fibre has lower latency and carries data, not only voice.

questions.stem: The manager of the Sunset Reef Hotel in Frigate Bay notices that guests' video calls to Europe run smoothly with almost no delay. Which statement BEST explains why fibre-optic submarine cables, rather than satellites, carry most of St. Kitts's international Internet traffic?
options: Cables are never damaged by storms or ships.
Satellites cannot send signals to small islands.
Fibre carries far more data (higher bandwidth) with much lower delay (latency) than satellite links.
Satellites only carry analogue television signals.

questions.stem:
The syllabus names four strands. Sort each milestone into its strand.

Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

Intel 4004, a CPU on one chip (1971)
questions.explain: A physical component: hardware.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

COBOL for business data processing (1959)
questions.explain: A programming language: software.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

ARPANET switches to TCP/IP (1983)
questions.explain: Network protocols: the Internet.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

Bell patents the telephone (1876)
questions.explain: Voice over a distance: telecommunications.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

The IBM System/360 family of compatible mainframes (1964)
questions.explain: A family of computers: hardware.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

Windows brings a GUI to most PCs
questions.explain: An operating system: software.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

The Domain Name System translates names into addresses
questions.explain: An Internet naming service.

questions.stem:
Hardware, software, Internet or telecommunications?

2G GSM brings digital mobile calls and SMS
questions.explain: A mobile network standard: telecommunications.

questions.stem:
You are helping the "Bits to Broadband" exhibition at a library in Port of Spain. Make the decisions a careful IT historian would make.

The organiser has 20 photos of old machines and asks how to arrange the hardware wall. What do you advise?
options: Arrange them by generation, labelling each with its defining component (tube, transistor, IC, microprocessor) and approximate period.
Arrange them alphabetically by manufacturer so they are easy to find.

questions.stem: A draft label says: "The IBM PC (1981) was a powerful mainframe used by banks." What do you do?
options: Correct it: the IBM PC was a microcomputer built around a microprocessor, designed for one user, and it ran MS-DOS.
Leave it. Visitors will not notice the difference.

questions.stem: The last panel covers telecommunications in Trinidad and Tobago. The organiser wants exact cable names and dates but has no source. What do you write?
options: Describe the history accurately in general terms (submarine fibre cables, the move to mobile networks and the growth of mobile broadband) and invite the local telecommunications providers to check any specific details before printing.
Make up plausible cable names and dates so the panel looks precise.

questions.stem:
The Seaview Guesthouse in Kingston keeps records about its guests and bookings. Sort each item.

Is this raw data or processed information?

14, 9, 22, 17, 30
questions.explain: A list of numbers with no labels or context is unprocessed, discrete data.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

Occupancy in March was 82%, the highest this year.
questions.explain: The figures have been calculated and compared, so they now have meaning: information.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

A pile of handwritten check-in cards.
questions.explain: The cards are unorganised and unprocessed: data.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

A bar chart showing that most guests book through the website.
questions.explain: The data has been summarised and presented in a meaningful format: information.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

USA, Canada, Netherlands, USA, Curaçao
questions.explain: Unprocessed country names with no count or context: data.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

Average length of stay for European guests is 9 nights.
questions.explain: An average is the result of processing, with a clear context: information.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

Room 12
questions.explain: A discrete chunk with no context: is it booked, dirty, empty? Data.

questions.stem:
Is this raw data or processed information?

Three rooms need repairs before Friday's cruise-season rush.
questions.explain: Organised and meaningful to the manager: information.

questions.stem:
The Bodden Town Community Clinic is collecting data. Choose the BEST description for each.

Each patient's blood pressure is measured with a digital monitor.
questions.explain: A measurement with units is objective: quantitative.

questions.stem: Patients write how they felt about the waiting time.
questions.explain: Feelings and opinions are subjective: qualitative.

questions.stem: Patients rate the cleanliness of the clinic from 1 to 5.
questions.explain: The number records an opinion, so it is still qualitative.

questions.stem: The pharmacy system logs every tablet dispensed, with time and batch number.
questions.explain: Every item is recorded in full: detailed.

questions.stem: A nurse surveys every tenth patient who visits in June.
questions.explain: Only a selection of patients is recorded: sampled.

questions.stem: A cleaner checks the water-cooler temperature at 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. only.
questions.explain: Two readings a day represent the whole day: sampled.

questions.stem:
The Antigua Storm Ready Committee must turn its shelter and storm data into information that different people can use. For each situation, choose the BEST option.

A fisherman already at sea off English Harbour needs a storm warning within the hour. Which MEDIUM is best?
options: A printed leaflet left at the fish market
A 20-page PDF on the committee website
questions.explain: Radio reaches him at sea in time. The leaflet and the PDF cannot reach him where he is, so the information would fail on medium and timeliness.

questions.stem: The committee wants its board to see how shelter use changed over the last five storms. Which FORMAT shows the trend most clearly?
options: A list of 2,000 individual sign-in times
A line graph of shelter use per storm
A voice note describing each storm
questions.explain: A line graph summarises the data and shows the trend at a glance. A raw list of sign-in times is still data.

questions.stem: A blind resident of All Saints needs to know the nearest shelter. Which choice suits this receiver?
options: A colour-coded chart emailed as an image
An audio message by phone call
A large colour map on a notice board
questions.explain: Format and medium must suit the receiver. Audio by phone is usable; anything purely visual is incomprehensible to this user.

questions.stem: Volunteers add up the cots used at each shelter and divide by the number of nights open. Which processing operation is this?
questions.explain: Totals and averages are calculations: processing that turns raw counts into information.

questions.stem: A clerk arranges the list of registered households alphabetically by street name. Which processing operation is this?
questions.explain: Putting records into a useful order is sorting and organising.

questions.stem: The committee stops posting letters about shelter openings and sends the same words as an SMS alert. What has it changed?
questions.explain: The words are the same; only the channel used to deliver them has changed, so this is a change of medium.

questions.stem: The Portsmouth Hardware store records every sale. At the end of the month the manager produces a report stating that "plywood sales rose by 65% in the week before the hurricane warning". Which statement BEST explains why the report is information rather than data?
options: The figures are quantitative, so they are automatically information.
The manager used the report to decide to order more plywood next year.
The sales figures have been processed and compared, giving them context and meaning for the manager.
The figures are stored on a computer rather than on paper.

questions.stem:
The New Amsterdam Medical Centre is reviewing how it handles patient information. Sort each situation by the characteristic it MOST illustrates.

Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

Only the treating doctor may read a patient's test results.
questions.explain: A rule about WHO may see sensitive information: confidentiality.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

A receptionist breaks the rules by reading results aloud in the waiting room.
questions.explain: Sensitive information reaches unauthorised people: a breach of confidentiality.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

Patient files are encrypted and each nurse logs in with a personal password.
questions.explain: Encryption and passwords are controls that protect information: security.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

Access rights let nurses view prescriptions but not change them.
questions.explain: Access levels are a security control.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

One vaccination schedule is posted online and every parent can open it at the same time.
questions.explain: Many people use the same information without using it up: shareability.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

Two doctors read the same lab report at once, and neither loses it.
questions.explain: Sharing information does not use it up: shareability.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

The records system stays online during a power cut because a generator starts.
questions.explain: Authorised users can still reach the information when needed: availability.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic does this situation illustrate?

An emergency doctor can pull up a patient's allergy list at 3 a.m.
questions.explain: Information accessible when and where it is needed: availability.

questions.stem:
The Regent Street Credit Union is reviewing problems with its information. Sort each problem by the group of characteristics it affects.

Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

Two branches show different balances for the same account.
questions.explain: Contradictory records: inconsistency, a trust problem.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

A loan report uses so many abbreviations that members cannot follow it.
questions.explain: Incomprehensible information cannot be understood.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

The monthly report reaches the board two weeks after the meeting.
questions.explain: Late information fails on timeliness.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

The report on a loan application leaves out the applicant's existing debts.
questions.explain: Missing key facts: completeness.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

A staff member emails member account numbers to a personal address.
questions.explain: A breach of confidentiality and security.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

The online banking system is down for two days.
questions.explain: Users cannot reach their information: availability.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

Interest-rate figures were mistyped when copied into the newsletter.
questions.explain: The meaning was changed in processing: distortion.

questions.stem:
Which group of characteristics does this problem affect?

Last year's rates are still on the website.
questions.explain: The information has passed its lifespan.

questions.stem: The Caribbean Market Insights Ltd collects data on shopping habits across Jamaica, Barbados and Guyana, processes it into regional reports and sells the reports to supermarket chains. This BEST illustrates which characteristic of information?

You are the operations manager of Island Fresh supermarket in Oistins. A tropical storm watch has been issued for Barbados. Make the best decisions with the data and information you have.

A staff member forwards a voice note saying "a Category 4 will hit tomorrow morning, everyone is buying water". What do you do first?
options: Check the latest official advisory and its issue time before acting.
Order three containers of water immediately based on the voice note.

questions.stem: The official advisory confirms a storm watch, with arrival in about 48 hours. To plan stock, which data do you use?
options: Detailed sales data from this store in the 48 hours before previous storm watches.
National average annual sales for all supermarkets in the Caribbean.

questions.stem: The report shows water, batteries and canned food sell three to five times faster before storms. You notice last year's battery figures were keyed in twice. What next?
options: Correct the duplicate entries, recalculate, then decide on order quantities and staff hours.
Ignore it; the numbers are close enough.

questions.stem:
Mango Scoop ice-cream parlour on Fort Street wants to decide which new flavour to launch for the cruise season. Sort each problem with its data.

Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

Some sales were keyed in twice on the till.
questions.explain: Duplicates make the data inaccurate: a quality problem.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

A cashier typed 1,000 cones instead of 100.
questions.explain: A data-entry error: the data is inaccurate.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

Half the survey forms have no answer to the flavour question.
questions.explain: Missing values: the data is incomplete.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

The flavour price list in the system has not been updated for three years.
questions.explain: Out-of-date data is a quality problem.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

The owner studies sales from a parlour in Canada during winter.
questions.explain: Accurate, perhaps, but from the wrong place and time: inappropriate.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

The owner looks at the shop's electricity bills to choose a flavour.
questions.explain: Correct data, but irrelevant to the decision: inappropriate.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

Staff, not customers, are asked which flavour customers would buy.
questions.explain: Wrong population: the data does not come from the people the decision is about.

questions.stem:
Is this a data-quality problem or an appropriateness problem?

Only customers on one quiet, rainy Monday are surveyed about busy cruise days.
questions.explain: The sample is from the wrong time, so it does not represent cruise-day customers.

questions.stem: A teacher at Seagrape Bay Secondary School in Barbados analyses mock-examination results. Which statement represents KNOWLEDGE rather than data or information?
options: The class average was 59% and four students scored below 50%.
Because students who practise past papers improve most on database questions, the class will do two timed database papers before the exam.
Most students lost marks on database questions.

questions.stem:
Students at Seagrape Bay Secondary School in Barbados are practising SO 1.3 questions. Judge each answer or question the way an examiner would.

Question: "Distinguish between data and information." Kemar writes only: "Data are raw, unprocessed facts."
options: Loses marks: only one of the two terms is defined
questions.explain: Distinguish needs a difference on the same feature for EACH term. Kemar must also say what information is, with an example.

questions.stem: Question: "Give an example of knowledge." Aaliyah writes: "Rainfall in Bridgetown was 40% above average in September."
options: Loses marks: this is information, with no decision
questions.explain: The statement is processed and meaningful, but nothing is decided. Adding "so the council will clear the drains in August" would make it knowledge.

questions.stem: Question: "Classify a 1-to-5 hotel room rating." Dwayne writes: "Quantitative, because it is a number."
options: Incorrect: it records an opinion, so it is qualitative
questions.explain: A rating records a subjective judgement. Being written as a number does not make it a measurement.

questions.stem: Question: "Explain timeliness." Shanice writes: "Information must be available in time for the decision it supports; a storm warning issued after landfall is useless."
questions.explain: Shanice gives the correct meaning (in time for the decision) and a reason with an example.

questions.stem: A Paper 02 question begins: "Identify TWO characteristics of quantitative data." What does the command word require?
options: Points for and against, with a conclusion
A detailed reason for each point
questions.explain: Identify means name or state; no explanation is needed for the mark.

questions.stem: Question: "Distinguish between confidentiality and security." Ravi writes one sentence saying they both mean "keeping data safe".
options: Loses marks: they are treated as one point
questions.explain: Confidentiality is the requirement that information be restricted; security is the set of controls that restrict it. Treating them as one loses the distinction.

questions.stem: Guadeloupe Tourism Survey Team wants to decide which new attraction to build for visitors. It uses an accurate, carefully checked spreadsheet of resident electricity bills for the last five years. Which statement BEST describes the problem with this data?
options: The data is of poor quality because it contains errors.
The data is qualitative, so it cannot be processed.
The data is inappropriate because it does not relate to visitors' preferences.
The data is incomplete because it covers only five years.

questions.stem:
Kayla, a Lower Six student at Seagrape Bay Secondary School in Anguilla, has interviewed people about how residents got news during Hurricane Irma in 2017. Sort each note from her research diary.

Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

Kayla asks the radio presenter a follow-up question about which stations stayed on air, and he explains straight away.
options: Advantage of people as a source
Disadvantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Interactive: you can ask follow-up questions and clarify. That is an advantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

Her grandmother in East End remembers the storm arriving on a different day from the official record.
options: Advantage of people as a source
Disadvantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Memory errors: recollections change over the years. That is a disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

The Sandy Ground shopkeeper describes selling goods by torchlight, something never written down anywhere.
options: Disadvantage of people as a source
Advantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Local, unpublished knowledge that exists only in people's experience: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

A manager she hoped to interview is too busy to meet her before her deadline.
options: Disadvantage of people as a source
Advantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Availability: experts may be busy or unwilling, and interviews take time to arrange. A disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

The shopkeeper insists his shop was the first on the street to reopen, but Kayla has no record to check this.
options: Advantage of people as a source
Disadvantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Hard to verify and possibly self-serving: a disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

A Flamboyant Heights College lecturer explains in plain language how radio signals travel, pitched at her level.
options: Advantage of people as a source
Disadvantage of people as a source
questions.explain: People can explain at a level that suits you: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

The interviews cost Kayla nothing except her time and a few phone calls.
options: Disadvantage of people as a source
Advantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Often free or low-cost: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Does this note show an advantage or a disadvantage of people as an information source?

Each person can describe only their own street, so her picture of the whole island is incomplete.
options: Advantage of people as a source
Disadvantage of people as a source
questions.explain: Limited to one person's experience, so not representative: a disadvantage.

questions.stem: The Seaside Pharmacy in Gros Islet wants to know why customers prefer its delivery service to collecting in store. Which source is MOST likely to give detailed, current insight into this question?
options: Interviews with a sample of regular customers
A DVD of pharmacy training videos
A printed textbook on retail management

questions.stem:
A Lower Six class from Flamboyant Heights College spends a morning with Mr. Hodge, a school librarian in St. John's, Antigua. For each situation, choose the best answer about books, catalogues and periodicals.

Tariq needs a full, structured explanation of how computers developed, and he has a week to read it at home.
questions.explain: Books give depth and a logical structure, with chapters and an index.

questions.stem: Tariq's library book on smartphones was printed in 2015. What is its main weakness for a report on this year's smartphones?
options: It needs a device to read it
It is likely to be out of date
questions.explain: Books take months or years to produce, so in fast-moving IT topics they date quickly.

questions.stem: Shania searches the library catalogue for "Caribbean history" and gets a list of titles with shelf numbers. What has the catalogue given her?
options: The full text of each book
The location of items so she can find them
An expert summary of each book
questions.explain: A library catalogue is a finding aid: it describes items and where they are, not their content.

questions.stem: Mr. Hodge compares laptops in a printed supplier catalogue before buying for the library. Which caution should he keep in mind?
options: The seller wrote it, so it presents the products favourably
It has been checked by independent experts
questions.explain: Product catalogues are written by the seller, and printed prices and models date quickly.

questions.stem: Devon needs expert research findings, with references, on solar power in small island states.
questions.explain: Journals publish research by specialists, often reviewed by experts, with reference lists.

questions.stem: Aaliyah wants to know what the government announced yesterday about road repairs in All Saints.
options: A book on the history of Antigua
questions.explain: Newspapers are the most current print source and cover local events.

questions.stem: Jaden wants a readable, illustrated review of new gaming consoles before Christmas.
questions.explain: Magazines offer readable reviews and illustrations for general readers.

questions.stem:
Mr. Hodge, a librarian at a St. John's school, is labelling the resources in his collection. Sort each source by its medium.

Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A printed copy of the daily newspaper
questions.explain: A printed newspaper needs no device: traditional.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A retired electricity company engineer who agrees to be interviewed
questions.explain: People are a traditional source.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A DVD of a documentary on Caribbean history
questions.explain: A DVD needs a player or computer: electronic.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A subscription database of journal articles
questions.explain: Electronic databases are accessed by computer: electronic.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A printed supplier catalogue of computer parts
questions.explain: A printed catalogue is a traditional source.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A wiki written by Form 5 students about local plants
questions.explain: A wiki is a collaboratively edited web site: electronic.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A printed computing journal on the library shelf
questions.explain: A printed journal is traditional. (The same journal online would be electronic.)

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

A tourism board's Instagram account
questions.explain: Social media is an electronic source.

questions.stem:
Is this a traditional or an electronic source?

An encyclopaedia on a CD-ROM
questions.explain: The content is the same type as a book, but the medium is a CD-ROM: electronic.

questions.stem:
Malik, an Upper Six student in Bridgetown, is using a public library for his Caribbean trade project. Sort each experience he has.

Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

A librarian shows Malik how to find three books on Caribbean trade in ten minutes.
questions.explain: Trained librarians help users find and choose sources: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

With his library card, Malik reads articles from an expensive journal subscription for free.
questions.explain: Free or low-cost access to costly sources: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

The only copy of the book Malik needs is out on loan for two weeks.
questions.explain: Limited copies and loan periods: a disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

The library closes at 5 p.m., but Malik can only study late at night.
questions.explain: Opening hours limit access: a disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

Old local newspapers from the 1990s are kept there and are not available online.
questions.explain: Libraries preserve local material: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

Malik's classmate lives far from town and has no transport to reach the building.
questions.explain: Users must travel to the building: a disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

Books are catalogued and shelved by subject, so related items sit together.
questions.explain: Sources are selected and organised: an advantage.

questions.stem:
Is this an advantage or a disadvantage of a library as an information source?

A small island library lost part of its collection when a storm flooded the building.
questions.explain: Physical collections can be damaged by storms: a disadvantage.

questions.stem: A student at Sandbox Tree College needs published research articles on renewable energy in small island states. Which statement BEST explains why the library's electronic database is a better choice than a general web search?
options: The database is free to everyone, while web sites charge a fee.
The database can be used without any Internet connection.
The database is always more up to date than any web site.
The database contains selected material from established publishers and allows precise filtering by subject and date.

questions.stem:
For each information need, choose the source that is MOST suitable.

Today's arrival delays at V. C. Bird International Airport in Antigua.
questions.explain: Live, official information: the airport's web site.

questions.stem: Peer-reviewed research on coral reef damage around Saba.
options: A scientific journal found through an electronic database
questions.explain: Expert research is published in journals, best found through a database.

questions.stem: How small shops in Road Town, Tortola, coped in the week after Hurricane Irma.
questions.explain: First-hand local experience comes from people.

questions.stem: The specifications and prices of laptops a supplier stocks.
questions.explain: A product catalogue lists specifications and prices.

questions.stem: An interactive science programme for a school in the Guyana interior with no Internet.
questions.explain: A DVD works offline and carries multimedia.

questions.stem: A detailed, structured explanation of computer history for a beginner.
questions.explain: A book gives depth and a logical structure.

questions.stem:
Jaden, a student at Calabash Point Secondary in Sint Maarten, is researching the 2017 hurricane season. Sort each item he collected.

Is this a primary or a secondary source?

A recorded interview with his uncle, who sheltered in Philipsburg during Hurricane Irma
questions.explain: First-hand account from someone who experienced the event: primary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

A textbook chapter on the causes of Atlantic hurricanes
questions.explain: It explains and summarises other work: secondary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

Photographs his neighbour took of damage in Simpson Bay the next morning
questions.explain: Original images captured at the time: primary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

A magazine feature reviewing recovery efforts five years later
questions.explain: It interprets events after the fact: secondary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

Wind-speed readings recorded by a weather station during the storm
questions.explain: Raw original data: primary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

An encyclopaedia entry on the 2017 Atlantic hurricane season
questions.explain: An encyclopaedia summarises other sources: secondary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

A blog post that compares several news reports about the storm
questions.explain: It analyses and compares other reports: secondary.

questions.stem:
Is this a primary or a secondary source?

A resident's live video posted to social media as the eye passed over
questions.explain: Original eyewitness content: primary, even though it is on social media.

questions.stem:
Each card describes a real research need in the region. Use the advantages of each type to decide whether a primary or a secondary source is the better choice.

Which type of source suits this need better?

The Portsmouth Water Sports wants to know what its own customers think of evening kayak tours.
options: A secondary source suits it better
A primary source suits it better
questions.explain: Only a primary source (its own survey) is specific to its customers.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A Lower Six student has one afternoon to get an overview of tourism trends across the Caribbean.
options: A primary source suits it better
A secondary source suits it better
questions.explain: Secondary sources are quick and give an overview someone has already put together.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A dive shop on Bonaire wants figures no one else has: how many divers saw turtles on its trips this month.
options: A secondary source suits it better
A primary source suits it better
questions.explain: Primary data gives unique, current information not available anywhere else.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A Form 4 student needs the causes of hurricanes explained in simple language.
options: A secondary source suits it better
A primary source suits it better
questions.explain: Secondary sources such as textbooks are easier for a beginner to understand.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A researcher wants to control and check exactly how her water samples from Carlisle Bay, Barbados, are collected.
options: A secondary source suits it better
A primary source suits it better
questions.explain: With primary data you control and can check the method of collection.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A small business in Grenada has no budget for its own survey but needs regional market information.
options: A primary source suits it better
A secondary source suits it better
questions.explain: Secondary sources are cheaper than collecting new data.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A journalist wants the exact words of a minister's speech, not someone's summary of it.
options: A primary source suits it better
A secondary source suits it better
questions.explain: A primary source has no added interpretation.

questions.stem:
Which type of source suits this need better?

A student new to a topic wants a reading list that will lead her to the original documents.
options: A primary source suits it better
A secondary source suits it better
questions.explain: Secondary sources give context and references that lead to primary sources.

questions.stem: A journal article written by a team at Coralstone College reports the results of their own survey of internet use among 2,000 households in Trinidad and Tobago. As an information source, this article is BEST described as
options: primary, because it reports original research carried out by the authors
secondary, because it is a printed traditional source
primary, because it was published in the Caribbean
secondary, because all journal articles are secondary sources

questions.stem:
For each situation in Jamaica and the wider region, decide which group of sources GENERALLY has the advantage.

In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

Two days after a hurricane there is no power or Internet in Montego Bay, and a student needs to revise.
questions.explain: Traditional sources need no equipment, power or connection.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A student on Carriacou needs to search thousands of articles for the word "desalination" in seconds.
questions.explain: Electronic sources allow fast keyword searching and filters.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A teacher wants students to watch an animation with narration explaining a process.
questions.explain: Electronic sources carry multimedia: audio, video and animation.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

Thirty students in different districts all need the same source at 10 p.m.
questions.explain: Electronic sources give many users access at once, 24 hours a day.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A reader wants an edited, checked account rather than unchecked blog and social media posts.
questions.explain: Books, journals and newspapers usually pass through editors.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A family in Martinique wants a source that costs nothing in data charges and needs no device.
questions.explain: Traditional sources need no device or data plan.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A researcher needs flight information that was updated this morning.
questions.explain: Online sources can be updated instantly.

questions.stem:
In this situation, which group of sources has the edge?

A record must still be readable in 30 years without worrying that its file format will become obsolete.
questions.explain: Paper does not depend on a file format or device, although it must be protected from water and fire.

questions.stem:
You are helping Amara, an Upper Six student, research the question: "How did cruise tourism in the British Virgin Islands recover after Hurricane Irma?" She has two weeks. Choose wisely.

Amara wants to start. Where should she begin to get an overview quickly?
options: Read a wiki article and a recent magazine feature for an overview, noting their references.
Copy facts straight from a wiki into her report and finish.

questions.stem: She now needs reliable figures on cruise passenger numbers before and after 2017. What next?
options: Search the school library's electronic database and official statistics web sites for published figures.
Use numbers quoted in social media comments under a cruise video.

questions.stem: Her teacher says the project needs first-hand evidence too. What does she add?
options: Nothing; secondary sources are always enough.
Interview a tour operator at the Castries cruise pier and a Bridge Street shop owner, recording and noting their answers.

questions.stem: A teacher in Dominica prefers a printed encyclopaedia to an encyclopaedia on CD-ROM for her classroom. Which reason is a VALID disadvantage of the CD-ROM version in this situation?
options: The CD-ROM content can be edited by any student.
The CD-ROM needs a constant Internet connection.
The classroom laptops have no optical drive, so the disc cannot be read.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: The Bayside Research Group sells a detailed report on tourism in the north-eastern Caribbean. It can be downloaded instantly from its web site, at any hour, for US$350. Which statement BEST identifies the characteristics of this source?
options: It has low currency because it is a report.
It is highly available but has a high cost.
It is unreliable because it is sold online.
It has low availability because it costs money.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
A Grade 12 student at Sea-Almond Secondary School in Dominica is gathering sources. For each source, decide whether its stand-out characteristic is depth (lots of detail on a narrow topic) or breadth (wide coverage, less detail).

Which characteristic stands out?

A 60-page engineering study of one desalination plant's energy use.
questions.explain: One plant, many pages of detail: depth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Which characteristic stands out?

A one-page fact sheet listing the capitals, populations and currencies of every CARICOM member.
questions.explain: Many countries, little on each: breadth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Which characteristic stands out?

A thesis on the history of a single Roseau street from 1900 to 1950.
questions.explain: A narrow topic studied in detail: depth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Which characteristic stands out?

An introductory textbook chapter surveying all major types of computer.
questions.explain: It surveys many types briefly: breadth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Which characteristic stands out?

A news round-up summarising ten stories from across the region.
questions.explain: Ten stories in brief: breadth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Which characteristic stands out?

An interview with an electricity company engineer explaining in detail how one substation was rebuilt after Hurricane Maria.
questions.explain: A single event explained thoroughly: depth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Holetown Marine Survey is sharing its findings in many ways. For each card, decide whether it names the format (how the information is arranged) or the medium (what carries it to the user).

Arrangement or carrier?

A table of water temperatures at six dive sites around Holetown.
questions.explain: A table is a way of arranging information: format.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

A printed booklet handed out at the Bridgetown cruise pier.
questions.explain: Paper is the carrier: medium.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

A narrated video showing coral damage after Hurricane Elsa.
questions.explain: Video is the form of the information: format.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

The survey's web site, read on a phone in Speightstown.
questions.explain: The web site delivers the information: medium.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

A bar chart comparing fish counts in 2017 and 2025.
questions.explain: A chart is an arrangement of data: format.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

A morning radio broadcast where a survey scientist explains the results.
questions.explain: The broadcast signal carries the spoken information: medium.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

A flash drive of results given to a Hummingbird Ridge High School teacher.
questions.explain: The flash drive stores and carries the files: medium.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Arrangement or carrier?

An audio recording of an interview with a local fisher.
questions.explain: Audio is the form the information takes: format.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Each comment comes from a Coralstone College student describing a source. Choose the characteristic the comment is MAINLY about.

"The only copy is in the reference section and cannot be taken home."
questions.explain: Where and how you can get it: availability.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: "The data was last updated in 2009."
questions.explain: How recent the information is: currency.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: "It covers every island from the Bahamas to Trinidad, but only one paragraph each."
questions.explain: Wide coverage across many islands: breadth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: "It is a podcast episode streamed through a mobile app."
questions.explain: Audio (format) delivered through an app (medium).

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: "The statistics office has published this survey every year using the same method, and it matches other sources."
questions.explain: A consistent, trustworthy track record: reliability.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: "Downloading the full dataset would use most of my monthly mobile data."
questions.explain: Mobile data is an indirect cost.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Portsmouth Fishers' Co-operative has three sources: (1) an interview with an experienced fisher, (2) a government fisheries report (PDF, 2019) and (3) the fuel dock price board and web page. For each need, use the sources' characteristics to choose the BEST source.

The treasurer needs today's price of boat fuel for the budget meeting tonight.
questions.explain: The price board is updated daily: the highest currency for this need, even though it is shallow.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A member wants catch figures for many species across the whole fishery over several years.
questions.explain: The report is broad and deep, with data tables across the fishery.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A journalist from a Roseau radio programme wants a first-hand account of how fishing at the reef has changed since the 1990s.
questions.explain: The fisher gives deep, first-hand experience over decades, though narrow and personal.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: The chairperson asks which source is most reliable for official catch statistics.
questions.explain: The report uses an official method and names its authors: high reliability for statistics.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A member working night shifts wants detailed data tables she can read online at 2 a.m. without paying anything.
questions.explain: The PDF is available online at any time and is free: high availability, low cost.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: The secretary notes that the fisher's memory of prices in the 1980s may be inexact. Which characteristic is she questioning?
questions.explain: Whether the source gives dependable information: reliability.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A student is researching whether a new solar farm would benefit Barbados. Which source is MOST likely to be biased?
options: A peer-reviewed journal article comparing solar output on several Caribbean islands.
An outdated encyclopaedia entry on solar energy.
A national statistics table of electricity consumption by year.
A brochure produced by SunCaribe Ltd, the company bidding to build the solar farm.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
A Flamboyant Heights College student is gathering sources for a report on hurricane-resistant housing in the Caribbean. Sort each source: was it checked by independent experts before publication (refereed) or not (un-refereed)?

Independent expert review before publication?

A peer-reviewed engineering journal article on roof failures during Hurricane Irma.
questions.explain: Peer-reviewed means independent experts checked it before publication: refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A blog by a San Fernando contractor describing the houses he has built.
questions.explain: A blog is published without expert review: un-refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A newspaper feature on rebuilding, checked by the paper's own editor.
questions.explain: An editor is quality control, but not independent subject experts: un-refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A conference paper accepted after review by three independent structural engineers.
questions.explain: Independent expert review before acceptance: refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A press release from a building-supply company announcing a new shutter.
questions.explain: Press releases are written by the organisation itself, with no independent review: un-refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A wiki page on hurricane straps that any user can edit.
questions.explain: Anyone can change a wiki without expert review: un-refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
Independent expert review before publication?

A scholarly book on Caribbean architecture from an academic press that sends manuscripts to outside reviewers.
questions.explain: Outside expert review before publication: refereed.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A Flamboyant Heights College student must include at least one refereed source in her report on mobile banking in Grenada. She checks how four articles were published. Which article is refereed?
options: An article that has been shared and linked by many Caribbean web sites.
An article in a local newspaper, checked by the paper's own editor before it was printed.
An article written by a single author who holds a university degree in finance.
An article evaluated by independent experts in banking and IT before it was published, who asked for revisions.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem:
A CAPE IT student at Palmetto Point Secondary is selecting web sources for a report on coral reefs around Saba. Read each clue and choose what it tells her.

The address is www.reefscience.edu/reports/saba. Who is most likely hosting the page?
questions.explain: .edu marks an academic organisation.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: The address is www.reefgearshop.com/sale. Who is most likely hosting the page?
questions.explain: .com and a sale page: a commercial organisation that wants to sell.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: The address is www.freepages-host.com/~tanya/reef-thoughts.html. Who is most likely hosting the page?
questions.explain: A personal name after a tilde on a free host: a private individual.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A page on a marine society's site says members' pages are reviewed under the society's publishing policy and offers a "Contact the Webmaster" link. What does this suggest?
options: It must be out of date
It has probably received some organisational approval
questions.explain: An approval policy and a Webmaster contact suggest organisational approval.

questions.topic: Characteristics of sources and criteria for selecting them
questions.stem: A page on reef diving permits shows "© 2018" and no last updated date, but she needs this year's rules.
