procedures guide users to protect the data stored on hardware
questions.explain: Users following a procedure protected the data held on hardware: the components support each other.

questions.stem: At Island Breeze Hotel, a new reservation program was installed on new computers, but staff were never given instructions on how to cancel a booking. Guests are now being double-booked. Which component of the information system has been neglected?

The Grand Anse Realty in St. George’s is setting up a company email system: a mail server running Microsoft Exchange, with Outlook on every PC. Sort each item into the component of the IT system it belongs to.

Which component of the IT system is this?

The new mail server in the back office
questions.explain: A physical device you can touch: hardware.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

The cables running from each desk to the back office
questions.explain: Cables are physical: hardware. The network is the sharing they make possible.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

Microsoft Exchange running on the mail server
questions.explain: The program that stores and routes mail: software.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

Outlook installed on each agent’s PC
questions.explain: The email client is application software.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

The office network that lets every PC share the server and the printer
questions.explain: Interconnected computers sharing resources: the network.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

The Internet link that carries mail to and from overseas clients
questions.explain: It connects the office to other networks: network.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

A letting agent, trained last week, who emails viewing times to tenants
questions.explain: She uses the system for her own work: an end user.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

The receptionist who books meetings in the shared calendar
questions.explain: Trained to use the system’s capabilities: an end user.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

The IT manager who creates mailboxes for new staff
questions.explain: Running and supporting the system: an IT professional.

questions.stem:
Which component of the IT system is this?

A database administrator (DBA) who looks after the tenant database
questions.explain: DBAs are IT professionals.

questions.stem:
The Bayside Insurance Agency in Charlestown, Nevis, is listing the hardware in its office. Sort each device by its main function.

What is the main function of this device?

Barcode reader at the reception desk
questions.explain: It captures codes directly into the computer: input.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Laser printer for policy documents
questions.explain: It produces hard copy: output.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Solid-state drive in the manager’s laptop
questions.explain: It keeps files and programs permanently: secondary storage.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Webcam used for online meetings
questions.explain: It captures images: input.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Multimedia projector in the boardroom
questions.explain: It displays soft-copy output on a large screen.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

External hard drive used for nightly backups
questions.explain: It stores copies of data: secondary storage (and a peripheral).

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Fingerprint scanner on the staff door
questions.explain: It captures biometric data: input.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

Speakers on the reception computer
questions.explain: They turn signals into sound: output.

questions.stem:
What is the main function of this device?

USB flash drive
questions.explain: A portable solid-state storage device.

questions.stem: The Sunset Supermarket in Frigate Bay needs printers at its eight checkouts. Receipts must print quickly and quietly, and the store wants to avoid buying ink or toner. Which printer is MOST suitable?

A technician at the Island Tech Repairs in Frigate Bay is explaining computer parts to customers. Sort each description by the processing device it describes.

Which processing device is this?

Executes the instructions of the accounting program and controls the other components
questions.explain: General instructions and control: the CPU.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

Draws the 3D scenes of a racing game sixty times a second using many small cores in parallel
questions.explain: Parallel graphics work: the GPU.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

The main circuit board with the processor socket and the RAM slots
questions.explain: It holds and connects the parts: the motherboard.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

Decides which file to retrieve from the SSD and compares two totals in a spreadsheet
questions.explain: Controlling retrieval and comparing values: the CPU.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

Renders the effects on a high-definition Carnival video while it is edited
questions.explain: Rendering images and video: the GPU.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

Its circuits and buses carry data between the processor, RAM, storage and ports
questions.explain: The connecting board: the motherboard.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

A customer’s laptop will not take more memory because there are no free slots on it
questions.explain: RAM fits into slots on the motherboard.

questions.stem:
Which processing device is this?

Contains the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit and registers
questions.explain: These are the parts of the CPU.

questions.stem:
Businesses and students around the Caribbean are making storage decisions. Read each situation and choose the BEST answer.

A laptop at the Harbour View Accounting switches off during a power cut. Which work survives?
options: Files already saved on the internal SSD
Both the saved and the unsaved work
questions.explain: RAM is temporary and volatile; the SSD stores files permanently.

questions.stem: A photographer in Port of Spain wants to carry finished photos to a client’s office in her pocket.
questions.explain: Removable storage is the medium you take out and carry.

questions.stem: The Holetown Marina office needs an extra 4 TB drive in its own case that can be unplugged each night and locked in a safe.
questions.explain: A drive in its own case, connected by cable: external storage.

questions.stem: A terminal at the Port Information Desk has no storage of its own. It shows only what a central server sends and forgets every setting when it restarts. What is it?
questions.explain: Without storage, a computer is a dumb terminal that saves no settings.

questions.stem: While a spreadsheet of cruise-passenger figures is being totalled, where are the figures held for the processor?
questions.explain: RAM stores and retrieves data during processing.

questions.stem: A Frigate Bay student copies her CAPE notes to a USB drive every Friday in case her laptop fails. What is the USB drive doing?
questions.explain: Flash cards and USB drives often serve as backup.

questions.stem:
A technician is setting up computers at the Frigate Bay Freight Services in Basseterre. Read each situation and choose the BEST answer.

A handheld barcode scanner is plugged into the warehouse computer by USB. What is it?
questions.explain: It is connected to and controlled by the computer, outside the CPU and memory, and it captures data: an input peripheral.

questions.stem: The RAM chips on the motherboard hold the stock program while it runs. Are they a peripheral?
options: No, main memory is part of the core
questions.explain: The core is the CPU and main memory, so RAM is not a peripheral.

questions.stem: An external hard drive is attached each evening to back up the delivery records. What kind of peripheral is it?
questions.explain: It keeps copies of data outside the core: a storage peripheral.

questions.stem: A Wi-Fi dongle lets an old desktop join the office network. What kind of peripheral is it?
questions.explain: A network adapter adds a way to communicate: a communication peripheral.

questions.stem: A new label printer prints nonsense until the manufacturer’s file is installed. What was missing?
questions.explain: A device driver lets the operating system communicate with that particular printer.

questions.stem: A new mouse works the moment it is plugged in because Windows finds and loads its driver by itself. What is this called?
questions.explain: Plug and play: the OS detects the device and loads its driver automatically.

questions.stem: A technician at the Marsh Harbour Medical Centre is listing the peripheral devices attached to a reception computer. Which item should NOT be on the list?
options: An external hard drive for backups

questions.stem:
Read each description and choose the BEST classification.

A spreadsheet program used by a Guyana rice farmer for budgets and by a Barbados teacher for marks.
questions.explain: Many users, many tasks: general-purpose application software.

questions.stem: A point-of-sale package sold to hundreds of supermarkets across the region.
questions.explain: One kind of task, sold to many businesses: special-purpose.

questions.stem: A booking system written only for the Saba Dive Centre by a hired programmer.
questions.explain: Written for one organisation’s exact needs: bespoke.

questions.stem: Android, running on a student’s phone and managing its memory, apps and touchscreen.
questions.explain: It manages the device’s resources: an operating system (system software).

questions.stem: A program that scans the hard disk and reorganises fragmented files.
questions.explain: It maintains the computer: a utility (disk defragmenter).

questions.stem: The chip and program inside a washing machine that runs the wash cycle.
questions.explain: A dedicated computer built into a larger device: an embedded control system.

questions.stem:
Application software reaches users in different ways and comes from different sources. Read each Caribbean situation and choose the BEST answer.

A new laptop bought on Young Street already has a calculator and a photo viewer the first time it is switched on.
questions.explain: Supplied with the operating system or the hardware: bundled.

questions.stem: The Georgetown Community Library buys a library management system from a vendor and downloads it on its own.
questions.explain: Bought and installed on its own: published separately.

questions.stem: The Frigate Bay Realty pays for a licence to use Microsoft Office; the company that makes it keeps its source code private.
questions.explain: Owned by a company, licence sold, code private: proprietary.

questions.stem: A teacher in Paramaribo installs LibreOffice free of charge; its source code is published so anyone can study and change it.
questions.explain: Published source code anyone may change: open-source.

questions.stem: Computing students at Sandbox Tree College build a bus-timetable app as their final-year project and share it with classmates.
questions.explain: Built by university students for study: a university project.

questions.stem: A student copies a flight simulator onto a computer that has no operating system installed. What happens?
options: It runs faster, with nothing else to slow it down
It cannot run, because application software needs system software
questions.explain: Application software cannot run without system software.

questions.stem:
Organisations around the region are choosing software. Sort each description by whether it fits proprietary or open-source software, as described in the extension table.

Proprietary or open-source?

The Montego Bay Realty pays a yearly licence fee for Microsoft Office
questions.explain: Bought from the company that owns it: proprietary.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A school lab in San Ignacio installs LibreOffice on every computer at no licence cost
questions.explain: In most cases free of charge: open-source.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A Coralstone College student downloads the source code of a program and changes it for her project
questions.explain: Source code provided and editable: open-source.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

The maker of the AccountsPro package keeps its code secret, so users cannot edit it
questions.explain: Source code not provided, uneditable: proprietary.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A firm relies on regular bug fixes and a support line from the developer of its software
questions.explain: Regular fixes and developer support are listed as a proprietary strength.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A small project is left without fixes after its only volunteer programmer moves on
questions.explain: Contributions may be unsupported if the programmer has left: an open-source risk.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A designer in Frigate Bay buys an Apple Mac running macOS
questions.explain: macOS is proprietary.

questions.stem:
Proprietary or open-source?

A server at the Island Web Hosting runs Red Hat Enterprise Linux
questions.explain: Red Hat is listed as open-source (businesses pay for support).

questions.stem:
Programmers around the region are translating their code. Sort each situation by the translator being described.

Which language translator is at work here?

A developer in Trinidad turns her whole C payroll program into an executable file to sell to clients
questions.explain: Whole program translated at once into an executable: a compiler.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

A Form 6 student’s Python program stops at line 14 and highlights a misspelt variable
questions.explain: Stopping at the first error, line by line: an interpreter.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

An engineer converts LOAD, ADD and STORE mnemonics for the chip in a water pump
questions.explain: Mnemonics into machine code: an assembler.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

The finished program runs quickly on clinic computers that have no translator installed
questions.explain: A compiled executable does not need the compiler at run time.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

Each time the script runs, every statement is translated again, so it runs more slowly
questions.explain: Retranslating on every run is the interpreter’s drawback.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

After translation, a list of three syntax errors appears and no executable is produced until they are fixed
questions.explain: Errors reported at the end of whole-program translation: a compiler.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

One low-level instruction becomes exactly one machine-code instruction for a hardware driver
questions.explain: One-to-one translation of assembly language: an assembler.

questions.stem:
Which language translator is at work here?

A teacher at Mahoe Grove High School demonstrates code line by line, running each statement as it is translated
questions.explain: Translate and execute one statement at a time: an interpreter.

questions.stem: A software developer in Trinidad has finished a payroll program and wants to give clients a file that runs quickly without the source code or any translator being installed on their computers. Which translator should she use?
options: A compiler, because it translates the whole program into a stand-alone executable
A utility, because it optimises the program for speed
An assembler, because it converts high-level code into machine code
An interpreter, because it translates one line at a time

questions.stem:
All of these are system software. Sort each into its group.

Which kind of system software is this?

Allocates RAM to each running program
questions.explain: Memory management is an OS function.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Converts a whole C program into an executable file
questions.explain: That is a compiler.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Copies the hard disk to the cloud every night
questions.explain: A backup utility.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Schedules turns on the CPU for several programs
questions.explain: Process management: OS.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Turns LOAD and ADD mnemonics into machine code
questions.explain: An assembler.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Reorganises scattered file fragments on an HDD
questions.explain: A disk defragmenter.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Runs a Python program one statement at a time
questions.explain: An interpreter.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Checks user names and passwords at log-in
questions.explain: Security is an OS function.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Shrinks a folder into a ZIP file
questions.explain: A compression utility.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Splits a new drive into separate sections for programs and data
questions.explain: A disk partitioning utility.

questions.stem:
Which kind of system software is this?

Manages the laptop’s Wi-Fi connection so programs can reach the Internet
questions.explain: Managing network connections is an OS function.

questions.stem:
Embedded systems are working all over the islands. Decide whether each one only watches and warns, or acts on the process by itself.

Does the computer act on the process?

A weather station in Barbados logs wind speed and air pressure and displays them for forecasters as a storm approaches
questions.explain: It records and displays readings; people decide what to do: monitoring.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

The air conditioner at the Coral Reef Hotel switches its compressor on and off to keep a room at 22 °C
questions.explain: It drives an actuator using feedback: control.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

A patient monitor at a Kingstown hospital shows heart rate and sounds an alarm for the nurse
questions.explain: It alerts a person, who acts: monitoring.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

Automatic irrigation on a farm in St. Kitts opens a valve when soil moisture falls too low
questions.explain: The valve is an actuator, so the system changes the process: control.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

A smart electricity meter records a home’s usage every half hour for the bill
questions.explain: It records usage only: monitoring.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

A pump keeps a hillside water tank in Portsmouth at the right level, switching on when the float sensor reads low
questions.explain: Sensor, comparison, pump (actuator) and feedback: control.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

A vaccine fridge sends a text to the pharmacist if it rises above 8 °C
questions.explain: A text to a person is an alert, not an actuator: monitoring.

questions.stem:
Does the computer act on the process?

Traffic lights on the Bridge Street change when sensors detect a queue of waiting cars
questions.explain: The lights act on the traffic automatically: control.

questions.stem: A pharmacy in Castries keeps vaccines in a refrigerator fitted with a temperature sensor. The system records the temperature every five minutes and sends a text message to the pharmacist if it rises above 8 °C. The pharmacist then moves the vaccines. Which BEST describes this system?
options: Application software, because the pharmacist uses it
A control system, because it uses a sensor
A control system, because it sends a text message as output
A monitoring system, because it records readings and alerts a person, who takes the action

questions.stem:
Embedded systems are everywhere in Antigua's shops, hotels and homes. Read each situation and choose the BEST answer.

A microwave in an English Harbour kitchen has a chip that reads the keypad and runs the timer. Is it an embedded system?
options: No: it has no keyboard or monitor
Yes: a programmable computer inside a device that is not a general-purpose computer
No: embedded systems must be connected to the Internet
questions.explain: A dedicated, programmable computer inside an appliance: an embedded system.

questions.stem: A student’s laptop runs a word processor, games and a web browser. What is it?
questions.explain: It can run many kinds of program: general-purpose.

questions.stem: A card terminal in a Market Street shop has not had a firmware update since it was installed six years ago. Why is this a risk?
options: Embedded systems are hard to update, so known vulnerabilities linger
Old terminals print receipts more slowly
The terminal will refuse cards after five years
questions.explain: Without updates, known weaknesses stay open while the terminal is connected.

questions.stem: In the Target breach, how was data from over 40 million cards stolen?
options: Through malicious software on connected point-of-sale systems
By stealing cards from customers’ wallets
By guessing PINs at cash machines
questions.explain: Attackers infected the connected POS tills, which captured card data at payment.

questions.stem: The Coral Reef Hotel has its door locks, tills and guest Wi-Fi all on one network. What is the BEST first step?
options: Separate the tills and locks from guest Wi-Fi and change default passwords
Connect more devices so they can share updates
Switch off the antivirus on the office PCs
questions.explain: Separating networks and changing defaults limits who can reach the embedded devices.

questions.stem: A smart TV in an English Harbour hotel lobby no longer receives updates from its maker. What should the hotel do?
options: Nothing: TVs do not contain computers
Keep it off the main network or replace it, because its flaws will not be fixed
Connect it to the payment network so it is monitored
questions.explain: An unpatched connected device is a lingering vulnerability.

questions.stem: The manager of the Sunset Supermarket in Holetown reads that over 40 million credit cards were stolen in the Target breach through point-of-sale systems. She asks why embedded tills like hers can stay vulnerable for years. Which answer is BEST?
options: They are general-purpose computers, so they run any software an attacker sends
Being embedded means they cannot be reached over a network
They have no processor, so they cannot run security checks
They are hard to update, so known vulnerabilities linger while they stay connected

questions.stem:
You are advising Harbour View Accounting, a new four-person firm in Montego Bay. It prepares clients’ accounts and payroll and must keep records safe through the hurricane season. Make the best choices.

The owner asks what software the firm needs to prepare accounts and payroll for many small businesses. What do you recommend?
options: Hire a programmer to write bespoke accounting software from scratch.
A special-purpose accounting and payroll package already used by many firms, plus a general-purpose office suite.

questions.stem: Next, hardware. Staff open large spreadsheets and the accounting package at the same time, and the old office laptops freeze. What do you prioritise?
options: Keep the old laptops but buy larger monitors.
Laptops with a multi-core processor, at least 16 GB of RAM and an SSD.

questions.stem: Finally, the owner remembers Hurricane Beryl. How should client records be protected?
options: Use a backup utility to copy records nightly to cloud storage, keep an encrypted external drive off-site, and keep antivirus up to date.
Save everything on one desktop hard disk in the office; it has never failed.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
The Seaside Pharmacy in Portsmouth collects data every day. For each situation, choose the BEST answer.

The till records "Panadol 24-pack, 1 unit, 10:14". On its own, this record is...
questions.explain: A single raw, unprocessed fact with no context or meaning is data.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The owner reads "Sales of sunscreen rose 35% in the week the number of cruise ships at the St. John’s cruise port doubled". This is...
questions.explain: The sales data has been processed, compared and given meaning for the owner: information.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The manager compares this month's overtime at each branch with the budget and cuts extra shifts at the branch that is over budget. Information is being used to...
questions.explain: Comparing actual with planned figures and taking corrective action is control.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The owners study a three-year sales forecast and set a goal of opening a branch in Roseau. Information is being used to...
questions.explain: Setting goals and deciding where resources will go is planning.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The sales system tells the stockroom which medicines the counter is running short of before the evening shift starts. Information is being used to...
questions.explain: Making departments work together (sales telling the stockroom what to restock) is coordination.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The pharmacy keeps every receipt for seven years so that the tax inspector can check its turnover. Information is being used to...
questions.explain: Keeping evidence of transactions for auditors and tax authorities is recording and compliance.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A 900-page list of every sale for five years is sent to the owner the night before she must decide on the new branch. Why does it have little value to her?
options: It was produced by a computer
It is not at the right level of detail, or in time, for that person
questions.explain: Information is a resource with value only when it reaches the right person, at the right time, at the right level of detail. A transaction list is far too detailed for an owner.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The department head of the Bayside Hotel in Negril compares occupancy figures for the last three months and decides how many extra housekeeping staff to hire for the coming winter tourist season. At which decision-making level is this decision MOST likely made?

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
The Grenadine Ferries company runs boats between St. Vincent, Bequia and Union Island. Sort each piece of information to the level that would MOST use it.

Which decision-making level needs this information?

A ten-year forecast of regional tourist arrivals from a tourism board report.
questions.explain: External, future-oriented and highly summarised: strategic.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

Today's passenger list for the 09:00 sailing to Bequia.
questions.explain: Detailed, current and needed now for one sailing: operational.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

A monthly report comparing fuel spending on each route with the budget.
questions.explain: Periodic, summarised and compared with budget: tactical.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

A competitor's plans to launch a fast catamaran service in the region.
questions.explain: External information about the environment that may change long-term direction: strategic.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

The number of life jackets checked on board this morning.
questions.explain: Detailed, internal and for a daily task: operational.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

A quarterly exception report listing routes with fewer than 50% of seats sold.
questions.explain: An exception report for a manager to adjust schedules and resources: tactical.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

A crew roster for this weekend's sailings.
questions.explain: Short-term scheduling of staff: operational.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which decision-making level needs this information?

A summary of five years of profits by route, shown as a trend chart.
questions.explain: Highly summarised, long time span, used to decide which routes to grow or drop: strategic.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
You are the information systems adviser to the Sunrise Wholesale company in Port of Spain. The managing director wants better decisions before, during and after hurricane season. Choose the best advice.

The managing director asks for "one big report" with every transaction from the last five years so she can decide whether to build a second warehouse in Chaguanas. What do you advise?
options: Print every transaction so she has all the detail.
Give her a summarised trend report of five years of sales, combined with external storm-risk and population forecasts.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The purchasing manager now wants to decide how many generators to pre-order for the season. What should the system give him?
options: A monthly summary of last year's generator sales, an exception report on items that sold out, and a what-if tool to test order sizes.
Nothing: let the system order a fixed number automatically every year.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: Warehouse clerks must decide, many times a day, when to reorder batteries and tarpaulins. How should these decisions be handled?
options: Set reorder levels in the stock system so it raises orders automatically, using accurate, real-time stock counts.
Ask the managing director to approve each reorder personally.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A network technician at the Kralendijk Clinic types "ping 192.168.1.1" at a prompt to test a printer's connection. A receptionist at the same clinic uses a screen that shows "1. Book appointment 2. Cancel appointment 3. Print list" and presses 1. Which statement BEST distinguishes the two interfaces?
options: The technician must recall and type commands in exact syntax, whereas the receptionist selects from options the computer displays.
Both use a natural language interface because they use English words.
The technician's interface is text based, whereas the receptionist's is not.
The technician uses a GUI, whereas the receptionist uses a command line.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Each card describes a system in Belize. Sort it to the type of HCI it MAINLY uses.

Which type of HCI is this?

A technician types "ipconfig /all" at a prompt to check a computer's network settings.
questions.explain: Typed commands in fixed syntax: command line.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

An ATM shows "1. Withdraw 2. Balance 3. Transfer" and the customer presses a button beside one.
questions.explain: The customer selects from a list of displayed options: menu.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A Coralstone College applicant enters name, date of birth and programme in labelled boxes, then clicks Submit.
questions.explain: Labelled fields for data entry: forms.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A student double-clicks a folder icon in a window and opens a document with the mouse pointer.
questions.explain: Windows, icons and a pointer: GUI.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A phone line says "Press 1 for billing, press 2 for faults".
questions.explain: A telephone menu of numbered options.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A hotel check-in screen with fields for passport number, arrival date and room type chosen from a drop-down list.
questions.explain: Several fields to complete, with validation and a drop-down list: forms.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A server administrator runs a saved script of commands to back up files every night.
questions.explain: Scripts of typed commands are a feature of the command line.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Which type of HCI is this?

A desktop where several windows are open, with a taskbar of icons along the bottom.
questions.explain: Multiple windows and icons: GUI.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
The right interface depends on the user and the task. For each user, choose the interface that suits them BEST.

An expert network technician at the Island Internet company must apply the same settings to 30 routers tonight.
questions.explain: An expert who knows the commands gains speed and can script the repeated task: command line.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: Cruise passengers who speak many different languages use an information kiosk at the Harbour Mall near the cruise pier.
options: GUI with icons and short text labels
questions.explain: Icons are language independent and easy for novices; short labels back up the less obvious ones.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: First-time applicants and experienced admissions clerks both enter applicant details at Coralstone College.
questions.explain: Forms copy familiar paper forms and suit all users, experts and novices, for data entry.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A mechanic at the Fort Street Garage is lying under a car with oily hands and needs to look up a part number.
questions.explain: Speech is hands-free and eyes-free, so it suits a user whose hands are busy.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: Waiters at a busy, noisy restaurant in San Fernando keep finding that their spoken orders are misheard by the ordering system.
questions.explain: Background noise is a key weakness of speech. A menu lets staff recognise and tap dishes quickly with no recall needed.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A designer at the Island Ads agency wants to resize and position a logo on a poster and see the result as she drags it.
questions.explain: Rapid, reversible actions on a visible object with immediate feedback: direct manipulation.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: Customers of the Island Power company want to report an outage in their own words without learning any menus or commands.
questions.explain: Natural language lets users communicate in everyday sentences, with nothing new to learn.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A student with a visual impairment at the Speightstown Library needs web pages read aloud to her.
questions.explain: Speech interfaces such as web readers and page scanners support users who cannot see the screen.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem:
Each situation is set in the Caribbean. Choose the type of HCI it MAINLY demonstrates.

A visitor drags a pin on a map app from Bridge Street to Gros Islet Beach and the route redraws instantly.
questions.explain: Acting on a visible object with immediate feedback is direct manipulation.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A driver in Kingston, Jamaica says "Call Mum" and the car dials the number.
questions.explain: Spoken input processed by speech recognition: speech.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A customer types "I want to change my delivery address to Portsmouth" into a courier's chat window.
questions.explain: Typed everyday sentences that the system interprets: natural language. It is typed, so not speech.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A Trinidad bank's online loan application asks for income, employer and loan amount in separate boxes.
questions.explain: Labelled fields for structured data entry: forms.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A student pinches a photo on a tablet to enlarge it.
questions.explain: Pinch to zoom acts directly on the object: direct manipulation.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A Guyanese technician types "shutdown /r /t 0" to restart a server.
questions.explain: An exact command with switches typed at a prompt: command line.

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: A tourist types "what time does the last ferry to Carriacou leave tonight" into a chat window on the Grand Anse Ferries website and receives a correct answer. Which type of HCI is MAINLY demonstrated?
options: Natural language, because the system interprets an everyday sentence
Speech, because the tourist is asking a question
Command line, because the tourist typed text
Forms, because the text was entered on a website

questions.topic: Data for decisions and types of HCI
questions.stem: The owners of Island Fresh supermarket chain are deciding whether to open a store in Curaçao within the next five years. Their adviser is preparing a briefing pack for them. Which of the following BEST describes the information the pack should contain?
options: Periodic summaries of internal performance compared with budget
Highly summarised, largely external and future-oriented, often uncertain
Lists of individual transactions produced in real time
Detailed, internal, current and highly precise

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Each situation below comes from a workplace or public service in the Caribbean. Decide which evaluation principle the evidence is mainly about, or which HCI type fits the user best.

At Holetown Grill, an experienced server orders two johnnycakes and a drink in four taps during the cruise-ship rush. Which principle does this show?
questions.explain: Few steps for someone who already knows the system is ease of use.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A tourist uses a bill-payment kiosk in a Castries supermarket for the first time and finishes without help because every screen shows one prompt and four labelled buttons. Which principle does this show?
questions.explain: A first-time user succeeding without training is ease of learning (recognition rather than recall).

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: Clerks at a Portsmouth insurance office often delete records by accident because there is no confirmation box and no Undo. Which principle is weak?
questions.explain: Error prevention and recovery are guidelines for ease of use.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A once-a-year online tax form shows "dd/mm/yyyy" inside the date box and a tooltip beside every field. Which principle do these features mainly improve?
questions.explain: Built-in help and examples help occasional users learn the form.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A telecoms company network technician configures routers all day and wants the fastest possible interface. Which HCI type suits her best?
questions.explain: A command line is very easy to use (fast and powerful) for a trained expert, even though it is hard to learn.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A voice assistant at a San Pedro hotel desk keeps mishearing guests with strong accents in a noisy lobby. Which principle is mainly reduced?
questions.explain: Misunderstood speech and background noise reduce ease of use of speech interfaces.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A network administrator at the San Pedro Data Centre can restart services across twenty servers with one typed command, but new interns need weeks of practice before they can use the command line. Which evaluation statement is MOST accurate?
options: The interface scores high on ease of use for experts but low on ease of learning.
The interface scores high on alignment because commands are typed in a line.
The interface scores poorly on ease of navigation because it has no colour.
The interface scores high on ease of learning but low on ease of use.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
An evaluation team has listed problems found in interfaces around Trinidad and Tobago. Sort each problem by the evaluation principle it MAINLY breaks.

Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Cashiers must re-type the same customer number on three separate screens for every sale.
questions.explain: Extra repeated steps for a trained user are an ease-of-use problem.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

A new parking app uses unlabelled icons that first-time visitors cannot work out.
questions.explain: First-time users cannot recognise what to do: a learnability problem.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

A ferry booking site has no Back button on the payment page, so users restart from the home page.
questions.explain: Users cannot get back: a navigation problem.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Form labels and boxes start at different points across the screen, so the eye zigzags.
questions.explain: Elements are not lined up on shared edges: an alignment problem.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Light grey text on a white background is almost unreadable in sunlight.
questions.explain: Poor contrast is a use-of-colour problem.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Error messages are shown only by turning a field red, with no text.
questions.explain: Relying on colour alone excludes colour-blind users.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

The help page is six sub-menus deep and has no search box.
questions.explain: Deep hierarchy and no search make it hard to find content.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

There is no on-screen help, no tooltips and no examples in the fields for a once-a-year tax form.
questions.explain: Occasional users need built-in help to learn the form.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Deleting a record has no confirmation and no Undo, so experienced clerks often lose data.
questions.explain: Poor error prevention and recovery reduce ease of use.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which principle does this problem mainly break?

Buttons on the same screen are placed randomly, some top-left and some bottom-right.
questions.explain: Inconsistent placement of buttons is an alignment issue.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
An evaluation team is visiting workplaces and testing devices around the Caribbean. For each one, choose the evaluation point that matters MOST in that setting or on that device.

Servers at an English Harbour seafood restaurant enter orders on a touchscreen POS during a full lunchtime rush.
options: Ease of use: few taps and large picture buttons
A dark theme for low light
questions.explain: Under pressure, speed (few taps, large targets) matters most in a restaurant.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: Nurses at a Portsmouth clinic record medication doses on a form.
options: Error prevention: validation, confirmation and aligned fields
questions.explain: A wrong entry could harm a patient, so error prevention and clear alignment outweigh speed.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A sound engineer in a Belize City recording studio edits a track late at night.
options: Ease of use for experts: drag-to-edit, shortcuts and a dark theme
questions.explain: Trained engineers want speed and direct manipulation; dark themes suit low light.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A technician in a school laboratory works with gloves on and must follow a test procedure.
options: Small icons to fit more on screen
Large touch targets and navigation that follows the procedure
questions.explain: Gloved hands need large targets, and steps should follow the lab procedure.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A family plays on a game console from the sofa, choosing options with a D-pad controller.
options: Short visual menus and text readable from a distance
questions.explain: Controller navigation through long lists is slow, so menus are short and readable from the sofa.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A cruise visitor opens the Bus KIN website on a phone in bright sunlight at the pier.
options: High contrast and a layout that adapts to a small screen
questions.explain: Outdoor glare tests contrast, and a web page must adapt to a phone screen for an untrained visitor.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A Grade 1 child uses a tablet reading game at a Castries primary school.
options: Touch GUI with large targets that is easy to learn
questions.explain: Tablets are very learnable through direct manipulation, as long as touch targets are large.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
For each setting, choose the evaluation principle that should carry the MOST weight.

A self-service ticket kiosk at the cruise pier used once by each visitor.
questions.explain: One-time public users have no training, so learnability decides success.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A pharmacy dispensing screen where a wrong dose could harm a patient.
options: Ease of use with error prevention
questions.explain: Error prevention (confirmation, validation) is part of ease of use and is critical here.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A security guard switching between 24 camera feeds during an incident.
questions.explain: Moving instantly between views is navigation.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A long online scholarship application form with 30 fields.
questions.explain: Aligned fields and grouped sections make long forms easier to complete accurately.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A traffic dashboard where operators must spot red, amber and green road status at a glance.
questions.explain: Colour carries the status here, so contrast, consistency and backup labels are essential.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
An IT professional works in one particular IT job role with the comprehensive skills for it. Anyone else using a system is an end user, even if they are "good with computers". Sort each person by the role they are playing in the situation described.

In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

Rhea, a trained network engineer, keeps the firewall and Wi-Fi running at a Grace Bay hotel in Providenciales.
questions.explain: A defined IT job role with specialist training: IT professional.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

The same web designer who builds hotel websites books a doctor's appointment on the Island Health portal.
questions.explain: Here he is using someone else's system for a personal task, so he is an end user (probably a novice on that portal).

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

Jerome, a teenager who games and builds PCs as a hobby, uses the school's learning platform to submit homework.
questions.explain: Being good with computers is not a profession. He is using the system for his own task: end user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

A database administrator at a Linden credit union sets up nightly backups of member records.
questions.explain: Protecting data is the DBA's professional role.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

A cashier at a Regent Street jewellery store processes sales on the POS.
questions.explain: She uses the system to do her job: end user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

A systems analyst with a degree in information systems writes the requirements for a new ferry booking system.
questions.explain: Special education and one particular IT role: IT professional.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

A help-desk technician resets a teacher's password at Calabash Point Secondary.
questions.explain: Supporting other users' systems is an IT professional role.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
In this situation, is the person acting as an IT professional or an end user?

A nurse who is very confident with apps enters patient notes on the clinic's records system.
questions.explain: Confidence does not make her an IT professional; she is an (expert) end user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: The San Fernando Logistics needs someone to work out what a new tracking system must do, estimate what it will cost, and act as the go-between for the managers and the programmers. Which IT professional should it hire?

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
All of these people are end users. Sort each one by whether they are acting as an expert user or a novice user of the system described, remembering that expertise is relative to each system.

Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

An accounts clerk at Bayside Shipping enters invoices with keyboard shortcuts after eight years on the same package.
questions.explain: Rich interaction knowledge and shortcuts: expert user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A first-year Sandbox Tree College student logs into the student portal for the first time.
questions.explain: New to the system and naïve about it: novice user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A grandmother in Dominica tries online banking for the first time and needs prompts on every screen.
questions.explain: Little experience and needs guidance: novice.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A Piarco airport check-in agent customises her screen layout and fixes minor glitches herself.
questions.explain: Customising and solving minor problems are signs of an expert user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A telecoms company router expert opens the Island Health patient system for the first time.
questions.explain: Expertise is relative to the system: on this system he is a novice.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A nurse with ten years on the records system knows the clinic's procedures and the software's shortcuts.
questions.explain: Task, domain and interaction knowledge together: expert.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Is this end user an expert or a novice on this system?

A cruise visitor using a bus route app once to reach Gros Islet.
questions.explain: Occasional, one-time use: novice.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: The Caribbean Credit Union is redesigning its teller software. Tellers range from new hires to staff with 15 years' experience. Which design BEST serves both groups?
options: A step-by-step wizard for every transaction that cannot be skipped.
A command-line interface only, because it is fastest.
A speech interface so tellers can talk to the system.
A menu-driven GUI with clear labels and help, plus keyboard shortcuts and customisable screens.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Places around Dominica are adapting their systems for different users. Sort each adaptation into the kind of interface it is: a non-visual interface, a sensor, or a built-in accessibility feature.

What kind of adaptive interface is this?

A telephone line at an utility office says "Press 1 or say 'billing'".
questions.explain: A spoken voice menu works without a screen: non-visual (audio).

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

A Braille display lets a blind clerk at a Roseau law firm read emails by touch.
questions.explain: Tactile output without a screen: non-visual.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

The raised dot on the 5 key of an ATM on Bridge Street.
questions.explain: A tactile marker lets users find keys without seeing: non-visual.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

Motion detectors open the doors automatically for travellers with luggage at Piarco Airport.
questions.explain: It detects a physical change (movement) as input: sensor.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

A smartwatch accelerometer detects that an older resident has fallen and alerts family.
questions.explain: An accelerometer detects movement: sensor.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

An eye-tracking camera lets a person with paralysis move a pointer by looking.
questions.explain: It senses eye movement as input: sensor.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

A student switches on high-contrast mode and larger text in the phone's settings.
questions.explain: Built-in settings for different abilities: accessibility features.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

Sticky keys let a user with one working hand press Ctrl+S one key at a time.
questions.explain: A built-in operating-system setting: accessibility feature.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
What kind of adaptive interface is this?

Automatic captions are turned on for a recorded Flamboyant Heights College lecture.
questions.explain: Captions are a built-in accessibility feature for deaf users.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
A Guyana government services portal is adding features. Sort each adaptation by the user characteristic it MAINLY addresses.

Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

Picture-based buttons with sound for a children's library catalogue.
questions.explain: Designed for young children who may not read well.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

A "large mode" with bigger text and slower screen time-outs for retirees.
questions.explain: Addresses age-related changes in eyesight and speed.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

Replacing jargon such as "authenticate credentials" with "sign in".
questions.explain: Plain language helps users with lower literacy or technical knowledge.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

A step-by-step wizard with examples for users who have never filled an online form.
questions.explain: Supports users with limited computer education.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

Alternative text on every image so screen readers can describe them.
questions.explain: Supports blind and low-vision users.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

Captions on all video guides.
questions.explain: Supports deaf and hard-of-hearing users.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

A language selector offering English, Dutch, Spanish and French.
questions.explain: Supports speakers of different languages.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
Which user characteristic is this adaptation mainly for?

Showing dates as "3 Apr 2026" instead of 03/04/2026.
questions.explain: Avoids confusion between different cultural date formats.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: The Gros Islet Hotel in Castries installs new room controls so that guests of all abilities, including blind guests, can use them. Which feature is a NON-VISUAL interface?
options: A touchscreen panel with large, high-contrast icons.
A website for booking spa treatments with alternative text on images.
A voice assistant that answers "What time is breakfast?" aloud and a light switch with a raised tactile marker.
A TV menu with a colour-blind-friendly palette.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem:
You are advising Island Health Services, which is placing self check-in kiosks in its clinics in Basseterre and Frigate Bay. Patients include older residents, visitors who speak little English, and people with disabilities.

The vendor's default kiosk has small text, English only and a long typed form. What do you recommend first?
options: Study the actual patients: their ages, languages, literacy and disabilities, then adapt the interface.
Install it as it is; patients will learn.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: Your survey finds many older patients and many Spanish and French speakers. What changes do you make to the screen?
options: Keep English only but add bright colours to make it friendlier.
Large high-contrast buttons, a language choice on the first screen, and touch-to-select menus instead of typing.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A blind patient and a wheelchair user report problems. What do you add?
options: A sign saying "Ask staff for help if you cannot use the kiosk".
Audio guidance through a headphone jack with a tactile keypad, and a lower, tiltable screen within reach of a seated user.

questions.topic: Evaluating HCI, users and adaptive interfaces
questions.stem: A Barbados tourism app shows hotel availability with green for "available" and red for "fully booked", with no other marker. Which evaluation is MOST complete?
options: It is fine, because red and green are universally understood.
It relies on colour alone, which fails users with red-green colour-vision deficiency, and colour meanings vary across cultures; adding icons and text labels such as "Full" fixes both.
It is an alignment problem because the colours are not lined up.
It should use more colours so each hotel has its own.

questions.stem: The Grand Anse Shipping office replaces the central device in its LAN. Staff notice that the network is faster and that a computer no longer receives data meant for other computers. Which change was MOST likely made?
options: A hub was replaced by a switch.
A switch was replaced by a hub.
A modem was replaced by a router.
A NIC was replaced by an access point.

questions.stem:
The Caribbean Cruise Services company in St. John’s runs several systems. Sort each one.

Which type of network is being used?

Tourists anywhere in the world view the public tour timetable.
questions.explain: Open to anyone: the Internet.

questions.stem:
Which type of network is being used?

Staff log in to read the employee handbook and apply for leave.
questions.explain: Staff only: an intranet.

questions.stem:
Which type of network is being used?

Approved bus companies log in to see tomorrow's passenger numbers.
questions.explain: Selected outside partners: an extranet.

questions.stem:
Which type of network is being used?

Managers share internal sales reports in a private web portal.
questions.explain: Internal and private: an intranet.

questions.stem:
Which type of network is being used?

A travel agent in Barbados logs in to book group tours directly.
questions.explain: An authorised outside partner: an extranet.

questions.stem:
Which type of network is being used?

The company posts a promotional video that anyone can watch.
questions.explain: Public: the Internet.

questions.stem:
Read each situation and choose the type of network that BEST fits.

Twenty computers in one office at Sandbox Tree College share a printer.
questions.explain: One building: a LAN.

questions.stem: A bank links its branches in Jamaica, Curaçao and Trinidad.
questions.explain: Several countries: a WAN.

questions.stem: A teacher at home opens the school server through an encrypted tunnel over the Internet.
questions.explain: Encrypted remote access over a public network: a VPN.

questions.stem: A taxi driver on the English Harbour road streams music through cell towers.
questions.explain: Cells and base stations: a mobile network.

questions.stem: A fibre network connects government offices across the Castries area.
questions.explain: A town or city: a MAN.

questions.stem: Approved suppliers log in to a supermarket's private ordering portal.
questions.explain: Trusted outsiders: an extranet.

questions.stem:
You are auditing networks for small and large organisations around the Caribbean. Sort each description into the configuration it shows.

Which configuration does this describe?

Hummingbird Ridge High School students log in with school accounts that one administrator creates and controls.
questions.explain: Central control of accounts by an administrator: client-server.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

Three laptops at the Guavaberry Café share one printer with no dedicated server.
questions.explain: Equal computers sharing directly with no server: peer-to-peer.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

The Dominica Credit Union backs up every member record from one central machine each night.
questions.explain: Central backups from a server: client-server.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

At a tiny boutique in George Town, each PC's user decides which folders to share.
questions.explain: Each user controls their own machine: peer-to-peer, with weaker security.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

When the main server at the Frigate Bay Clinic failed, nobody could open patient files.
questions.explain: A server failure stopping everyone is the classic client-server weakness.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

Two freelance designers in English Harbour copy files directly between their computers to avoid buying a server.
questions.explain: Low cost and no server: peer-to-peer.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

Island Breeze Hotels group buys a network operating system and hires a skilled administrator.
questions.explain: Higher cost for central management: client-server.

questions.stem:
Which configuration does this describe?

Files at the Cayman Brac Dive Shop are scattered across four PCs, so backups are hard to organise.
questions.explain: Scattered files and difficult backups: peer-to-peer.

questions.stem: The Dominica Credit Union has 45 staff, stores confidential member records and needs daily backups and controlled user permissions. Which configuration is MOST suitable?
options: Peer-to-peer, because every user can manage their own files.
Client-server, because it never stops working if the server fails.
Client-server, because a server allows central control of security, permissions and backups.
Peer-to-peer, because it is cheaper to install.

questions.stem:
You are a network consultant taking calls from clients across the Caribbean. For each situation, choose the BEST answer.

A cruise terminal office at the Bridgetown Port will keep adding check-in desks and wants one broken cable to affect only one desk.
questions.explain: Star: each desk has its own cable to the switch, so one fault affects one desk and expansion is easy.

questions.stem: A provider links towers across the island and wants traffic to take another route if hurricane damage cuts one link.
questions.explain: Mesh gives alternative routes, so one cut link does not isolate a district.

questions.stem: A one-day event in Frigate Bay needs four laptops linked with the least cable and lowest cost, accepting that a backbone break stops everything.
questions.explain: Bus uses the least cable and is cheapest for a few devices.

questions.stem: A network must give orderly data flow with no collisions under heavy load, accepting that one failed node could stop the loop.
questions.explain: Ring: data passes in order around the loop with no collisions.

questions.stem: The Caribbean Union Bank wants a full mesh linking its 5 branches. How many links are needed?
questions.explain: n(n-1)/2 = 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10. Twenty forgets to divide by 2.

questions.stem: Every PC in the Georgetown Law Office star LAN lost its connection at the same moment. What MOST likely failed?
questions.explain: The central switch is the single point of failure in a star.

questions.stem:
Saba Eco Lodge is choosing transmission media. Sort each statement into the medium type it describes.

Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Pulses of light travel through glass strands.
questions.explain: Fibre-optic cable is a wired, guided medium.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Guests move freely around the lodge with their phones online.
questions.explain: Mobility is the key advantage of wireless.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Copper pairs are twisted to reduce interference.
questions.explain: Twisted pair is a wired medium.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Signals are relayed through a satellite for a remote site.
questions.explain: Satellite links are wireless.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Someone must physically connect to the cable to intercept data.
questions.explain: Physical access is needed, which makes wired media more secure.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Thick stone walls weaken the signal.
questions.explain: Wireless signals are affected by walls and distance.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

A central copper core is wrapped in a metal shield.
questions.explain: That is coaxial cable.

questions.stem:
Does this describe wired or wireless transmission?

Point-to-point dishes need a clear line of sight.
questions.explain: Microwave links are wireless.

questions.stem:
You are advising the Boardwalk Bean Café in Bridgetown, which wants to offer a free customer hotspot and also runs its till and stock system on the same premises. Make the best decisions.

The owner plans to connect the tills, the office PC and customers' phones all to one open Wi-Fi network. What do you advise first?
options: Separate the networks: a password-protected staff network for the tills and office, and a separate guest hotspot.
Keep one open network; it is simpler for everybody.

questions.stem: The router connects the café to the Internet. Which protection do you switch on at the router?
options: The router's firewall, with rules that block unrequested incoming connections, and a new strong admin password.
Nothing. A firewall slows things down.

questions.stem: The manager wants to check stock figures from home at night. How should she connect?
options: Through a VPN that encrypts her connection to the café network.
Open the stock system directly to the Internet with no login so it is quick.

questions.stem:
Follow a contract sent by the Gros Islet Realty to a client in Curaçao, then answer each question about the communication.

Ana at the Gros Islet Realty emails a sales contract from her laptop. In this communication her laptop is the...
questions.explain: The device that creates and sends the message is the sender.

questions.stem: The client's computer in Curaçao accepts the email and opens the contract. It is the...
questions.explain: The device that accepts and interprets the message is the receiver.

questions.stem: A home modem in Gros Islet varies the frequency of a carrier wave so digital data can travel along the telephone line. This is...
questions.explain: Changing a carrier wave to carry the data is modulation.

questions.stem: At the far end, the modem recovers the digital data from the analogue wave. This is...
questions.explain: Recovering the data at the receiver is demodulation.

questions.stem: A Sandbox Tree College student downloads a 40 MB lecture video on a 10 Mbps link. What is the minimum time?
questions.explain: 40 MB × 8 = 320 megabits; 320 ÷ 10 = 32 seconds. Four seconds forgets to convert bytes to bits.

questions.stem: The English Harbour Tours office upgrades its link from 10 Mbps to 100 Mbps so more staff can stream at once. What has increased?
questions.explain: Bandwidth is the channel's capacity in bits per second.

questions.stem: Ana's laptop and the client's computer both follow the same agreed rules so the email can be understood. These rules are a...
questions.explain: Agreed rules for communication are protocols.

questions.stem:
Choose the communication mode for each situation.

A Guyanese radio station broadcasts the news to listeners.
questions.explain: Listeners cannot reply on the same channel: simplex.

questions.stem: Port crew use two-way radios: one speaks while the other waits.
questions.explain: Both directions but one at a time: half duplex.

questions.stem: A student in Saba talks to her teacher on a phone call; both can speak at once.
questions.explain: Simultaneous two-way: full duplex.

questions.stem: A keyboard sends key presses to the computer.
questions.explain: One direction only: simplex.

questions.stem: A videoconference between campuses in Barbados and Jamaica.
questions.explain: Participants see and hear each other at the same time: full duplex.

questions.stem:
The human resources office of a regional company based in The Valley, Anguilla, is reviewing how staff work and meet. Sort each situation.

Which network application is this?

A claims officer at the Anguilla Insurance Agency works from home three days a week, logging in over a VPN.
questions.explain: Working away from the office through the network: telecommuting.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

Managers in St. Kitts, Antigua and Guyana dial in to an audio-only conference call.
questions.explain: A meeting by audio link: teleconferencing.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

A guest lecturer in Curaçao teaches a Sandbox Tree College class live; students see and hear her.
questions.explain: Live video and audio between locations: videoconferencing.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

After Hurricane Irma closed its office, staff at a firm in The Valley kept working from home by email and VPN.
questions.explain: Continuing normal work from home: telecommuting.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

Hotel managers on two islands switch on webcams and share screens in their weekly meeting.
questions.explain: Webcams and live pictures: videoconferencing.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

A speakerphone in the boardroom links three branch heads by voice only.
questions.explain: Voice only: teleconferencing.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

Needs webcams, microphones, software and high bandwidth in full duplex.
questions.explain: Those are the requirements for videoconferencing.

questions.stem:
Which network application is this?

Replaces the daily drive through Kingston traffic with a network connection.
questions.explain: Replacing the commute: telecommuting.

questions.stem: Marisol works for the Cayman Islands Insurance Agency. Three days a week she works at home, logging in to the office system over a VPN and sending reports by email. This arrangement is BEST described as

At Breadfruit Valley Secondary, video lessons freeze whenever a whole class streams at once, although the network cabling and devices are working correctly. Which network characteristic is MOST likely insufficient?

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Mr. Hodge, a network technician at Breadfruit Valley Secondary, is explaining to a Form 6 class why networks need standards and layered models. Answer each of his questions.

A student's Dell laptop connects without any problem to the Huawei Wi-Fi router in the school library. Which idea makes this possible?
questions.explain: Both makers follow the same published standards (such as Wi-Fi, IEEE 802.11), so their equipment works together: interoperability.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The computer lab moves from Ethernet cables to Wi-Fi, yet every web browser still uses HTTP exactly as before. Which benefit of a layered model does this show?
options: Wi-Fi removes the need for protocols
Every layer must be rewritten when one changes
Each layer can change without rewriting the others
questions.explain: Only the lowest layer changed; HTTP at the top was untouched. Layers are independent.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: When the Internet drops in the staff room, Mr. Hodge checks the cable first, then the IP settings, then the browser. Which benefit of layering is he using?
options: It divides the problem so each layer can be checked on its own
questions.explain: Layering divides communication into separate jobs, so a technician can troubleshoot one layer at a time.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: HTTP sets out exactly how a browser at the Bay Times newsroom requests a page and how the server must reply. HTTP is best described as a...
questions.explain: A protocol is a set of rules for formatting, sending, receiving and acknowledging data. HTTP is a protocol.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Ethernet was formally agreed and published by the IEEE, so any manufacturer can build network cards that work with everyone else’s. This makes Ethernet a...
questions.explain: A standard is a protocol or specification that has been formally agreed and published.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: As an email travels down the layers on a teacher’s laptop in Port of Spain, each layer adds its own header to the data. What is this process called?
questions.explain: Adding a header at each layer on the way down is encapsulation; removing them on the way up is de-encapsulation.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Follow one day of network activity across St. Kitts. For each event, choose the OSI layer that is doing the job.

A reporter at the Bay Times on Fort Street in Basseterre presses Send, and her email program hands the story to SMTP.
questions.explain: SMTP is an Application-layer protocol: it provides the email service to the user’s program.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Before a Coralstone College student’s photo is sent, it is compressed to JPEG and encrypted with TLS.
questions.explain: Compression and encryption change the format of the data: Presentation layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: A 600 MB video upload from Frigate Bay drops halfway when the Wi-Fi fails, then resumes from the last checkpoint instead of starting again.
questions.explain: Checkpoints (synchronisation) and managing the conversation are Session-layer jobs.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: A banking app at the Basseterre Credit Union splits data into numbered segments and sends them to port 443 using TCP.
questions.explain: Segments, sequence numbers, port numbers and TCP all belong to the Transport layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: A router at Caribbean Connect ISP reads the destination IP address of each packet and forwards it towards a server in Miami.
questions.explain: IP addressing and routing of packets happen at the Network layer, where routers work.
