questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: A switch in the Palmetto Point Secondary computer lab reads the MAC address on a frame and sends it out of one port only.
questions.explain: Frames and MAC addresses belong to the Data Link layer, where switches work.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Pulses of light carry 1s and 0s along the undersea fibre-optic cable that links the island to the rest of the world.
questions.explain: Transmitting raw bits as signals on a medium is the Physical layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
The IT technician at Kralendijk Hardware is labelling a poster for staff training. Sort each protocol or job into its TCP/IP layer.

Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

HTTPS
questions.explain: HTTPS delivers secure web pages to the browser: Application layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

DHCP gives a new laptop its IP address
questions.explain: DHCP is an Application-layer service, even though it hands out IP settings.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

IMAP
questions.explain: IMAP retrieves and synchronises email: Application layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

UDP
questions.explain: UDP is the connectionless Transport protocol.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

Port numbers direct data to the right program
questions.explain: Port numbers are a Transport-layer feature (port 443 for HTTPS).

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

TCP three-way handshake
questions.explain: TCP sets up a reliable connection: Transport layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

IPv6
questions.explain: IP, version 4 or 6, is the Internet-layer protocol.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

Routers choose a path for each packet
questions.explain: Routing by IP address is the Internet layer’s job.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)
questions.explain: Ethernet frames and cabling belong to Network Access.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which TCP/IP layer does this belong to?

Wi-Fi radio signals (IEEE 802.11)
questions.explain: Wi-Fi moves frames over radio on the local network: Network Access.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The Arima Sports Network streams live football matches online. The engineers accept that a few frames of video may be lost, but they cannot accept delays caused by resending data. Which protocol, at which layer, should carry the video stream?

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Kezia is making a revision poster that compares the two networking models for her Form 6 class at Breadfruit Valley Secondary. Sort each statement onto the right part of her poster.

Which model does this statement describe?

Has seven layers
questions.explain: OSI has seven layers; TCP/IP has four.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Has separate Presentation and Session layers
questions.explain: Only OSI separates them; TCP/IP puts their jobs inside one Application layer.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Has separate Data Link and Physical layers
questions.explain: OSI separates them; TCP/IP combines them as Network Access.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Designed by ISO as a general reference model
questions.explain: The OSI model was designed by ISO as a reference model before protocols were fixed.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Has four layers
questions.explain: TCP/IP: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Combines Data Link and Physical into a Network Access layer
questions.explain: Network Access is the TCP/IP layer that covers OSI Layers 1 and 2.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Grew from working ARPANET protocols and is the model the Internet runs on
questions.explain: TCP/IP is the practical model of the Internet.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Is layered, with each layer serving the layer above
questions.explain: Both models are layered.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Has a Transport layer that uses TCP or UDP
questions.explain: Both models have a Transport layer with TCP and UDP.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which model does this statement describe?

Uses encapsulation as data moves down the layers
questions.explain: Encapsulation happens in both models.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Kezia is revising for Paper 01 in the Mahoe Grove High School library. Answer each question she is stuck on.

Which OSI layer is responsible for compression and encryption?
questions.explain: Presentation handles format: translation, encryption and compression.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: A switch forwards frames using...
questions.explain: Switches are Layer 2 devices and read MAC addresses.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Which TCP/IP layer corresponds to OSI Layers 5, 6 and 7?
questions.explain: The single TCP/IP Application layer covers Application, Presentation and Session.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The PDU at the OSI Network layer is called a...
questions.explain: Network = packet. Transport = segment. Data Link = frame.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Which protocol keeps email synchronised on the server across several devices?
questions.explain: IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it; POP3 downloads to one device; SMTP sends.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Which protocol automatically assigns an IP address to a phone joining a network?
questions.explain: DHCP assigns IP settings automatically. DNS converts names to IP addresses.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The Oranjestad Print Shop has eight PCs connected to a hub. Staff complain that the network slows down whenever several people print large files, and the owner worries that any PC can capture the accounts clerk's data. Which change BEST solves both problems?
options: Replace the hub with a switch
Change the SSID of the Wi-Fi network
Replace the hub with a second hub

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Business owners across the island bring their Wi-Fi questions to the Kingston Tech Clinic. Choose the best answer for each one.

The Montego Bay Bakery has turned on MAC filtering and says it no longer needs Wi-Fi encryption. Why is this unsafe?
options: MAC filtering changes the SSID every day
MAC addresses are sent unencrypted and can be copied (spoofed), and filtering does not scramble traffic
MAC filtering makes the network too slow
questions.explain: MAC filtering is only an extra layer: an attacker can spoof an allowed address, and without WPA2/WPA3 the traffic is readable.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The router at the Negril Beach Bar offers "WPA2-TKIP" or "WPA2-AES". Which should the owner choose?
questions.explain: AES is the strong cipher; TKIP is outdated and WEP is broken.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: An attacker records the WPA2 handshake outside the Ocho Rios Dive Shop and tries millions of password guesses at home. Which WPA3 feature stops this?
questions.explain: SAE replaces the WPA2 handshake, so every guess must be a live attempt against the network.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The Port Antonio Guesthouse has older tablets that cannot use WPA3 and new phones that can. Which router setting lets both connect securely?
options: An open network with no key
questions.explain: Transitional mode lets WPA3 devices use WPA3 while older devices still use WPA2 with AES.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: The Mandeville Pharmacy uses WPA3. The owner asks what "AES" on the settings page means.
options: The symmetric encryption algorithm used inside WPA3 (and WPA2)
Another name for the network key
A list of allowed MAC addresses
questions.explain: WPA2 and WPA3 are security protocols; AES is the symmetric encryption algorithm they use.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: An attacker discovers the Wi-Fi key of Frederick Street Boutique, which uses WPA3. Can she decrypt traffic she captured there last month?
options: Only if MAC filtering was off
No, because WPA3 provides forward secrecy
questions.explain: Forward secrecy means a key discovered later cannot unlock traffic captured earlier.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
The Saba Island Library is securing its network. Sort each measure: does it mainly protect the wired network or the wireless network?

Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Lock the switch and router in a cabinet
questions.explain: Physical security of cabled equipment is a wired measure.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Disable unused wall sockets at the switch
questions.explain: Disabling unused ports stops visitors plugging into the wired LAN.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Port security: allow only known MAC addresses on each switch port
questions.explain: Switch port security controls cabled connections.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Run cables inside trunking and ceilings
questions.explain: Protecting cables from tapping or damage is wired security.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Turn on WPA3
questions.explain: WPA3 encrypts and authenticates Wi-Fi connections.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Choose AES rather than TKIP on the access point
questions.explain: AES is the encryption cipher used by WPA2/WPA3 Wi-Fi.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Use a long network key and change it when staff leave
questions.explain: The network key controls who joins the Wi-Fi.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
Which part of the network does this measure mainly protect?

Rename the default SSID and avoid personal details
questions.explain: The SSID is the wireless network name.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Statia Fuel Depot uses WPA2-Personal with an eight-character network key. An IT consultant recommends moving to WPA3-Personal. Which statement BEST explains the security benefit?
options: WPA3 replaces AES with a stronger cipher called TKIP.
WPA3 hides the SSID so attackers cannot find the network.
WPA3 automatically blocks all devices whose MAC address is not on a list.
WPA3 uses SAE, so an attacker cannot capture the handshake and guess the key offline.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem:
You are the IT consultant for the Bay View Guesthouse near Gros Islet. The owner, Mr. Arrindell, needs a network for the reception PC, the office PC, a card machine and Wi-Fi for staff and guests.

Mr. Arrindell has an old 8-port hub and asks if he can use it to connect the reception and office PCs. What do you advise?
options: Use a switch instead: it sends frames only to the destination port, which is faster and keeps traffic private.
Use the hub; it does the same job and saves money.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Next, he wants guests and staff to share one Wi-Fi network called "Arrindell-Family-Home" with no password, "so guests don't complain". What do you recommend?
options: Keep one open network but hide the SSID so only people who know the name can join.
Two SSIDs without personal details: a staff network with WPA3 (AES) and a strong network key, and a separate guest network with its own key, isolated from the staff LAN.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: Finally, you log in to the router and find the administrator password is still "admin", and there is no firewall rule set. What do you do?
options: Leave it: guests only use the Wi-Fi, they will not try to log in to the router.
Change the router password to a strong one, enable the firewall to block unrequested inbound traffic, turn off remote administration, and add MAC filtering on the staff SSID.

questions.topic: Networking standards and designing simple networks
questions.stem: In a network diagram for Dominica Coffee Exporters, the designer draws a brick-wall shape between the router and the switch. What does this shape represent, and why is it placed there?
options: An Ethernet patch panel, placed there to organise cables
A wireless access point, placed there to broadcast the SSID
A hub, placed there to repeat signals to every PC
A firewall, placed there so all traffic between the WAN and the LAN is filtered

questions.stem:
A technician is turning the network design for the Seaside Pharmacy in Frigate Bay into a working network. Sort each job she does into the physical half or the logical half of configuration.

Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She runs an Ethernet cable from the dispensary PC to a LAN port on the router.
questions.explain: Connecting a cable as the diagram shows is physical work.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She plugs the cable from the ISP's fibre terminal into the router's WAN port.
questions.explain: Choosing and connecting the correct port is part of the physical set-up.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She types a new SSID, SP-Staff, into the router's management page.
questions.explain: Entering a setting in the management page is logical configuration.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She chooses WPA3-Personal with AES in the wireless settings.
questions.explain: Security modes are settings, so this is logical configuration.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She places the point-of-sale terminal and the printer exactly where the diagram shows them.
questions.explain: Placing devices to match the design is physical work.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She switches on the router's firewall and saves the settings.
questions.explain: Turning on the firewall is done in the settings: logical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She sets the DHCP range to 192.168.1.100 to 192.168.1.199 and reserves an address for the printer.
questions.explain: IP addressing is part of the logical half.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical configuration step?

She mounts the router in a locked cabinet behind the counter.
questions.explain: Positioning and securing the hardware is physical.

questions.stem:
A technician is describing the networks she has set up around the island. Sort each description into the topology it belongs to.

Which topology is being described?

A terminator is fitted at each end of the main cable.
questions.explain: Terminators at both ends of a single backbone are the signature of a bus.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

Each PC is cabled to the next PC, and the last PC is cabled back to the first.
questions.explain: A closed loop of node-to-node links is a ring.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

Every device has its own Ethernet cable running to one central hub.
questions.explain: All cables meeting at a central device makes a star.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

Data passes from node to node in one direction until it reaches its destination.
questions.explain: Data travelling round a loop through each node is a ring.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

If the central hub loses power, every device is cut off.
questions.explain: The central device is the single point of failure in a star.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

It uses the least cable because all devices share one backbone.
questions.explain: One shared backbone means least cable: a bus.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

A damaged cable at one desk disconnects only that desk.
questions.explain: Separate cables isolate faults in a star.

questions.stem:
Which topology is being described?

A single break in the backbone cable stops the whole network.
questions.explain: Every device depends on the backbone in a bus.

questions.stem: The San Pedro Tours office in Belize City has four PCs cabled to a hub. Staff can share files with each other, but none of the PCs can reach the Internet. The ISP's fibre terminal is working. Which device must be added and configured so that the LAN can reach the WAN?
options: A terminator at each end of the hub
A router, with its WAN port connected to the fibre terminal and a LAN port connected to the hub
A second hub, connected to the first hub
Longer Ethernet cables, so the PCs can reach the fibre terminal

questions.stem:
You are helping the Montego Bay Tours office on King Street, Kingston, wire up its new network. For each situation, choose the best device, port, cable or term.

The cable from the ISP's fibre terminal must go into the new router. Which port should it use?
questions.explain: The WAN port joins the router to the ISP; LAN ports are for local devices.

questions.stem: Six desk PCs need wired connections, but the router has only four LAN ports. What extends the star?
options: a hub or switch cabled to one of the router's LAN ports
questions.explain: A hub or switch gives more ports and connects to the router through one LAN port.

questions.stem: The manager does not want every booking PC to receive every other PC's traffic. Which central device is better?
options: a switch, because it sends data only to the intended port
a hub, because it repeats data to every port
questions.explain: A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards data only to the right port; a hub repeats to all.

questions.stem: The PC in the back store room would need a 130-metre cable run to reach the hub. What is the problem?
options: the PC needs its own WAN port
Ethernet cannot connect PCs to hubs
Ethernet runs should not exceed about 100 metres
questions.explain: A single twisted-pair Ethernet run is limited to about 100 metres.

questions.stem: The network links only the PCs and printer inside the Albert Street office. What type of network is it?
questions.explain: A network inside one building, owned by the organisation, is a LAN.

questions.stem: ipconfig on a booking PC shows its default gateway as 192.168.1.1. Which device has that address?
questions.explain: The router's LAN address is the default gateway for every device on the LAN.

questions.stem:
The technician for the Bayside Family Clinic in Portsmouth is tightening security on the clinic's wired network. Sort each measure she takes.

What kind of security measure is this?

The router blocks all unrequested inbound connections from the Internet for every device on the LAN.
questions.explain: Protecting the whole LAN at the boundary is the job of the hardware firewall in the router.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

Remote management of the router from the WAN is switched off on the router.
questions.explain: This is part of configuring the router's firewall so outsiders cannot reach the management page.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

Windows Defender Firewall on the reception PC blocks a games program from accepting incoming connections.
questions.explain: A firewall installed on one computer, controlling its programs, is a software (host) firewall.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

An allow rule on the records PC lets the records program receive data on TCP port 5050 from LAN addresses only.
questions.explain: A rule for one program on one computer belongs to that host's software firewall.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

The router and hub are moved into a locked cupboard.
questions.explain: Locking equipment away is physical security, not a firewall.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

The unused network socket in the waiting room is disconnected at the hub.
questions.explain: Disabling unused ports stops a visitor plugging in a laptop.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

The router's firmware is updated to the latest version.
questions.explain: Up-to-date firmware closes known weaknesses in the router's own software.

questions.stem:
What kind of security measure is this?

Only the clinic's own PCs, listed by MAC address, can receive an address on the wired ports.
questions.explain: MAC filtering on wired ports admits only listed devices.

questions.stem:
You are configuring the network for the Bayside Family Clinic in San Fernando from the designer's diagram: a star LAN, a router to the ISP, staff Wi-Fi and a waiting-room guest Wi-Fi. Make the best decisions.

You have cabled everything. The router came with the admin login admin / admin. What do you do first in the management page?
options: Leave it; nobody outside will know the address of the management page.
Change the router password to a long, unique one.

questions.stem: Now the wireless settings. A few older tablets support only WPA2. Which security setting do you choose?
options: WPA2/WPA3 transitional mode with AES and a 16-character network key, with a plan to replace the old tablets.
Open network with no key, so the old tablets can connect easily.

questions.stem: Patients want Wi-Fi in the waiting room. What do you set up?
options: A separate guest SSID, isolated from the LAN, with its own key, and the firewall left on.
Give patients the staff network key.

questions.stem:
You are the technician for the Island Hop Travel agency in Bridgetown. For each piece of evidence, choose the most likely cause.

ping 8.8.8.8 gets 4 replies, but ping www.example.com says "could not find host".
questions.explain: The Internet path works by IP address, so name resolution (DNS) is failing.

questions.stem: ipconfig shows "Media disconnected" for the Ethernet adapter.
options: no physical link: cable or port
questions.explain: Media disconnected means the network card sees no link at all: check the cable and port.

questions.stem: All PCs are offline and the router's Internet light is red; LAN lights are normal.
options: a fault on the WAN side: ISP line or WAN settings
questions.explain: The LAN is working; the link to the ISP (WAN) is down.

questions.stem: Wired speed test gives 95 Mbps; Wi-Fi in the back office gives 12 Mbps.
options: weak Wi-Fi signal or interference in that room
questions.explain: The line is fine when cabled, so the wireless link is the bottleneck.

questions.stem: A new staff laptop sees the SSID and accepts the network key but never connects; other devices are fine.
options: the gateway is wrong for everyone
MAC filtering has not been updated with its address
questions.explain: Only the new device is refused: its MAC address is probably missing from the allow list.

questions.stem: ping to a colleague's PC times out, but she can browse the web normally.
options: her PC has no IP address
her software firewall blocks incoming ping
questions.explain: Her connection works, so her host firewall is most likely blocking inbound ICMP echo requests.

questions.stem: A user at the Saba Dive Shop reports "the Internet is down". The technician finds that ping 8.8.8.8 receives 4 replies with 0% loss, but nslookup www.example.com returns "DNS request timed out". Which action is MOST appropriate next?
options: Call the ISP to report that the line is down
Change the DNS server setting, then test again with nslookup

questions.stem: A teacher's PC at the San Pedro Learning Centre has a fast new SSD, but it freezes whenever several programs are open and the drive light flashes constantly. The CPU is only moderately busy. Which upgrade is MOST likely to improve performance?

Staff at the English Harbour Learning Centre have logged performance complaints. For each one, choose the best explanation.

The video-editing PC has a new SSD and 32 GB of RAM, but renders still crawl and Task Manager shows the old processor at 100%.
options: The SSD is too fast for the RAM.
The CPU is the bottleneck: it sets the speed limit.
questions.explain: Storage and RAM are feeding the CPU well; the processor itself limits how fast work can be done.

questions.stem: The office PC has 4 GB of RAM. With the accounts package, email and a browser open it slows badly, and the drive light never stops flashing.
options: RAM is full, so the PC keeps swapping to virtual memory.
questions.explain: Constant drive activity with many programs open shows swapping between RAM and virtual memory; more RAM would reduce it.

questions.stem: The centre bought faster PCs, but web pages load no faster over its old, slow office connection.
options: Upgrading one part leaves the outdated part limiting the whole system.
Web pages do not use the network.
questions.explain: A system performs only as well as its parts work together; the slow connection still limits web browsing.

questions.stem: The payroll program prints correct payslips, but it takes an hour and uses all the PC's memory.
options: It is efficient because the output is right.
It is accurate but inefficient: the input-output ratio is adverse.
questions.explain: Correct output does not make a system efficient if it uses far too much time and memory to produce it.

questions.stem: Receptionists needed nine clicks to book a class; the redesigned screen needs only three.
options: Usability has improved: the goal is reached with fewer steps.
questions.explain: Usability efficiency means reaching goals with as few resources (time, steps, effort) as possible.

questions.stem:
The St. Kitts Seaview Hotel is choosing new equipment. Sort each manager's comment by the feature it compares.

Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

The SSD opens the booking system in seconds; the old hard drive took a minute.
questions.explain: How quickly a task is done is speed.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

The laptops use a third of the electricity of the old desktops.
questions.explain: Useful work for less power is efficiency.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

Housekeeping staff can carry the tablets from room to room.
questions.explain: Ease of carrying and using elsewhere is portability.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

The desktop's RAM can be upgraded in five minutes; the sealed laptop cannot.
questions.explain: Ease of repair and upgrade is maintainability.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

The new server holds 8 TB of guest records; the old one held 500 GB.
questions.explain: Capacity to hold data is storage.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

Fibre between the two buildings is unaffected by the kitchen's electrical equipment, unlike the copper cable.
questions.explain: Comparing how media carry data is transmission.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

The booking software receives regular updates and has a clear manual.
questions.explain: Updates and documentation make software maintainable.

questions.stem:
Which SO 2.15 feature does this comment compare?

Wi-Fi lets guests connect anywhere in the lobby, but cabled PCs at reception get a steadier signal.
questions.explain: Wired versus wireless links is a transmission comparison.

questions.stem:
You are advising the Statia Harbour Office on how to store and send its data. For each need, choose the best option.

The office must keep ten years of shipping records as a cheap archive that is only ever read from start to finish.
options: A flash drive kept in a desk drawer
Tape, because sequential access is enough and it is cheap for large backups
questions.explain: Tapes allow only sequential access, but that suits a large, cheap archive.

questions.stem: The live berth-booking database must jump straight to any vessel's record.
options: Disk, because it allows direct (random) access
An optical disc read in sequence
questions.explain: Disks allow any file organisation, including direct access to a record.

questions.stem: Records must survive if the building is badly damaged in a hurricane.
options: A second hard drive in the same office
questions.explain: Only an off-site copy is safe from a local disaster; RAM is volatile.

questions.stem: The office PC loads programs slowly from its spinning hard disk. Which storage would load them much faster?
questions.explain: An SSD has no moving parts, so access is much faster than an HDD.

questions.stem: The harbour radio link lets each side transmit, but only one side at a time.
questions.explain: Both directions, one at a time, is half-duplex.

questions.stem: Video calls with the Willemstad office need both sides sending at the same time.
questions.explain: Both directions at once is full-duplex.

questions.stem: Large blocks of cargo data are sent in a steady stream timed by a shared clock.
questions.explain: Blocks in a steady stream timed by a clock is synchronous transmission; asynchronous sends a character at a time with start and stop bits.

questions.stem: Cargo records sent from Statia arrive as gibberish in Curaçao because the two systems interpret the bits differently.
options: No common data encoding standard was used.
questions.explain: Sender and receiver must follow the same standards, such as data encoding, to interpret the bits the same way.

questions.stem: The Statia Harbour Office must link two buildings 400 metres apart. The cable route passes beside heavy electrical machinery, and data must be hard to intercept. Which transmission medium BEST meets ALL these needs?
options: Wi-Fi access points in each building

questions.stem: Dominica Craft Co-op keeps 2 TB of product photos on one office hard disk drive. The manager wants faster access and wants the photos to survive if the office is damaged in a hurricane. Which combination BEST meets both needs?
options: Move working files to an SSD and keep a synchronised cloud backup
Copy the photos onto flash drives kept in the office desk
Keep the hard disk drive and print the photos as backup
Add more RAM to the office PC

questions.stem:
The IT officer at the Bayview Credit Union in New Amsterdam has noted how access control works during a normal week. Sort each event into the part of access control it shows.

Which of the four parts of access control is this?

The manager decides that tellers may record deposits but may not approve loans.
questions.explain: Deciding who is approved and exactly what they may use is authorisation.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

A teller types her user ID, TELLER07, at the log-in screen.
questions.explain: Stating who you are with a user ID is identification.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

The system checks her password and the code on her hardware token.
questions.explain: Verifying the claimed identity is authentication.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

An auditor's report lists every change TELLER07 made to member accounts last month.
questions.explain: Tracing actions to an individual for reporting and auditing is accountability.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

A member gives her account number at the counter so the teller can find her record.
questions.explain: An account number is a form of username: it identifies the member.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

The member's fingerprint is compared with her enrolled template to confirm she is the account holder.
questions.explain: Checking that she really is the person she claims to be is authentication.

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

Only the IT officer is approved to create new user accounts.
questions.explain: Approving who may use which resource is authorisation (policy definition).

questions.stem:
Which of the four parts of access control is this?

The log shows that the shared "frontdesk" account deleted a record, so nobody can be held responsible.
questions.explain: This is a failure of accountability: the action cannot be traced to one person.

questions.stem:
Access control is everywhere, from a car door in San Pedro to a business computer in Belize City. Judge each situation.

Kezia locks her car outside the Belize City market and takes the key with her. In access-control terms, the lock and key...
options: protect a resource so that only those allowed can use it
questions.explain: A lock and key is an everyday access control: only the key holder can open or start the car.

questions.stem: At a Frederick Street cash machine, Jaden's bank card works only after he types four secret digits. This everyday access control is a...
questions.explain: A PIN controls use of a bank or credit card.

questions.stem: The Island Fresh Supermarket locks its cash office and puts passwords on its stock database. The cash office is a...
questions.explain: Buildings and rooms are physical assets; computer systems and data are computing resources.

questions.stem: Every night at 2 a.m. a backup program at the supermarket logs in to copy the stock file. Why does the IT definition of access control say "who or what"?
options: Users may be people or computer processes
questions.explain: Users may be people or computer processes, and both must be controlled.

questions.stem: A Grenadian bank gives staff a small device that shows a new six-digit code every minute, typed in when logging in. This technology is a...
questions.explain: Hardware tokens are one of the access-control technologies businesses use, with passwords, biometrics and certificates.

questions.stem: Before the new till system goes live, the supermarket manager sets the rule "cashiers may record sales; only supervisors may approve refunds". Which phase is this?
questions.explain: Deciding in advance who may do what is policy definition (authorisation).

questions.stem: Next morning, the till refuses a cashier's attempt to approve a refund. Which phase is this?
questions.explain: Granting or rejecting a request using the authorisations already defined is policy enforcement.

questions.stem: At the Sunrise Hardware store in Holetown, all six cashiers log in to the till system with one shared account, "till1". A generator was sold at a heavily discounted price, and the store cannot tell which cashier entered it. Which part of access control is MOST clearly missing?

The Grand Anse Marina Hotel is reviewing its security. Sort each measure by what it protects.

Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

A security guard checks staff ID badges at the back entrance.
questions.explain: A guard controls entry to the building, so this is physical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

Front-desk staff can view bookings but cannot change room rates.
questions.explain: Access rights set in software decide what each user can do with data: logical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

The server cabinet is kept in a locked room.
questions.explain: A locked room protects the hardware itself: physical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

The booking system locks an account after five wrong passwords.
questions.explain: The software is controlling log-in attempts: logical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

A swipe card is needed to open the staff-only corridor.
questions.explain: The card opens a door, so it controls physical entry.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

Guest credit-card numbers are stored in encrypted form.
questions.explain: Encryption protects the data itself through software: logical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

Each laptop is chained to the desk with a cable lock.
questions.explain: A cable lock stops the hardware from being carried away: physical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

The manager logs in to the accounts PC with a fingerprint.
questions.explain: Here the fingerprint opens a computer system, not a door, so it is logical.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

The barrier at the staff parking lot lifts only for registered staff cards.
questions.explain: Parking lots, like buildings and IT rooms, are protected by physical access controls.

questions.stem:
Is this a physical or a logical access control measure?

Each employee has a unique username and password for the hotel network.
questions.explain: A unique username and password limits connections to the network and its data: logical.

questions.stem:
Staff at the Princess Port Hotel in Bridgetown and other Barbadian organisations are sorting out who controls access and how users are identified. Answer each question.

The barrier at the hotel's staff parking lot needs reprogramming so that new staff cards open it. Who is MOST likely responsible?
questions.explain: Parking lots, buildings and rooms are physical access, usually the facilities manager's responsibility.

questions.stem: The hotel's IT manager decides that housekeeping supervisors can view room status but not guests' payment details. She is using...
questions.explain: Computer-system managers use logical access controls to decide who enters a system and which tasks they can perform.

questions.stem: The IT manager sets every hotel PC to lock after five idle minutes and blocks software installation. This shows that computer-system managers can also...
options: influence how staff use the system
questions.explain: Logical access settings shape how staff use the system, not just who gets in.

questions.stem: A caller to the Bayview Credit Union gives her account number so the clerk can find her record. The account number is acting as a...
questions.explain: A username may take the form of a user ID, an account number or a PIN.

questions.stem: An employee of a Speightstown firm scans his card at a reader to lift the car-park barrier. Which identification method is this?
questions.explain: Smart cards are swiped or scanned through a reader to grant entry to parking facilities, buildings and rooms.

questions.stem: A Holetown laboratory recognises staff at the door from the pattern of their iris. Which identification method is this?
questions.explain: Biometrics recognises a person through physical or behavioural traits.

questions.stem: A Mahoe Grove High School student types her username at the network log-in. Why must the system still ask for a password?
options: The username only claims an identity, which must then be authenticated
questions.explain: Identification claims who you are; authentication proves it.

questions.stem:
The Sunset Reef Resort at Dickenson Bay, Antigua, is replacing metal keys with key cards. The manager has listed what she has noticed in the first month. Sort each observation.

Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

A housekeeper reports her card missing at 9 a.m.; the IT officer cancels it in two minutes without changing any locks.
questions.explain: Lost cards can be cancelled instantly in software, unlike a lost metal key.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

A delivery driver walks into the staff corridor right behind a waiter before the door closes.
questions.explain: This is tailgating: the card opened the door for one person, but two got in.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

The log shows exactly which card opened the server room at 11:42 p.m. on Saturday.
questions.explain: Each card has a unique code, so the system keeps an audit log of entries.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

A guest lends her room card to a friend, who uses the pool gate without being registered.
questions.explain: A card proves possession, not identity. Whoever holds it gets in.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

Guest cards stop working automatically at noon on the check-out date.
questions.explain: Access can be restricted by time, so old guests cannot return.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

During a power cut, the card readers on the side doors stop working.
questions.explain: Readers and controllers need electricity, unlike a simple key lock.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

The cleaners' cards open offices only between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m.
questions.explain: Access can be limited by time and by door for each card.

questions.stem:
Is this a benefit or a drawback of using key cards?

A magnetic stripe card stops working after being left next to a phone speaker.
questions.explain: Magnetic stripes can be wiped by magnets and wear out with swiping.

questions.stem: At Basseterre Data Centre, staff open the server-room door with a proximity key card. One afternoon an unauthorised visitor enters using a card that an employee left on a café table in Fort Street. Which statement BEST explains the weakness this incident exposes?
options: Proximity cards can be read only when the power is off.
Key cards are a logical access control and cannot protect rooms.
The card must have been encrypted incorrectly.
A key card authenticates possession of the card, not the identity of the person holding it.

questions.stem:
Organisations in Guyana have reported what happened after they installed biometric systems. Sort each report.

Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

At Linden Construction Ltd., nobody can clock in for an absent friend, because each worker must place their own finger on the reader.
questions.explain: Presence: the person must be physically present to authenticate.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

Staff at a Georgetown insurance office no longer call the help desk about forgotten passwords.
questions.explain: Memory: there is nothing to remember.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

An intruder cannot copy a manager's iris pattern the way he once copied a door key.
questions.explain: Imitation: biometrics are hard to fake.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

An employee who left her staff badge at home still gets into the office with her fingerprint.
questions.explain: Convenience: lost IDs are not a problem.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

The fingerprint reader rejects a mason whose fingertips are worn from years of laying blocks.
questions.explain: Changing traits: physical characteristics may change, causing false rejection.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

A clerk with limited hand movement cannot use the hand-geometry terminal.
questions.explain: Accessibility: physically disabled users may struggle with fingerprint, hand-geometry or signature systems.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

The Island Credit bank finds voice recognition works well by phone but fails in its noisy branch lobby.
questions.explain: Suitability: techniques differ in effectiveness for different uses.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

At shift change, a queue forms because the face scanner at a cruise-pier tour office takes several seconds per person.
questions.explain: Time and cost: response time may be too slow.

questions.stem:
Does this report show an advantage or a disadvantage of biometrics?

The Seaside Pharmacy decides retina scanners are too expensive for its two-door shop.
questions.explain: Time and cost: the required devices can be expensive.

questions.stem:
Organisations across the region are trying out biometric devices. Judge each situation using what you know about biometrics.

At Linden Construction Ltd., a mason with a freshly cut finger is refused by the fingerprint time clock, even though he is enrolled. This is a...
questions.explain: A genuine, enrolled user being refused is a false rejection.

questions.stem: A Jamaican bank lets callers into telephone banking by checking the pitch and tone of their speech. Which biometric is this?
questions.explain: Pitch, tone and speech patterns are measured by voice recognition.

questions.stem: A Roseau gym's fingerprint database is hacked. Why is this worse than a hacked password file?
options: A fingerprint cannot be changed like a password can
questions.explain: A stolen password can be reset, but a person cannot get new fingerprints.

questions.stem: A Trinidad factory switched from paper sign-in sheets to a fingerprint clock. What problem does this mainly solve?
options: Forgotten passwords on the stock system
Workers clocking in for absent friends
questions.explain: A fingerprint cannot be lent, so one worker cannot clock in for another ("buddy punching").

questions.stem: Signing on a pad at a Curaçao courier office measures how a person writes. This kind of biometric is...
questions.explain: Signature and typing rhythm measure how a person behaves, so they are behavioural biometrics.

questions.stem: An enrolled worker at the San Fernando Shipping Agency places her finger on the reader. What does the system compare her sample with?
questions.explain: The sample is converted into a template and compared with the template stored at enrolment.

questions.stem:
Students in a Coralstone College computer lab have asked you to check their password habits. Answer each question.

Aaliyah uses "aaliyah05" because it is easy to remember. Which characteristic does it fail MOST clearly?
questions.explain: It contains her own name, which anyone who knows her could guess. Being alphanumeric is a strength, not a failure.

questions.stem: Marco changes "sunsetbeach" to "SunsetBeach". Which characteristic has he added?
questions.explain: He added capital letters, so the password now uses mixed case. It still has no digits.

questions.stem: Keisha's password is 10 mixed-case alphanumeric characters. What happens to the number of possible combinations if she adds one more such character?
questions.explain: Each extra position multiplies the possibilities by the number of characters available, so length is very powerful.

questions.stem: Shania writes her school password on a sticky note on her monitor. The best advice is to...
options: use a memorable passphrase and remove the note
make it shorter so she remembers it
share it with her best friend as a backup
questions.explain: A passphrase is long but memorable, so she no longer needs the note.

questions.stem: Why does the school system show dots instead of the letters as you type?
options: Masking stops onlookers reading the password
questions.explain: Masking prevents shoulder-surfing. Encryption is a different process that scrambles stored or transmitted data.

questions.stem:
The IT officer at the Bayview Credit Union in St. George’s is reviewing staff habits and the log-in system. Judge each situation.

A loan officer has used the same password since she joined the credit union six years ago. This is called a...
questions.explain: A static password is seldom, if ever, changed, so an attacker who learns it can use it for a long time.

questions.stem: The credit union now makes staff change passwords every 90 days. The MAIN benefit is that...
options: passwords no longer need to be secret
an attacker has less time to use a stolen password before it changes
questions.explain: A shorter lifespan reduces an attacker's opportunity to compromise and use the password.

questions.stem: A teller wants to use her work password on a cooking forum and for her personal e-mail. Following good practice, she...
options: should write it down to avoid mixing them up
may reuse it anywhere if it is strong
should not reuse her work password; reuse is only for non-critical resources
questions.explain: Only reuse a password for resources considered non-critical. A work password protecting member data is critical.

questions.stem: Someone tries 40 different passwords on the manager's user ID in one minute. Which system feature guards against this?
options: Disabling the user ID after consecutive failed logons
questions.explain: Lockout after consecutive failed logons guards against repeated password guesses.

questions.stem: A cashier changes from "Sun7!" to the passphrase "Sunrise over San Fernando at 7!". Compared with the short password, the passphrase is...
options: generally harder to guess, because it is longer and has several words
the same, because both contain a number
questions.explain: A passphrase is longer and usually has more than one word, so it is harder to guess and somewhat more secure.

questions.stem: Passwords are the oldest and most common way to authenticate staff at the credit union. They are also usually considered...
questions.explain: Passwords can be guessed, shared, observed or forgotten, so they are the weakest common method.

questions.stem: The credit union's loan system holds sensitive member data. Which log-in follows the guidance for sensitive or critical systems?
options: A password plus a code from a hardware token
questions.explain: Use at least two of the three factors for sensitive or critical systems. A password and a passphrase are both things you know, so they count as one factor.

questions.stem:
Staff and customers across Jamaica prove who they are in many ways. Sort each authentication method into its factor.

Which authentication factor is being used?

A customer types a 4-digit PIN at a bank machine on King Street.
questions.explain: A PIN is a secret the user knows.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A telephone company technician taps a contactless badge to enter the exchange building.
questions.explain: The badge is a physical token the technician holds.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A teacher unlocks her laptop by looking at its camera (face recognition).
questions.explain: Her face is a characteristic of who she is.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

An online banking user enters a one-time code sent by text to his registered phone.
questions.explain: The code proves he has the phone, so it is a possession factor.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A caller answers "What was the name of your first school?"
questions.explain: A security question tests something the user knows.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

An NMIA worker places her finger on a reader to enter the baggage area.
questions.explain: A fingerprint is an inherence factor: something she is.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A student types his password into the school network.
questions.explain: A password is the classic knowledge factor.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A Jamaican bank checks the caller's voice before discussing the account.
questions.explain: Voice recognition measures a characteristic of the person.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A manager at the Bayview Credit Union types her passphrase "Kites over Hellshire at 6!".
questions.explain: A passphrase, like a password, is something you know.

questions.stem:
Which authentication factor is being used?

A courier in Spanish Town signs on a pad that checks the speed and pressure of her signature.
questions.explain: A signature measured as it is written is a characteristic unique to the person.

questions.stem: The Anguilla Island Bank wants to introduce two-factor authentication for online banking. Which of the following log-in designs is a TRUE example of two-factor authentication?
options: A password followed by a one-time code sent to the customer's registered phone
A password followed by a four-digit PIN
A password followed by a security question about the customer's first school
A username followed by a password

questions.stem: A laptop holding the Saba Dive Centre's customer list is stolen from a car. The hard drive was fully encrypted and the thief does not have the key. Which statement BEST describes the effect of the encryption?
options: It prevented the laptop from being stolen.
The thief has the data but cannot read it, because it is stored as ciphertext.
It allows the dive centre to track the laptop's location.
The data has been corrupted and can no longer be used by anyone.

questions.stem:
After Hurricane Irma, the Road Town Water Board records office is reviewing what went wrong and what protects its data. Sort each item.

Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

The power failed while the billing file was being saved.
questions.explain: An interrupted save leaves a partly written, corrupted file.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

A UPS keeps the server running long enough to shut down safely.
questions.explain: The UPS prevents corruption from sudden power loss.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

Rainwater leaked onto an external hard drive.
questions.explain: Physical damage can make stored data unreadable.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

A range check rejects any meter reading below zero.
questions.explain: Validation stops unreasonable data entering the system.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

A file was copied over an unstable network link and some bits changed.
questions.explain: Transmission errors alter data in transit.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

Every night a backup is copied to a server off the island.
questions.explain: An off-site backup allows correct data to be restored.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

A clerk pulled out a flash drive while files were still being written.
questions.explain: Improper removal interrupts writing and corrupts files.

questions.stem:
Is this a cause of data corruption or a safeguard for data integrity?

A checksum is compared after each file transfer.
questions.explain: Checksums detect data changed in transmission.

questions.stem:
The Leeward Medical Laboratory in Kingstown has listed incidents that better access control could prevent. Sort each one by the purpose of access control it relates to.

Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A visitor photographs a patient's results on an unattended screen.
questions.explain: Disclosure to an unauthorised person is a data security failure.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A former employee whose account was never disabled logs in and deletes a folder of reports.
questions.explain: Unauthorised deletion is a data security failure; disabling leavers' accounts prevents it.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A courier reads a printed list of test results left in an unlocked room.
questions.explain: Disclosure to an unauthorised person: physical access control would have prevented it.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A receptionist with full rights accidentally changes a glucose result from 5.2 to 52.
questions.explain: Only authorised users should modify data; read-only rights for reception would keep results accurate.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

Lab technicians enter results, but only the senior scientist may amend a result after it is approved.
questions.explain: Restricting who may modify data keeps it accurate and consistent.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

Two staff update the same patient record in different ways, and nobody can tell which is correct.
questions.explain: Data should be accurate and consistent; limiting who may modify records protects integrity.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A hacker guesses a weak password and plants a virus that scrambles the results database.
questions.explain: Malicious access led to corrupted data.

questions.stem:
Which purpose of access control does this incident relate to?

A visitor plugs an infected USB drive into an unlocked lab PC, and files are damaged.
questions.explain: Physical and logical access controls reduce vulnerability to viruses that corrupt data.

questions.stem:
You are the IT consultant for the Harbourview Medical Clinic on Hincks Street, Bridgetown. It has a small server, six PCs and paper-free patient records. Make the best security decisions.

The server sits under the reception desk, where visitors wait. The owner asks what to do first.
options: Leave it there; a strong password on the server is enough.
Move the server into a locked room opened only by staff key cards, with a UPS.

questions.stem: Staff all log in with the shared account "clinic" and password "harbour1". What do you recommend?
options: Keep the shared account but change the password to "Harbour2".
Give each person a unique user ID, require effective passwords, and set access rights by role.

questions.stem: The clinic backs up to a USB drive kept in the same room as the server. Patient forms often contain impossible dates of birth. What next?
options: Nothing more is needed; the server room is locked.
Encrypt the backups, store a copy off-site, and add validation checks to the patient form.

questions.stem: The Statia Fuel Depot's database is fully protected by key cards, passwords and encryption, and no outsider has ever accessed it. However, managers find that several delivery quantities were entered with an extra zero. Which concept has been compromised?
options: Data security, because the data is incorrect
Encryption, because the data was scrambled
Authentication, because the staff were not verified
Data integrity, because the data is not accurate

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
After Hurricane Irma in 2017, a class surveyed how people in The Valley, Anguilla, got back online. Sort each statement: does it describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Technicians repair the cables and routers that link homes in Sandy Ground to the rest of the world.
questions.explain: Cables and routers are network infrastructure: the Internet.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

A student clicks from a news page about Irma to a weather report stored on another server.
questions.explain: Moving between linked hypertext documents is using the web.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

A family in Blowing Point makes a video call to relatives in Curaçao.
questions.explain: Video calling is a different service carried by the Internet, not the web.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Documents are joined to one another by hyperlinks and viewed in a browser.
questions.explain: Interconnected hypertext documents viewed in a browser are the web.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Data travels between networks using TCP/IP.
questions.explain: TCP/IP is the Internet's main set of protocols.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Pages are requested from web servers using HTTP.
questions.explain: HTTP is the protocol of the web.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

Its forerunner, ARPANET, dates from 1969.
questions.explain: The Internet is the older system; the web was built on top of it.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe the Internet or the World Wide Web?

It was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989.
questions.explain: Berners-Lee proposed the web, which runs on the existing Internet.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Dante, a Lower Sixth student from San Pedro, is revising hypertext with his study group. Answer each question about what they see.

Dante reads the printed manual for his family's car from page 1 to the last page, in the order the author chose. He is processing the information...
questions.explain: Reading from start to finish in the author's order is linear.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Belize City Motors puts the same manual online as short topic pages, and Dante clicks straight to "Warning lights". This is...
options: a hypertext approach: the user chooses the order and selection of topics
questions.explain: Hypertext lets the user, not the author, choose the order.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: On a Flamboyant Heights College course page, Aaliyah moves her pointer over a photo of the library and the arrow becomes a small pointing hand. The photo is...
questions.explain: Images can be links; the hand pointer shows a link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Aaliyah clicks a link on a St. John’s page and a document loads from a server in Europe, though she never sees where it came from. Why does hypertext suit networks so well?
options: The user only needs to activate the link, not know where the document is stored
All the documents are on one computer
The user must type the server's IP address first
questions.explain: The location is largely unseen: the user just activates the link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A link on a Belize tourism page jumps to the "Beaches" heading lower down the same page. A hyperlink can point to...
options: another place in the same document or a different document
questions.explain: Links can target the same document or a different one.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Kemar says: "The web and the Internet are the same thing." The best correction is...
options: The web is the cables and the Internet is the pages
The web is a service, a subset, accessed on the Internet
The Internet is a service that runs on the web
questions.explain: The WWW is one service on the Internet, not the whole Internet.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A gamer in San Pedro clicks a link that opens an online game in her browser. This shows that hyperlinks...
options: have expanded to video, sound, interactive programs and gaming
questions.explain: The original web was text-only; links now reach any form of information.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
A class is auditing web pages used around the Caribbean. Sort each page: is it static or dynamic?

Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

Grand Anse Guest House "Our history" page shows the same text to every visitor all year.
questions.explain: Same content every time it is viewed: static.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

The Bequia Ferries page shows today's departure times, updated as each boat leaves.
questions.explain: Content that changes each time it is accessed: dynamic.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

A student logs in to the Sixth Form portal and sees her own name and her own assignments.
questions.explain: Built for each visitor from stored data: dynamic.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

The Montego Bay Bakery page lists its address and opening hours; the owner edits it twice a year.
questions.explain: It changes only when the author edits the file: static.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

A weather page for Bridgetown shows a new temperature every time it is refreshed.
questions.explain: New data on each visit: dynamic.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

A Flamboyant Heights College student's one-page CV, unchanged since she uploaded it.
questions.explain: A stored file sent exactly as written: static.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

An online shop page shows a different basket total for every customer.
questions.explain: Different content for each visitor: dynamic.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this a static or a dynamic web page?

The menu of a King George V Street café, saved once as an HTML file.
questions.explain: Same content each time: static.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Kiara, a Lower Sixth student at Sea-Almond Secondary School, is helping the Seaside Pharmacy in San Fernando understand its new web site. Answer each question.

She types https://www.seasidepharmacy.tt/services/refills.html. Which part tells the browser to use secure, encrypted rules?
questions.explain: https:// is the protocol (scheme). The s means HTTP secured with encryption.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: In the same URL, /services/ is the...
questions.explain: The path names the folder on the server that holds the file.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The .sx at the end of the domain name shows...
options: the country-code top-level domain for Sint Maarten
the file type of the page
questions.explain: .sx is the TLD for Sint Maarten, like .jm for Jamaica and .tt for Trinidad and Tobago.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A customer mistypes the file name as refils.html. The domain works, but the server cannot find that file. Which status code comes back?
questions.explain: 404 means the server was reached but no file exists at that address.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The refill form sends a customer's name and prescription number. Which HTTP method sends the data in the body of the request rather than in the URL?
questions.explain: POST sends data in the request body. GET adds it to the URL, which is fine for searches but not private data.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The pharmacy's server treats every request as brand new, with no memory of the customer's last click. HTTP is therefore...
questions.explain: HTTP is stateless: each request is handled on its own.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The browser asks the server for the page and the server replies with a status code and the file. This model is called...
questions.explain: HTTP works on a request-response model between client (browser) and server.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

questions.explain: The server answers HTTP requests.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:

questions.explain: The address bar is part of the browser.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe a web server or a web browser?

Lets a Flamboyant Heights College student go back and forward through the pages she has traversed.
questions.explain: Traversing information resources is a browser function.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

A computer in a data centre that hosts the web sites of several Caribbean businesses.
questions.explain: A computer that hosts sites is a web server.

Opens an HTML file saved in the student's own Documents folder.
questions.explain: Browsers can also open files in the local file system.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe a web server or a web browser?

Holds the pages of a school intranet so staff on the private network can view them.
questions.explain: Servers can serve private networks too.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Island Data Services in Oranjestad builds both web pages and data feeds. Sort each statement.

Does this describe HTML or XML?

Its main purpose is to display content in a browser.
questions.explain: Displaying content is the role of HTML.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

The author invents tags such as cruiseship and arrivaltime.
questions.explain: User-defined tags are what make XML extensible.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Uses a fixed set of tags such as p, h1 and table.
questions.explain: HTML tags are predefined.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Used to send port schedules from one computer system to another.
questions.explain: Transporting data between systems is a typical XML use.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

A file fails if a single tag is left unclosed.
questions.explain: XML is strict: it must be well-formed.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Browsers will usually still show the page even if a closing tag is missing.
questions.explain: Browsers are tolerant of HTML errors.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Tags are case-sensitive, so Status and status are different.
questions.explain: XML is case-sensitive; HTML is not.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Describes how a heading, a list and an image are laid out on a page.
questions.explain: Structuring and presenting a page is HTML.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Island Data Services uses it to create a new markup language for cruise schedules, with rules that are enforced.
questions.explain: XML is a language for creating markup languages whose rules are enforced.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

Supports many rules but has no mechanism to enforce them, so the browser does its best with mistakes.
questions.explain: HTML rules are not enforced; browsers tolerate errors.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Does this describe HTML or XML?

A cruise schedule file that a port officer and a computer program can both read easily.
questions.explain: XML documents are designed to be both human-readable and machine-readable.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

options: The HTTP protocol on the web server
The browser's ability to follow hyperlinks
The HTML code of the home page

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Malik works part-time at the Holetown Computer Repairs. Help him answer customers' questions about addresses and names.

Malik reads three addresses from customers' laptops. Which one is a valid IPv4 address?
questions.explain: Four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by three dots. 256 is too high, and 10.4.7 has only three numbers.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A customer in Speightstown notices her home connection gets a different IP address every time it reconnects. She has a...
questions.explain: An address that changes each time you log on is dynamic.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

questions.explain: A static address is always the same.

questions.stem: Who assigns a home in Oistins its IP address on the Internet?
questions.explain: The ISP assigns the static or dynamic address.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A business in Port of Spain uses a name ending in .tt. This country-code suffix mainly helps identify...
options: the location and audience of the site
questions.explain: Country codes such as .tt and .sx point to location and audience.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A Barbados animal-rescue charity registers a name ending in .org. This suffix is often used by...
questions.explain: .org is often used by non-profit organisations; .com by commercial sites.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: In https://www.anguillakayaks.com/tours, which part is the domain name, strictly speaking?
questions.explain: The domain name starts after // and www is not part of it; it ends at the single slash.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Why do customers type anguillakayaks.com instead of the server's IP address?
options: Domain names are easier to remember than numbers
questions.explain: Names are easier to recall; DNS turns them back into IP addresses.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The Gros Islet Ferries company runs its booking web site on its own server in Rodney Bay. Customers reach it by domain name, and the owner wants that name to keep pointing to the server without anyone updating records. Which type of IP address should the ISP assign to the server?
options: No IP address, because customers use the domain name

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Kiara in Frigate Bay is sending a large photo to her teacher at Seagrape Bay Secondary School. Sort each job: is it done by TCP or by IP?

Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Checks that every packet of Kiara's photo arrived at her teacher's computer.
questions.explain: Verifying delivery is TCP's job.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Moves each packet from node to node across the network towards its destination.
questions.explain: Moving packets between nodes is IP's job.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Asks for packet 7 to be sent again because it never arrived.
questions.explain: Re-requesting missing packets is part of verifying delivery: TCP.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Labels each packet with the sender's and receiver's IP addresses.
questions.explain: Addressing packets so they can be routed is IP.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Puts the packets back in the correct order before the photo is opened.
questions.explain: Reassembling in order is TCP.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Lets routers between Jamaica and Miami pass each packet on to the next node.
questions.explain: Forwarding packets between nodes is IP.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Verifies that a downloaded lecture file is complete before it is saved.
questions.explain: Verified delivery is TCP.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Is this the job of TCP or IP?

Gives each device a numeric address so packets can be routed to it.
questions.explain: IP addresses belong to the Internet Protocol.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
Aaliyah is building a page for the Saba Hiking Club. Choose the HTML she needs each time.

The largest, most important heading on the page uses...
questions.explain: h1 is the top-level heading. The head element is the non-visible section of the document.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: To force a new line inside a paragraph without starting a new paragraph, she uses...
questions.explain: br is a line break. hr draws a horizontal line; p starts a new paragraph.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A note to other developers that will not appear on the page is written as...
options: a comment opened with an exclamation mark and two dashes
