questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: To make one heading dark green using inline styling, she adds...
questions.explain: The style attribute takes property: value pairs, and the property is spelt color.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: To centre a paragraph, the style property is...
questions.explain: text-align: center; aligns text horizontally.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The text shown on the browser tab comes from the...
questions.explain: The title element in the head sets the tab text.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

The steps to take before a storm (secure shutters, charge phones, fill water tanks) must be done in order. Which list?
questions.explain: An ordered list (ol) numbers the steps because order matters.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The hurricane-kit items (water, torch, batteries) can appear in any order. Which list?
questions.explain: An unordered list (ul) gives bullets when order does not matter.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: A glossary of storm terms (watch, warning, storm surge) with a meaning for each needs...
questions.explain: A description list pairs each term (dt) with its description (dd).

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Each bullet or numbered step inside ul or ol is marked with...

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: She wants the steps lettered A, B, C instead of 1, 2, 3. She adds to the ol start tag...
questions.explain: The type attribute sets the numbering style; start sets the first number.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

questions.explain: src (source) gives the file name, path or URL.

It must be closed with an end tag.
It stores the picture inside the HTML file.

options: The width attribute was set too small for the picture to appear.

The Bridge Street Craft Market is adding links across its small web site. Sort each link by type.

What kind of hyperlink is this?

The Products page links to contact.html, stored in the same folder.
questions.explain: A file name on the same site with no protocol is a relative link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

The Contact page links to https://www.example.org/library on another site.
questions.explain: A full URL with protocol and domain name is an absolute link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

A "Back to top" link at the foot of a long page uses href="#top".
questions.explain: # followed by an id jumps within the same page: a bookmark link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

An "Email the manager" link uses href="mailto:manager@example.sx".
questions.explain: mailto: opens the visitor's email program.

questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

The menu jumps to the "Opening hours" section further down the same page.
questions.explain: Moving to a section of the same page needs a bookmark link to an id.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

Every page has a navigation bar with href="index.html" to return to the home page.
questions.explain: index.html on the same site is a relative link; it keeps working if the folder moves to a new server.

questions.stem:

questions.explain: Full URLs to other sites are absolute links, often opened with target="_blank".

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
What kind of hyperlink is this?

Clicking "Ask about custom orders" opens a new message addressed to orders@example.sx.
questions.explain: Opening an email program addressed to someone is a mailto: link.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem:
The Montego Bay Youth Football Club asks you to build its first web page before the new season. Make the best decisions.

You open a blank file in a text editor. What do you write first?
options: The DOCTYPE declaration, then html containing a head (with a title) and a body.
Start straight away with the fixtures table; structure can be added later.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: The coach wants the weekly fixtures (date, opponent, venue) on the page. How do you present them?
options: One long paragraph with all the matches separated by commas.
A table with a header row of th cells and one tr per match with td cells.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Parents must register players online, choosing one age group (U10, U12 or U14). Which form control do you use for the age group?
options: Radio buttons sharing the same name, plus a submit button, inside a form with method="post".
Checkboxes, so parents can tick as many age groups as they like.

questions.topic: The Internet, the Web and HTML
questions.stem: Finally, the club wants its logo at the top and a link to the league's web site. What do you write?
options: An img with src and alt="Montego Bay Youth Football logo", and an a element with the league's full URL in href and target="_blank".
An img with only src, and the league's name typed in bold with no a element.

questions.stem:
Each card comes from a problem in a Caribbean community. Decide whether it describes the current state (how things are now), the desired state (how the people affected want things to be) or only a symptom (a visible sign of the problem).

Which part of the problem does this card describe?

The Seaside Pharmacy in Gros Islet tracks insulin stock on paper and only reorders when the shelf is empty
questions.explain: This is how things work at the pharmacy now: the current state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Seaside Pharmacy always has insulin in stock when a patient arrives with a prescription
questions.explain: This is how the pharmacy wants things to be: the desired state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Patients leave Seaside Pharmacy angry and empty-handed twice a week
questions.explain: Angry, turned-away patients are a visible sign that something is wrong. They point to the problem but are not the problem itself.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Ms. Ollivierre's tomato plants in Mesopotamia are infested with whitefly and are producing a third less fruit
questions.explain: This describes her situation now: the current state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Ms. Ollivierre harvests a full crop and meets every weekly order from the Calliaqua restaurants
questions.explain: This is the outcome she wants: the desired state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Yellow, curling patches appear on Ms. Ollivierre's tomato leaves
questions.explain: Curling, yellow leaves are what you can see. They are a symptom; the whitefly infestation and its effect on her harvest are the problem.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Bookings at the Carenage Water Taxi are written in one paper diary shared by two staff
questions.explain: This is how bookings are handled now: the current state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Every cruise passenger booked with Carenage Water Taxi is collected on time at the St. George’s cruise port
questions.explain: This is what the company wants to achieve: the desired state.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem does this card describe?

Long queues and loud complaints build up at the water taxi desk on cruise-ship days
questions.explain: Queues and complaints are visible signs. The underlying problem is the double-booking caused by the paper diary.

questions.stem:
Business owners and clubs around the Caribbean are tackling problems. Decide whether each approach follows a structured problem-solving process or is unstructured trial and error.

Which approach is this?

The owner of the Belmopan Bakery buys a new oven the day sales fall, without checking why customers stopped coming
questions.explain: This jumps straight to the first idea without defining or analysing the problem: trial and error.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

The IT club at Seagrape Bay Secondary School writes down exactly who is affected by the slow printer queue, and how, before suggesting any fixes
questions.explain: Defining the problem before acting is the first stage of a structured process.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

Arima homework club compares three ways to speed up its laptops before choosing one
questions.explain: Generating and comparing several options is part of a structured process.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

A Bridge Street shop owner keeps buying faster routers because the card machine fails, but never checks what is causing the failures
questions.explain: This treats the symptom again and again without finding the cause: trial and error.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

Three months after installing a booking system, the Carenage Water Taxi counts how many double bookings still happen
questions.explain: Checking the outcome against the original problem is evaluation and review, the last stage of the process.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

The Harbourview Grill in Kingston tries one ordering app, then another, then another, with no record of why each failed
questions.explain: With no analysis or review, each attempt is a guess and money is wasted: trial and error.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

The manager of the Seaside Pharmacy explains to the owner, with reasons, why an inventory app was chosen over a larger weekly order
questions.explain: A choice justified with reasons is a feature of a structured process.

questions.stem:
Which approach is this?

A farmer sprays whatever chemical the farm shop has in stock and never checks whether the damage has stopped
questions.explain: No definition, no comparison and no review: this is trial and error.

questions.stem: Stock keeps running out on cruise days at two Bay Street souvenir shops. Shop A's owner buys a new till at once. Shop B's owner defines the problem, finds its causes, compares three options, chooses one with reasons, installs it and checks the results. Why is Shop B's approach called a problem-solving process?
options: It required Shop B's owner to write a computer program.
It started by buying the best technology available.
It follows an ordered set of stages, from understanding the problem to checking that the chosen solution worked.
It produces one correct answer, like a mathematics problem.

questions.stem:
Each phrase comes from a problem statement written for a business or person. Sort it into the part of the statement it provides.

Which part of the problem statement is this?

Ms. Ollivierre's tomato and sweet pepper crops in Mesopotamia
questions.explain: This names who and what is affected.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

whitefly damage has reduced the harvest by one third
questions.explain: This describes how the crops are affected, with a measurement.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

she will lose her two restaurant contracts and her main income
questions.explain: This is what happens if nothing is done: the consequence.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

cruise passengers booked with San Pedro Water Taxi
questions.explain: These are the people affected.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

boats are double-booked, leaving about five groups a week waiting at the pier
questions.explain: This is how they are affected.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

the company will lose customers to competitors and receive poor reviews
questions.explain: This is the consequence of leaving the problem unsolved.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

students in the San Fernando homework club
questions.explain: This identifies who is affected.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

the shared laptops take 15 minutes to start, cutting study time
questions.explain: This explains how the students are affected.

questions.stem:
Which part of the problem statement is this?

students will miss assignment deadlines and their grades may fall
questions.explain: This is the consequence if nothing changes.

questions.stem: Ms. Ollivierre records which plants are infested each week, notices that the worst damage is next to a patch of weeds, and lists her budget limit and the restaurants' requirement for low-residue produce. Which stage of the problem-solving process is she carrying out?

The East End Bakery loses customer cake orders written on scraps of paper. The owner has a budget of US$600 and is comparing a shared spreadsheet, an online order app and a custom-built system. Use a weighted scoring matrix and strong justification to help her choose.

Cost has a weight of 3. The shared spreadsheet scores 5 out of 5 for cost. What is its weighted score for cost?
questions.explain: Weighted score = weight × score, so 3 × 5 = 15. Adding the weight and score (8) is a common slip.

questions.stem: The weighted totals are: shared spreadsheet 38, custom-built system 31, online order app 44. Which option does the matrix select?
options: The custom-built system, because custom is always best
The online order app, because it has the highest weighted total
The shared spreadsheet, because it is the cheapest
questions.explain: The option with the highest weighted total gives the best overall balance across the criteria, so the app is selected.

questions.stem: Which of these is the STRONGEST justification for choosing the online order app?
options: The app is the best choice because it is modern.
The app is the best choice because it is cheap.
Unlike the spreadsheet, the app sends every order to one list so none are lost, and unlike the custom system it fits the US$600 budget.
questions.explain: A strong justification links the choice to the cause (lost paper orders), the constraint (budget) and compares it with each alternative.

questions.stem: The owner's nephew says, "Pick the spreadsheet because it is free." What is wrong with this as a justification?
options: It mentions cost, which is never a criterion
Nothing: the cheapest option is always optimal
It gives one reason only and does not compare the options against the requirements
questions.explain: Cost is a valid criterion, but one reason with no comparison is weak. The spreadsheet scored lower overall because it does not stop orders being missed.

questions.stem: A weakness of the app is that the two counter staff need training. What should a strong justification do with this weakness?
options: Admit it and explain how it will be managed, such as a short training session before launch
Hide it so the choice looks better
questions.explain: Admitting a weakness and saying how it will be managed makes a justification more convincing.

questions.stem:
You are a student volunteer helping the farmer Mr. Desmond Brooks, who grows callaloo and cabbage near Christiana, Jamaica. Caterpillars are eating his crop. Guide him through the problem-solving process.

Mr. Brooks says, "Just tell me which poison to buy." What do you do first?
options: Help him write a problem statement: who and what is affected, how, and what happens if nothing is done.
Recommend the strongest pesticide in the farm shop straight away.

questions.stem: The statement is agreed: caterpillars have destroyed about 40% of his cabbage in a month, and if this continues he will lose his market income. What next?
options: Order insect netting online now, because netting always works.
Analyse: check when and where damage occurs, identify the caterpillar, and list his budget and time limits.

questions.stem: You find that damage is worst after moths are seen at dusk, and his budget is small. You list hand-picking and a biological spray, netting, and chemical spray. How do you choose?
options: Evaluate each option against cost, effectiveness, time and safety, then select the best and justify it by comparing it with the others.
Pick whichever option his neighbour used last year.

questions.stem: He chooses hand-picking plus a biological spray and puts it into action. A month later, what should happen?
options: Evaluate and review: compare the damage now with the 40% in the problem statement and decide whether to adjust.
Nothing; once a solution is implemented the process is finished.

questions.stem:
The Arima homework club has slow shared laptops. Name the stage for each action.

The club leader writes: "Students wait 15 minutes for laptops to start, losing study time; if this continues, they will miss deadlines."
questions.explain: A statement of who, how and consequence is the problem definition.

questions.stem: A volunteer discovers the laptops have nearly full hard drives and old start-up programs.
questions.explain: Finding the causes is analysis.

questions.stem: The leader lists three options: clean up the laptops, upgrade the memory, or buy new laptops, with pros and cons of each.
questions.explain: Listing and judging alternatives is identifying and evaluating possible solutions.

questions.stem: She chooses the clean-up plus memory upgrade because it fixes the cause for a fraction of the price of new laptops.
options: select and justify the optimal solution
questions.explain: Choosing with reasons compared to alternatives is selecting and justifying.

questions.stem: Volunteers remove unused programs and fit the new memory on Saturday.
questions.explain: Putting the solution into action is implementation.

questions.stem: A month later, she times start-up again and asks students whether they finish more work.
questions.explain: Measuring results against the original problem is evaluation and review.

questions.stem:
Students often confuse the first two stages with the last one. Sort each activity from the Seaside Pharmacy case into the correct stage.

Which stage does this activity belong to?

Writing that patients are turned away twice a week and will miss doses if this continues
questions.explain: Who, how and consequence: this is the problem definition.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Discovering that stock is only counted when a shelf is empty
questions.explain: This finds a cause, so it is analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Listing the budget limit and the need for the system to work offline during power cuts
questions.explain: Constraints and requirements are identified during analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Counting how many patients were turned away in the three months after the app was installed
questions.explain: Measuring results after implementation is evaluation and review.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Asking pharmacists whether the low-stock alerts are useful after using them
questions.explain: Feedback on a solution in use is part of evaluation and review.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Agreeing with the owner on exactly which problem is being solved
questions.explain: Agreeing the problem is part of defining it.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Breaking the problem into ordering, recording and supplier parts
questions.explain: Decomposing the problem is analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage does this activity belong to?

Deciding to return to analysis because shortages still happen with one supplier
questions.explain: A review that sends you back to an earlier stage is evaluation and review.

questions.stem:
Sixth Form students at Calabash Point Secondary are choosing a real problem to investigate as practice for Paper 03. Decide whether each choice is suitable or unsuitable. A suitable problem is real, can be investigated, has an information component and is bounded.

Is this a suitable problem to research?

Late-fee records at the Harbourside Community Library are kept on index cards and are often lost
questions.explain: Real, local, bounded to one process and full of information to collect: a suitable choice.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

Crime in the Caribbean
questions.explain: Far too broad. It is not bounded, and one student cannot investigate it properly.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

An aunt's hair salon in New Amsterdam double-books clients because appointments are written in a notebook
questions.explain: A real problem the student can observe, with a clear information component (appointments): suitable.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

"The school needs a new canteen building"
questions.explain: This names a solution, not a problem, and a building has little information component for an IT-based solution.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

The Frangipani Hill Academy sports club loses track of who has paid fees because payments are written on loose sheets
questions.explain: Bounded, real and information-based: a suitable choice.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

Climate change around the world
questions.explain: Global and unbounded. Choose one local business process instead.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

A business in Jamaica that the student has never visited and cannot contact
questions.explain: The student cannot gather facts, interview people or observe the problem, so it cannot be properly researched.

questions.stem:
Is this a suitable problem to research?

The Frigate Bay Taxi Association cannot see which drivers are free when a cruise ship docks
questions.explain: Real, local, bounded and about information (driver availability): suitable.

questions.stem: The Saba Dive Centre must replace its paper booking forms. Option X is free but does not prevent double bookings. Option Y costs US$40 a month, prevents double bookings and works on phones. Option Z is custom-built for US$12,000, far above the centre's budget. Which is the BEST justification for selecting Option Y as the optimal solution?
options: Z is the best because it is custom-built for the centre.
Unlike X, Y removes the cause of double bookings, and unlike Z it fits within the budget, so it best meets the requirements and constraints.
Y is the most modern technology available.
X is free, so it must be the optimal solution.

questions.stem:
Every problem is a gap between a present situation and a goal situation, and information is needed at every stage of closing it. Read each short Caribbean situation and choose the best answer.

Kezia, a Breadfruit Valley Secondary student, has failed her last two CAPE IT Unit 1 tests and wants a Grade II in the final exam. "She has failed her last two tests" describes her...
questions.explain: Where she is now is the present situation. The Grade II she wants is the goal situation; problem solving closes the gap between them.

questions.stem: For the same student, "a Grade II in the final CAPE IT Unit 1 exam" describes her...
questions.explain: Where she wants to be is the goal situation.

questions.stem: A farmer in Guyana whose bora bean plants are being eaten asks an agricultural officer to identify the insect and count the damaged plants per row. At which stage of problem solving is this information mainly used?
options: Select and justify the best solution
questions.explain: Identifying the pest and measuring the damage tells the farmer exactly what is wrong and how serious it is: defining and analysing the problem.

questions.stem: Three months after moving its shelves to make space for a cold drinks fridge, the Belmopan Minimart compares its new monthly sales with last year's figures. At which stage is this information used?
questions.explain: Checking new figures after the change shows whether the solution worked: evaluate and review.

questions.stem: A clinic in Port-au-Prince has enough nurses, beds and medicine, but patients wait for hours because staff cannot see which patients have appointments at which times. What does the clinic mainly lack?
questions.explain: The materials, people and equipment are there. What is missing is knowledge of who is booked when: an information resource.

questions.stem: A Noord family reads its electricity bills, sees that usage jumped after their old fridge began to leak, and uses those figures to decide to replace the fridge. Which step of "understand → inform → solve" is the decision to replace the fridge?
questions.explain: Using the information to choose a response is the solve step. Reading the bills helped them understand; the figures informed the decision.

questions.stem: Before her first evening lecture at Coralstone College, Nadia checks the campus map to find room B12. Which everyday research habit is this?
questions.explain: Locating a room is "find a place", one of the simple research habits we use every day.

questions.stem: Marcus, a student in Port of Spain, wants to buy his first used car with money saved from a summer job. Which item of information is MOST necessary to solve his problem?
options: The colours each model is available in
The year the car manufacturer was founded
Which cars his favourite celebrity drives
The total amount of money he has available, including insurance and registration costs

questions.stem:
Like the guava jelly exporter, many organisations think they are short of materials, people or equipment when they are really short of information. Sort each Caribbean situation by what is REALLY missing.

Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

A jelly exporter's buyers return from the markets with too little fruit, although many farmers have ripe guavas they would sell. The exporter does not know which farmers they are.
questions.explain: The guavas exist. The exporter does not know where to find them: an information gap.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

Farmers with ripe guavas let the fruit rot because they do not know the exporter wants to buy it.
questions.explain: The producers lack information about the buyer. An information gap on the other side.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

A San Pedro restaurant says it "cannot get" local fish, while fishermen land good catches at Oistins and Speightstown on days the restaurant does not know about.
questions.explain: The fish is there. The restaurant does not know which boats land where and when: an information gap.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

Parents on Saba miss free vaccination days because the dates are not announced, although the clinic has the vaccines in stock.
questions.explain: The vaccines are in stock. The missing piece is the dates: an information gap.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

After Hurricane Irma, two classrooms at a primary school in The Valley, Anguilla, have no roof.
questions.explain: The school needs roofing materials and builders: a physical resource gap.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

The only oven at the Sweet Hands Bakery in Salem has broken, and no spare parts are on the island.
questions.explain: Knowing more will not bake the bread. The bakery needs a working oven: a physical resource gap.

questions.stem:
Is the real gap in physical resources or in information?

A St. Kitts fishing co-operative knows exactly where the deep-water fish are, but its boats' engines are too small to reach them safely.
questions.explain: The co-operative has the information. It lacks bigger engines: a physical resource gap.

questions.stem:
Sort each problem into the syllabus category it BEST fits.

Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

A student must choose between two scholarship offers.
questions.explain: One person decides and lives with the result: personal.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

A Jan Thiel restaurant needs to cut its food waste costs.
questions.explain: A business trying to protect its profit: commercial.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

Researchers want to know why sargassum arrivals have increased.
questions.explain: Investigated through measurement and data: scientific.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

A community wants to reduce youth unemployment in its district.
questions.explain: It affects society and needs collective action: social.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

A family wants to lower its monthly electricity bill.
questions.explain: A household decision: personal.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

A car rental firm near Grantley Adams International Airport must decide how many vehicles to keep for the high season.
questions.explain: A trading business planning stock and demand: commercial.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

Scientists test whether a new crop variety survives drought in Guyana.
questions.explain: Controlled experiments and measurements: scientific.

questions.stem:
Is this a personal, commercial, scientific or social problem?

Flooding regularly blocks roads in a low-lying neighbourhood during rainy season.
questions.explain: A shared community and government problem: social.

questions.stem:
The Lagoon Water Taxi wants to launch an online booking system so tourists can book rides across the lagoon. Sort each item of information.

How important is this information to the booking solution?

The departure times and number of seats on each boat.
questions.explain: Without times and seats, no booking can be taken. Essential.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

The ticket price for each route.
questions.explain: Customers cannot pay and the business cannot charge without prices. Essential.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

Which hotels most customers stay at, so pick-up points can be suggested.
questions.explain: Useful for a better service, but bookings work without it. Desirable.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

Customer reviews from previous trips.
questions.explain: Helpful for marketing and improvement, but not needed to take a booking. Desirable.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

The history of how the lagoon was formed.
questions.explain: Interesting, but irrelevant to booking a ride. Extraneous.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

The owner's favourite cricket team.
questions.explain: No bearing on the problem at all. Extraneous.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

A staff member's assurance that "the boats are never full", given instead of actual seat counts.
questions.explain: It looks like capacity information but masks the missing seat figures, so it cannot guide bookings. Cosmetic.

questions.stem:
How important is this information to the booking solution?

A note that "tourists love us online", with no figures on how many people would actually book.
questions.explain: It sounds like demand information but masks the missing booking figures. Cosmetic.

questions.stem:
Each item of information is paired with a problem. Choose the category it belongs to FOR THAT PROBLEM.

The tide times for Prince Rupert Bay, Dominica, for a fisherman deciding when to launch his boat.
questions.explain: Launching safely depends on the tide. Essential.

questions.stem: The tide times for Prince Rupert Bay, for a student choosing a laptop.
questions.explain: Tides have nothing to do with choosing a laptop. Extraneous.

questions.stem: Customers' birthdays, for a Paramaribo bakery deciding how many loaves to bake tomorrow.
questions.explain: Birthdays do not predict daily bread demand. Extraneous for this problem.

questions.stem: Customers' birthdays, for the same bakery planning a birthday-cake promotion.
questions.explain: Now the promotion cannot work without them. Essential.

questions.stem: A manager's statement that "dengue is under control", sent to the health department without any case figures.
questions.explain: It sounds like useful information but masks the missing case numbers, so it cannot guide a decision. Cosmetic.

questions.stem: Last year's exam results, for a teacher planning revision for this year's CAPE IT class.
questions.explain: They help target weak areas, but revision can be planned without them. Desirable.

questions.stem: The St. Vincent Tours company is building a website to sell island tours. Which of the following is BEST described as cosmetic information for this problem?
options: The price and duration of each tour
The number of goats on a neighbouring island
A partner's assurance that "cruise passengers will definitely buy online", with no figures on how many actually book tours online

questions.stem:
Use common sense first, then the validity questions. For each Caribbean situation, choose the best answer.

A flyer on Broad Street claims that a new app "doubles your phone's battery life overnight". Before checking anything else, what is the sensible first reaction?
options: Accept it, because it is printed
Accept it, because the app is free
Take it with a pinch of salt: it fails common sense
questions.explain: An unbelievable claim fails the common-sense test first. Then check it against the concrete criteria.

questions.stem: A tour company's web page about diving off Saba lists only the good points of its own trips and none of the risks or costs.
questions.explain: The source favours a particular point (its own trips): it is subjective, so bias is the question it fails.

questions.stem: A report on school attendance in Belize is full of typing errors, and its total does not match its own table.
questions.explain: Is it correct as presented, without typographical errors? No: accuracy fails.

questions.stem: A guide to "Caribbean eating habits" treats the whole region as one, and a health team wants to use it for a campaign in one Curaçao neighbourhood.
questions.explain: The guide is generalised, not specific to the community in the problem: a cultural context question.

questions.stem: A budget guide for Flamboyant Heights College students leaves out accommodation costs and is written in jargon most students cannot follow.
questions.explain: Vital pieces are missing and it is hard to understand: both are completeness questions.

questions.stem: A list of mobile data prices on the island was last checked in 2017, and a student wants to use it to compare plans today.
questions.explain: How current is it? Not current enough for today's prices: currency fails.

questions.stem: A Barbados student researching how to reduce flooding in Bridgetown finds a detailed, well-referenced report written in 2024 by engineers about flood control in the Netherlands, where many areas lie below sea level and rivers are the main flood source. Which criterion gives the STRONGEST reason to be cautious about using it directly?

A Sandbox Tree College student researching how rising sea temperatures affect coral near Tobago sorts the publications she has found by their level of scholarship.

Who is the intended audience?

A refereed marine biology journal article with its methods, data tables and a reference list.
questions.explain: Written for specialists, refereed and in depth: scholarly.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

A local newspaper feature in which divers describe the bleaching they have seen.
questions.explain: Newspapers are written for the public: general audience.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

An academic book from a university press that sends manuscripts to outside experts.
questions.explain: A reputable academic publisher with expert review: scholarly.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

A tourism magazine article titled "Tobago's ten best dive sites".
questions.explain: Written to interest tourists, not to analyse coral science: general audience.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

A conference paper presented to coral reef scientists, with a full bibliography.
questions.explain: Prepared for specialists and fully referenced: scholarly.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

A popular science website that sums up a study in simple words, with no references.
questions.explain: Easier to understand, but it lacks in-depth analysis: general audience.

questions.stem:
Who is the intended audience?

A blog post by a Saba dive shop owner about what he saw on Sunday's dive.
questions.explain: A personal account for the public: general audience, and un-refereed.

questions.stem:
Each item gives a research topic and a source. Decide whether the source is fit for THAT research.

Topic: which laptops Palmetto Point Secondary should buy this year. Source: a Computer Science book on hardware published in 1980.
options: Likely outdated: reject for this research
questions.explain: Computing has changed completely since 1980, so the book is outdated for a purchase today.

questions.stem: Topic: the history of computing in Caribbean schools. Source: the same 1980 hardware book.
questions.explain: For historical research, an old book can be extremely relevant evidence of its time.

questions.stem: Topic: how doctors treated yellow fever in the early twentieth century. Source: a Medicine book published in 1925.
questions.explain: The research is historical, so a 1925 book is a valuable source, even though it is outdated for treating patients today.

questions.stem: Topic: comparing views on the current telecommunications regulatory framework in Jamaica. Source: opinion columns by an operator, a consumer group and a commentator.
options: Accept: this research must rely on subjective views
questions.explain: Comparing views requires subjective publications. Label each view and balance them.

questions.stem: Topic: whether well water in Belmopan is safe to drink. Source: a resident's strong opinion that "it tastes fine".
options: Rely on objective information, such as laboratory test results
Accept the opinion as the main evidence
questions.explain: Water safety is an empirical question, so it needs objective measurements, not opinions.

questions.stem: Topic: whether a new treatment for coral disease works near Saba. Source: a refereed article reporting the measured results of a controlled experiment.
options: Reject: scientific articles are too technical
Accept: an empirical question answered with objective evidence
questions.explain: An empirical scientific question should rely primarily on objective, refereed results like these.

questions.stem: Kayla, a CAPE IT student in Kingston, is researching how residents, mobile operators and consumer groups view the current telecommunications regulatory framework. A friend tells her to reject every opinion piece she has found because it is subjective. Which response is BEST?
options: Replace them with a Computer Science textbook from 1980, because textbooks are objective.
Reject them all: subjective information must always be rejected.
Keep only the opinion piece she agrees with, because it is the most convincing.
Keep the opinion pieces: research comparing views must rely on subjective publications, so she should label each view and balance them.

questions.stem:
A CAPE IT student in Warrens is collecting web pages on hurricane-resistant roofing. Sort each page by who is most likely to have published it.

Who is hosting this page?

www.windloadstudies.edu/reports/roofs-2025
questions.explain: .edu marks an academic organisation.

questions.stem:
Who is hosting this page?

www.coastalengineering.ac.uk/research/hurricanes
questions.explain: .ac before a country code (.uk) marks an academic organisation.

questions.stem:
Who is hosting this page?

www.roofstrongsupplies.com/hurricane-straps
questions.explain: .com and a product page: a commercial organisation that wants to sell.

questions.stem:
Who is hosting this page?

www.islandhardware.lc/specials
questions.explain: A business using St. Lucia's country code, with a "specials" page: commercial.

questions.stem:
Who is hosting this page?

www.freepages-host.com/~kevinroofs/tips.html
questions.explain: A tilde and a personal name on a free hosting site: a private individual.

questions.stem:
Who is hosting this page?

www.windloadstudies.edu/~mbrown/my-roof-tips.html
questions.explain: The host is academic, but the tilde shows a personal page published by an individual, which the university may not have checked.

questions.stem: Marlon, a CAPE IT student in Grand Anse, has two undated web pages on making drinking water safe after a storm. Page X is linked from the regional public health agency's website and from a university library guide. Page Y is linked only from a few anonymous forums. Why does this make Page X more acceptable?
options: Reliable pages link to it, and an authoritative publisher is unlikely to undermine its authority by linking to unreliable pages.
Search engines rank pages by the number of links, so Page X must be correct.
Any page that is linked to has been refereed.
Links show that Page X has been updated recently.

questions.stem:
You are an intern at an environmental consultancy in Bridgetown. Your manager asks you to gather information for a report to beach-front hotels on how to deal with sargassum seaweed. Make good information decisions.

Before searching, your manager asks what you will gather first. What do you say?
options: First list the information we NEED (essential): arrival forecasts, volumes, removal methods and costs, and health guidance. Then search for it.
Collect everything online about seaweed and sort it out later.

questions.stem: You find a viral video claiming that sargassum "can be burned safely on the beach". It has 2 million views but no named expert. What do you do?
options: Treat it as un-refereed and unverified; check health guidance and refereed research before using any of it.
Include it in the report because so many people have watched it.

questions.stem: You find a refereed study from 2012 and a Caribbean government advisory from this year that partly disagree on the best removal method. Which do you rely on?
options: Use both: note the study's age, prefer the current regional advisory for local practice, and explain the difference to the hotels.
Use only the 2012 study, because refereed sources are always right.

questions.stem: Your draft report is ready. A colleague suggests adding a two-page history of the Sargasso Sea's discovery and a line saying "hotels report that sargassum is no longer a serious problem", although no hotel figures were collected. What do you do?
options: Leave out the history as extraneous; treat the "no longer a serious problem" line as cosmetic, because it hides missing hotel figures, so collect the figures or remove it.
Add both: the history fills pages and the line sounds reassuring.

questions.stem: Jada, a CAPE IT student in Scarborough, Tobago, is researching the health effects of rotting sargassum. She finds a refereed journal article and a popular blog post on the same topic. Which of the following BEST explains why the journal article is generally considered more reliable?
options: It has been evaluated by independent experts in the field before publication.
It is always more up to date than a blog post.
It has been read and shared by more people.
It is printed on paper rather than published online.

questions.stem:
Windward Customs Brokers in Roseau is having its declarations software built with the Waterfall model. Sort each thing that happens on the project as an advantage or a disadvantage of Waterfall.

Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

Before work starts, the developer gives the brokers a fixed price and a delivery date that both sides can rely on.
questions.explain: Detailed up-front planning makes cost and time easy to estimate, which suits a fixed-price contract.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

A new programmer joins halfway through and gets up to speed by reading the signed-off design document.
questions.explain: Thorough documentation at every stage helps staff changes and later maintenance.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

The manager checks progress each month against clear milestones: analysis signed off, design signed off, coding complete.
questions.explain: Clear stages and deliverables make Waterfall simple to manage and progress easy to measure.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

The brokers are busy with cruise season and only need to attend meetings at the start and the end.
questions.explain: Waterfall needs little customer time during the project, an advantage when users are not available.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

In month five the owner asks for a new report, but the design is already signed off, so two stages must be redone.
questions.explain: Waterfall is inflexible: changes after sign-off are costly because earlier stages must be repeated.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

Staff see working screens for the first time only in month eight, near the end of the project.
questions.explain: Working software appears late in Waterfall, so users cannot react to it early.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

During final testing, the team finds that a field required by Customs was missed during analysis.
questions.explain: Testing comes late, so requirement errors surface late, when they are expensive to fix.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage of Waterfall?

At handover the owner admits he did not really know what he needed at the start, and the system misses some needs.
questions.explain: Waterfall assumes users know all their requirements at the start; if they do not, the whole investment is at risk.

questions.stem: Four organisations in Trinidad and Tobago each want new software and are asking a Port of Spain developer which model to follow. For which project would the Waterfall model be MOST appropriate?
options: Leeward Ferries’ ticket-pricing module, built to a fixed government fare formula, under a fixed-price contract that requires full documentation
A Frederick Street tourism kiosk whose client says, "I will know what I want when I see it"
A San Fernando start-up’s website that must go live in two weeks and then grow feature by feature
A Chaguaramas youth group’s social app, whose features will be decided by watching how early users react

questions.stem:
Each event happened on a Caribbean prototyping project. Decide what each one shows.

At Harbour Gems Jewellers, the owner sees a clickable catalogue on Friday and asks why it cannot go live with real stock on Monday.
options: Advantage: lower risk of building the wrong system
Disadvantage: users mistake the prototype for the finished system
questions.explain: The prototype has no stock database or security behind it. Users thinking it is finished is a classic prototyping disadvantage.

questions.stem: Volunteers for the Island Relief Network try a registration screen and immediately notice there is no field for the number of children in a household.
options: Disadvantage: hard to plan and cost
Advantage: missing functions are spotted early
questions.explain: Users evaluating a working model find missing functions early, before the full system is built.

questions.stem: After eleven rounds of changes, the developer of the Bright Smile Dental Clinic booking system finds the code so tangled that a small fix breaks two other screens.
options: Disadvantage: poorly structured code that is hard to maintain
questions.explain: Constant quick changes to an evolutionary prototype can leave the code poorly structured and hard to maintain.

questions.stem: St. Kitts tourism board could not describe its kiosk, but after trying a model for one week it produced a clear list of the six screens it needs.
options: Disadvantage: needs a lot of user time
Disadvantage: users may stop giving feedback
questions.explain: "I will know it when I see it" became a concrete list: clarifying requirements is the main advantage of prototyping.

questions.stem: Sea Breeze Marina asks how many weeks the berth-booking prototype will take. The developer honestly cannot say how many feedback cycles will be needed.
options: Disadvantage: difficult to plan and cost
questions.explain: No one knows in advance how many build-evaluate-refine cycles are needed, so prototyping is hard to plan and cost.

questions.stem: A Bridgetown insurer’s busy claims staff miss three feedback sessions in a row during the tourist season.
options: Disadvantage: prototyping needs a lot of user time
questions.explain: Prototyping depends on users trying each version; busy users who stop giving feedback stall the process.

questions.stem:
Each event comes from a Caribbean project. Does it show incremental development (adding a new working part) or iterative development (repeating the cycle to refine what already exists)?

Adding a part or refining by repeating?

Harbour Water Taxi Co-operative’s system goes live with seat booking; two months later online card payment is added.
questions.explain: A new working part (payment) is delivered on top of what exists: incremental.

questions.stem:
Adding a part or refining by repeating?

The Caribbean Islands Credit Union releases transfers as a new section of its app, after balances went live in June.
questions.explain: Transfers are a new increment adding functionality: incremental.

questions.stem:
Adding a part or refining by repeating?

The Guyana licensing system delivers vehicle licences first; business licences follow as a separate module.
questions.explain: Delivering the system module by module is incremental development.

questions.stem:
Adding a part or refining by repeating?

After members complain the balance screen is slow, the credit union team redesigns and rebuilds that same screen in the next cycle.
questions.explain: Revisiting and improving an existing part through another cycle is iterative.

questions.stem:
Adding a part or refining by repeating?

The water taxi team repeats analysis, design, build and review on the booking screen three times, improving it each time from passenger feedback.
questions.explain: Repeating the whole cycle to refine the same product is iterative development.

questions.stem:
Adding a part or refining by repeating?

A Bayleaf Hill Secondary club app’s sign-up form is reworked in a second cycle because students found the layout confusing.
questions.explain: The same form is refined in a repeated cycle: iterative.

questions.stem:
Each event happened on a Caribbean project using iterative/incremental development or Agile. Decide which advantage or disadvantage it shows.

Members of the Caribbean Islands Credit Union can check balances on the app in month two, long before transfers and loans are ready.
options: Incremental advantage: early delivery of core functions
Agile disadvantage: needs a committed customer representative
questions.explain: The core increment is in use early, so the credit union benefits sooner: the key incremental advantage.

questions.stem: When the loans module of the credit union app is added, it uses a different member-number format from the balances module and the two will not link.
options: Incremental disadvantage: later increments do not integrate cleanly
Incremental advantage: easier to test small parts
questions.explain: Later increments that do not fit earlier ones are a recognised incremental disadvantage, which is why good up-front design is needed.

questions.stem: A bug in the payment increment of the Harbour Water Taxi system is found and fixed in one afternoon because only that small part changed.
options: Incremental disadvantage: total cost can be higher
Incremental advantage: small increments are easier to test and debug
questions.explain: Testing a small increment is easier than testing a whole system at once.

questions.stem: The Island Hop Tours owner moves WhatsApp booking to the top of the backlog, and it is working two weeks later.
options: Agile advantage: changes are built into the next iteration at low cost
Incremental disadvantage: hard to define the full scope
questions.explain: Agile welcomes change; a new priority is simply built in the next sprint.

questions.stem: The Daily Island Deals website asks for a final price for its Agile project, but the developer can only quote per sprint because the scope keeps changing.
options: Agile disadvantage: final cost and date are hard to predict
questions.explain: Because scope changes, the total cost of an Agile project is hard to predict, so it suits fixed-price contracts poorly.

questions.stem: The manager acting as product owner for a Barbados hotel app is called away for a month, and the team cannot get priorities approved.
options: Agile disadvantage: needs a committed customer representative
Incremental advantage: feedback improves the next iteration
questions.explain: Agile depends on an available customer representative; without one the process breaks down.

questions.stem: A year after the tour app launches, a new developer struggles to maintain it because only short notes were ever written.
options: Agile disadvantage: light documentation makes maintenance and handover harder
questions.explain: Agile’s "just enough" documentation can make maintenance and handover to new staff difficult.

questions.stem: The owner of the Island Hop Tours in Montego Bay hears four claims about the Agile approach her developers want to use for her excursion app. Which claim about Agile software development is ACCURATE?
options: The team will value working software more than comprehensive documentation, but will still document where it adds value
She will receive the complete app only at the end of the project
Agile works best if she stays away from the developers until the end
The team will do no planning, so it can respond to change

questions.stem:
Sort each statement to the model it describes BEST.

Which model is this?

Requirements are frozen after analysis and signed off.
questions.explain: Freezing requirements early is the defining feature of Waterfall.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

Users try a working model and say, "Move that button, add a search box."
questions.explain: Users evaluating a model to refine requirements is prototyping.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

The core module goes live first; payments are added in the next release.
questions.explain: Delivering in working parts that add functionality is incremental development.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

A product owner reprioritises the backlog before every two-week sprint.
questions.explain: Product owners, backlogs and sprints are Agile practices.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

Testing begins only after all the code is written.
questions.explain: Late testing of the whole system is a feature (and weakness) of Waterfall.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

A quick model is built just to find out what users want, then discarded.
questions.explain: This is a throwaway prototype.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

The team holds a brief stand-up meeting every morning.
questions.explain: Daily stand-ups are a typical Agile practice.

questions.stem:
Which model is this?

Each cycle revisits the design and improves what was built before.
questions.explain: Repeating and refining through cycles is iterative development.

questions.stem:
For each project, choose the most suitable development model.

A Barbados bank must replace its interest-calculation engine. The rules are set by regulation and every stage must be documented for auditors.
questions.explain: Stable, regulated requirements and heavy documentation needs point to Waterfall.

questions.stem: A Saba dive shop owner wants a booking website but says, "Show me something and I will tell you what I like."
questions.explain: Vague requirements that become clear on seeing a model: prototyping.

questions.stem: A Guyana ministry needs a large licensing system. Vehicle licences are urgent; business and firearm licences can follow later.
questions.explain: The urgent core can be delivered first and other modules added later: incremental.

questions.stem: A Curaçao music-streaming start-up changes priorities every month based on user data. The founder works alongside the developers daily.
questions.explain: Constant change plus a customer working daily with the team: Agile.

questions.stem: A Dominica school wants a simple exam-mark system. Requirements are clear, small and unlikely to change; the teacher has little time for meetings.
questions.explain: Clear, stable requirements and little user time favour Waterfall.

questions.stem: An Anguillan insurer’s staff cannot agree what the claims screens should look like, but once they agree, the system must be built under a fixed-price contract with full documentation for the regulator.
questions.explain: Models can be combined: a throwaway prototype settles the unclear screens, then plan-driven Waterfall builds the documented, fixed-price system.

questions.stem:
You are a junior developer advising the Harbour Bites restaurant group, which has restaurants in Kingston and Montego Bay. Choose wisely.

The owner, Mr. Richardson, wants an online ordering app. He says: "I don't really know what it should look like. I'll know when I see it. And I need customers ordering before carnival season in April." Which approach do you propose first?
options: Write a complete, signed-off requirements specification and then follow Waterfall.
Build a quick prototype of the ordering screens for him and some customers to try.

questions.stem: The prototype works well. Customers love the menu screen. Mr. Richardson now wants ordering, card payment, delivery tracking and a loyalty scheme, but April is close. How do you plan the build?
options: Build all four features together and release everything at once.
Deliver in increments: menu and ordering before April, then payment, then tracking and loyalty.

questions.stem: After launch, Mr. Richardson is in the office every day and keeps changing priorities as customer feedback arrives. How should the team continue?
options: Work in two-week Agile iterations, with Mr. Richardson as product owner reprioritising the backlog.
Freeze all remaining requirements now and refuse further changes until the end.

questions.stem: Statia Fuel Terminal needs control software for a fuel pump safety system. Requirements are fully defined by an international safety standard and the regulator must approve the design before any code is written. Which is the BEST justification for using the Waterfall model?
options: The requirements are stable and fully defined, and Waterfall requires the design to be completed and approved before development, matching the regulator’s demand
Agile delivers working software quickly, which is important for safety systems
Waterfall lets users test an early prototype of the pump controls
Waterfall is the oldest model, so it is the most reliable

questions.stem:
Each statement refers to a model named in brackets. Sort it as an advantage or a disadvantage of that model.

Advantage or disadvantage?

(Waterfall) Cost and time are easy to estimate at the start.
questions.explain: Up-front planning makes Waterfall predictable, an advantage for fixed budgets.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Waterfall) Users see working software only near the end.
questions.explain: Late visibility means errors in requirements are found late.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Prototyping) Users may mistake the prototype for the finished system.
questions.explain: Unrealistic expectations are a known disadvantage of prototyping.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Prototyping) Vague requirements become clear when users try a model.
questions.explain: Clarifying requirements is the main advantage of prototyping.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Incremental) The core system is delivered and used early.
questions.explain: Early delivery of core functions is the key advantage of incremental development.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Incremental) Later increments may not integrate cleanly with earlier ones.
questions.explain: Integration problems are a common disadvantage.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Agile) The final cost and end date are hard to predict.
questions.explain: Because scope changes, Agile is hard to cost in advance.

questions.stem:
Advantage or disadvantage?

(Agile) Changes in requirements can be added in the next iteration.
questions.explain: Flexibility to change is Agile’s chief advantage.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Bayside Bakery project in New Amsterdam is described below using the nine phases from the class slides. For each activity, choose where it sits in the six CAPE syllabus stages (your exam framework).

The analyst interviews the bakers and the owner about the order book and writes a System Proposal stating the problem, objectives, terms of reference, constraints and expected benefits (problem definition).
questions.explain: Problem definition is the opening part of the syllabus feasibility study stage.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: After the "go" decision, a Project Management Plan and a Gantt chart are drawn up (project planning).
options: Between the feasibility study and analysis
questions.explain: Project planning follows the go/no-go decision of the feasibility study and leads into analysis; the plan then controls every later stage.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The Requirements Specification lists what the system must do and how fast and securely it must do it (analysis).
questions.explain: Specifying requirements is the analysis stage in both models.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Testers run black box and regression tests and write the Test Report (testing).
questions.explain: In the syllabus six, testing is part of development.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Order records are converted, staff are trained and the new system goes live (implementation).
questions.explain: Install, convert, train and change over: implementation in both models.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: A year after go-live, a developer fixes a fault and adds a gluten-free option, recorded in a Maintenance Report (evaluation and maintenance).
questions.explain: Evaluation and maintenance correspond to the syllabus review stage.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Cornerstone Code in Belize City is building a fee-payment system for a secondary school. A trainee has written notes on how different people approached the job. Sort each note: is it a software engineering practice, or an informal "just code it" approach?

Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

The team writes down and agrees the school's requirements with the bursar before any code is written.
questions.explain: Formal, agreed requirements are a core software engineering practice.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

Every programmer follows the company coding standards: meaningful variable names, comments and separate modules.
questions.explain: Coding standards make the code maintainable: software engineering.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

Each change is saved in version control so that an earlier working version can be restored.
questions.explain: Version control is a disciplined engineering practice.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

Testers follow a test plan with normal, boundary and erroneous fee amounts and record the actual results.
questions.explain: Planned testing against a test plan is software engineering.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

A technical manual is written so that another developer can maintain the system next year.
questions.explain: Documentation for maintenance is part of the engineering discipline.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

A student programmer starts typing code on her laptop the same day she hears about the project.
questions.explain: Coding with no requirements or design is trial and error.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

The program is "tested" by trying a few payments to see whether anything crashes.
questions.explain: Random checks with no planned data or expected results are not systematic testing.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Software engineering practice or informal trial and error?

Nobody records why the code was written that way, so only the original programmer can fix it.
questions.explain: Undocumented code makes the organisation depend on one person: the opposite of engineering.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The Cornerstone Code in Bridgetown is building a school fee-payment system. Instead of letting one programmer "just code it", the firm documents requirements, designs the database, tests against a test plan and writes manuals. Which statement BEST describes software engineering, the approach the firm is using?
options: Repairing computer hardware so that software can run correctly.
Choosing which software package an organisation should buy.
Writing program code in a high-level programming language.
The application of a systematic, disciplined approach to developing, operating and maintaining software.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Carenage Water Taxi company is considering an online ticketing system. Sort each finding from its feasibility study into the type of feasibility it concerns.

Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

The ticket booth has no Internet connection and the nearest fibre line is 200 metres away.
questions.explain: Whether existing technology can handle it is technical feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

No current employee knows how to configure a payment gateway.
questions.explain: Whether existing staff can handle the technology is technical feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

The system will cost about USD 18,000 but should save USD 9,000 a year in cash-handling costs.
questions.explain: Do benefits justify cost? A cost/benefit comparison is economic feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

Online sales are expected to increase bookings from cruise passengers.
questions.explain: A tangible benefit counted in the cost/benefit analysis: economic.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

Tickets would still be checked at the boarding gate exactly as now, so the boarding procedure barely changes.
questions.explain: Does it fit existing procedures? That is operational feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

The new process removes the need to count cash at the end of each shift, which fits how managers already close the day.
questions.explain: Fit with existing business procedures is operational feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

Long-serving boat captains dislike using smartphones and may refuse to scan e-tickets.
questions.explain: Can users adapt? Attitudes and resistance to change are social/behavioural feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

Booth staff worry that online tickets will cost them their jobs.
questions.explain: Fear of job losses affects whether users will adapt: social/behavioural.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

The owners want it live before the cruise season starts in eleven weeks.
questions.explain: Can it meet the deadline? That is time (schedule) feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which type of feasibility does this finding address?

The developer estimates fourteen weeks for the full build and testing.
questions.explain: Comparing time needed with time available is time feasibility.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Seaview Medical Centre is replacing its paper appointment diaries. The practice manager has a pile of notes. Decide whether each belongs in the documents of the feasibility study stage, the system proposal or feasibility report (should we do it?), or in the project management plan (after the "go" decision: how, who and when?).

Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Doctors are double-booked because receptionists keep three separate paper diaries.
questions.explain: The problem definition is set out in the system proposal.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Option 1: buy a clinic package. Option 2: commission a custom system.
questions.explain: Alternative solutions are compared in the feasibility report.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Set-up will cost about USD 12,000 and save about 15 receptionist hours a week.
questions.explain: Cost/benefit findings (economic feasibility) belong in the feasibility report.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Recommendation: buy the package, because it is cheaper and can be live sooner.
questions.explain: A justified go/no-go recommendation ends the feasibility report.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Design: 4 weeks; development: 8 weeks; implementation: 3 weeks.
questions.explain: Timescales for each remaining stage are in the project plan.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Milestone: the test plan must be approved before coding ends.
questions.explain: Milestones are part of the project plan.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

The IT contractor builds the database; the practice manager signs off the screen layouts.
questions.explain: Responsibilities are set out in the project plan.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Proposal/feasibility report or project plan?

Risk: the contractor may be away in August, so a backup developer is named.
questions.explain: Risks and how they will be handled are in the project plan.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The manager of the Harbour Gems Jewellers asks for a document showing each task in the new sales-system project, who is responsible for it, its start and finish dates, and the budget allocated. Which deliverable is she asking for?

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Here are lines from the requirements specification for the Seaview Medical Centre appointment system. Sort each requirement.

Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

The system books an appointment with a chosen doctor at a chosen time.
questions.explain: Booking is an action the system performs: functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

The system sends an SMS reminder to the patient the day before the appointment.
questions.explain: Sending a reminder is something the system does: functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

The system prints a daily appointment list for each doctor.
questions.explain: Producing an output is a function: functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

The system cancels a booking and frees the slot for another patient.
questions.explain: Cancelling is an action: functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

Only clinic staff with a password can view patient details.
questions.explain: A security quality: non-functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

A new receptionist can book an appointment after ten minutes of training.
questions.explain: A usability quality: non-functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

A booking is confirmed within five seconds, even at the busy Monday-morning peak.
questions.explain: A performance quality: non-functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Functional (what it does) or non-functional (a quality it must have)?

Online booking is available 24 hours a day, including weekends.
questions.explain: An availability quality: non-functional.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The design team for the Harbour Ferry Line booking system has produced the items below. Decide whether each is part of the logical design, the physical design or a prototype.

Logical design, physical design or prototype?

Each booking must link one passenger to one sailing.
questions.explain: A statement about the data needed, with no technology chosen: logical design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

The system needs to record each passenger's name, phone number and nationality.
questions.explain: What data is needed, not how it is stored: logical design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

A process "check seats available" takes a sailing and returns the number of free seats.
questions.explain: A process described without any language or platform: logical design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

The Bookings table has a six-character text field, BookingID, as its primary key.
questions.explain: Exact field names and data types are the blueprint: physical design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

The system will be a web app on a cloud server, written in Java.
questions.explain: Platform and programming language are physical design decisions.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

The booking form uses a drop-down list for sailing times and a date picker.
questions.explain: The actual form layout is part of the physical design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

Ticket clerks click through a model of the booking screens and ask for a larger "Pay" button.
questions.explain: Users inspecting a working model before development: prototype.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Logical design, physical design or prototype?

A mock-up of the boarding pass screen is shown to the operations manager for approval before coding.
questions.explain: A model shown to the customer before development: prototype.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Harbour View Guesthouse booking system accepts stays of 1 to 14 nights, entered as a whole number. You are completing the test plan. Classify each test value.

What type of test data is this?

A guest books 5 nights.
questions.explain: 5 is a typical valid value: normal data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

A cruise-ship crew member books 10 nights.
questions.explain: 10 is valid and not at an edge: normal data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

A guest books 1 night.
questions.explain: 1 is the lowest valid value: boundary data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

A guest books 14 nights.
questions.explain: 14 is the highest valid value: boundary data.
