questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

A guest tries to book 15 nights.
questions.explain: 15 is just outside the range and should be rejected: erroneous data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

The receptionist enters 0 nights by mistake.
questions.explain: 0 is outside the valid range, so it is erroneous, not boundary.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

The receptionist types "two" instead of a number.
questions.explain: Wrong data type: erroneous data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
What type of test data is this?

The receptionist enters -3 nights.
questions.explain: A negative value is invalid: erroneous data.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The Saba Dive Centre is developing a booking system. Choose the SDLC stage in which each activity takes place.

The owner is told the project would cost more than three years of the savings it brings, and is advised not to proceed.
questions.explain: Deciding whether the project is worth it is the feasibility study (economic feasibility).

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: An analyst interviews dive instructors to find out why bookings are lost.
questions.explain: Investigating the current system in detail is analysis.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Screen layouts for the booking form are drawn and the database tables are specified.
questions.explain: Deciding how the system will look and store data is design.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Programmers enter a booking for 0 divers to check that it is rejected.
questions.explain: Carrying out tests from the test plan happens during development.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Last year's bookings are transferred into the new database and staff attend a training session.
questions.explain: Data conversion and training are part of implementation.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Six months after go-live, the owner checks whether lost bookings have fallen as the objectives promised.
questions.explain: Evaluating the system against its objectives is the review stage.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
The King Street Jewellers in Kingston is checking its new sales system. Decide whether each check is verification (are we building the product right?) or validation (are we building the right product?).

Verification or validation?

Checking that the turnover tax on each sale is calculated exactly as the design specification states.
questions.explain: Checking against the specification: verification.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Verification or validation?

A code review confirms the receipt module follows the agreed design and coding standards.
questions.explain: Is it built right? Verification.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Verification or validation?

Black box tests show every report matches the expected results in the test plan.
questions.explain: Matching the planned expected results: verification.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Verification or validation?

The owner tries the system and finds it cannot record layaway payments, which the shop relies on.
questions.explain: Is it the right product for the business? Validation.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Verification or validation?

Sales staff confirm they can now serve cruise passengers faster, as the system proposal promised.
questions.explain: Checking against the real need in the proposal: validation.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Verification or validation?

The manager checks that the stock report shows the information she actually needs to reorder.
questions.explain: Does it meet the user's real need? Validation.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Harbour Gems Jewellers' new sales system passes every test in its test plan: totals, receipts and reports all match the design specification. In acceptance testing, however, staff find it cannot record layaway payments, which many customers use. Which statement BEST describes the situation?
options: The system has failed regression testing.
The system has been verified but not validated.
The system has failed white box testing of its code.
The system has been validated but not verified.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
You are assembling the documentation for the University Book Corner's new sales system. Decide which manual each item belongs in.

Which manual should contain this?

Step-by-step instructions, with screenshots, for processing a sale.
questions.explain: Task instructions for operators belong in the user manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

What to do when the message "Card declined" appears.
questions.explain: Error messages and responses help end users: user manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

A list of frequently asked questions from cashiers.
questions.explain: FAQs support users: user manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

The data dictionary listing each field, its data type and length.
questions.explain: Database detail is for developers: technical manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

Commented program listings for the discount module.
questions.explain: Code is for maintainers: technical manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

Installation steps and the minimum server specification.
questions.explain: Installation and hardware requirements are technical.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

The completed test plan with expected and actual results.
questions.explain: Test evidence helps maintainers: technical manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Which manual should contain this?

A plain-language glossary of terms such as "void" and "refund".
questions.explain: A plain glossary helps users: user manual.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Five months after the Statia Port Authority began using a new cargo-tracking system, a team compares the number of lost container records with the target in the original system proposal and surveys staff about the system. This activity belongs to which SDLC stage?
options: Implementation, because the system is new
Development, because the system is being tested
Review, because the live system is being evaluated against its objectives
Analysis, because staff are being surveyed

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
You are the systems analyst for Island Wheels Car Rentals, which has branches at the airport and in Bridgetown and wants to replace its paper booking cards with a computerised system. Make the key decisions.

The owner says: "My nephew can code. Let him start building tomorrow." What do you recommend?
options: Define the problem and carry out a feasibility study first, presenting a system proposal and feasibility report that compare options.
Agree: starting to code early saves time.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The proposal is approved. Development is finished and tested. Bookings are critical, and the owner cannot afford lost reservations during the tourist season. Which changeover method do you put in the conversion plan?
options: Phase it in by location: the Bridgetown branch first, keeping backups of the paper cards, then NMIA.
Direct changeover at both branches on the first day of the season.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The system is live at both branches. Four months later, the owner asks whether the project was a success. What do you do?
options: Carry out a review: compare results with the proposal's objectives, survey staff and customers, and produce an evaluation report.
Tell him it is working, so nothing more is needed.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: The Caribbean Mutual Bank is replacing its customer-account system. Accuracy is critical, the bank must be able to prove every balance is correct, and cost is a lesser concern. Which changeover method is MOST appropriate?

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem:
Apply the class scenarios. For each situation, choose the BEST option and read the feedback for the justification. (Extension: beyond the CXC Unit 1 syllabus, except the changeover question.)

Scenario 1: The Sunset Boutique on Albert Street needs a payroll system for its eight staff within a month and has a very limited budget.
questions.explain: A ready-made package is cheapest and fastest, and payroll is a common need, so having no competitive advantage hardly matters. The trade-off is vendor dependence.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 2: The Windward Commercial Bank in Castries needs software that matches its unique loan products, and it has a strong in-house IT team.
questions.explain: In-house development fits unique needs fully, and the bank has the IT staff to build and maintain it. It is costly, but a package would not fit.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 3: Accounts staff at the Island Builders' Supply want to automate a spreadsheet process. No programmers are available, so they will build it themselves. What is this approach?
questions.explain: Staff who are not programmers building their own solution with a spreadsheet is end user development. It can suit a small, low-risk task.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 3 (continued): What is the MAIN risk of the Island Builders' Supply staff building it themselves?
options: Spreadsheet errors that go unnoticed, and a system that is hard to maintain
questions.explain: End user development is prone to errors and hard to maintain: it is rarely tested or documented, so mistakes slip through and nobody else can fix it.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 4: On the Coastline Tours booking project, users and developers keep misunderstanding each other's requirements, and the project is slipping. Which approach could fix this?
questions.explain: Joint application development brings programmers and users together, so there is less miscommunication.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 4 (continued): Which phase does joint application development MAINLY affect on the Coastline Tours project?
questions.explain: Requirements are gathered and agreed in analysis, which is where the misunderstandings arise.

questions.topic: The system development life cycle and software engineering
questions.stem: Scenario 6: The Bayview General Hospital in Castries is replacing its patient records system. A fault could harm patients, and results must be checked against the old system.
questions.explain: Parallel running keeps old and new side by side until fault free so results can be compared; patient safety justifies the cost. Pilot running is a defensible cheaper compromise; direct is far too risky.

questions.stem: Bayside Freight is replacing its cargo-tracking system. The analyst needs detailed information about the needs of the company's five department managers, including the reasons behind their current procedures. Which fact-finding tool is MOST appropriate?

The Carenage Water Taxi company in Grenada is replacing its paper ticketing. Sort each situation by the fact-finding tool that suits it BEST.

Which tool fits this situation best?

Find out the owner's goals and budget for the new system.
questions.explain: One key decision-maker with detailed, personal goals: interview.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Collect satisfaction ratings from 300 regular passengers.
questions.explain: Many people, the same rating questions: questionnaire.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

See how ticket sellers really handle a queue when a cruise ship docks.
questions.explain: Real day-to-day work under pressure is best seen by observation.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Identify every field on the current paper ticket and daily sales sheet.
questions.explain: The data items are written on existing documents: review of printed material.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Ask the two senior captains why boarding procedures are done in a certain order.
questions.explain: A small number of experts and the reasons behind procedures: interview.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Count how often 40 part-time staff use each feature, using rating scales.
questions.explain: A large group answering quantitative questions: questionnaire.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Time how long it takes to issue one ticket at the St. George's kiosk.
questions.explain: Timing a task as it happens is observation.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Read last year's procedures manual and monthly sales reports.
questions.explain: Studying existing manuals and reports is review of printed material.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Bring eight ticket sellers, captains and office staff together to discuss and agree what the new booking screen should show.
questions.explain: A guided group discussion in which users build on each other's ideas: focus group.

questions.stem:
Which tool fits this situation best?

Gather six regular passengers to react together to a proposed mobile ticket and talk through their concerns.
questions.explain: A small group reacting to a proposal through discussion: focus group.

questions.stem:
Sunset Supermarkets chain, with branches in Port of Spain, San Fernando and Arima, is planning a new stock system. Its analyst must plan interviews, design a questionnaire, run a focus group, observe staff and write the requirements. Judge each decision.

The analyst asks every branch manager the same ten prepared questions in the same order, so their answers can be compared. What type of interview is this?
questions.explain: The same prepared questions in the same order for everyone is a structured interview; answers are easy to compare.

questions.stem: With the owner, the analyst prepares a few questions but follows up on anything interesting she says about opening a branch in St. Kitts. What type of interview is this?
questions.explain: Prepared questions plus freedom to follow up is semi-structured, the most common type in practice.

questions.stem: The questionnaire asks cashiers: "Rate the speed of the current till system from 1 to 5." What kind of question is this?
options: An open question giving qualitative data
A closed question giving quantitative data
questions.explain: A rating scale offers fixed answers, so it is a closed question producing numbers that are quick to total and chart.

questions.stem: A draft question reads: "Don't you agree the old system is far too slow?" What is wrong with it?
options: It is too short to be useful
It is a leading question that pushes respondents towards one answer
questions.explain: The wording suggests the "right" answer, so results would be biased. Use neutral wording.

questions.stem: Before sending the questionnaire to 150 staff, the analyst tries it on five cashiers in San Fernando. Why?
options: To pilot it and find confusing questions
questions.explain: Piloting on a few users finds misunderstood questions before the full survey goes out, when they can no longer be changed.

questions.stem: Shelf-packers in Arima worked unusually fast on the one day the analyst watched them. What should the analyst do?
options: Observe over several days and compare with the stock-system logs
questions.explain: This is the Hawthorne effect. Several visits let staff get used to the analyst, and logs cross-check the timings.

questions.stem: Managers say a stock count takes 20 minutes, but observation shows it takes an hour. What is the analyst doing by comparing the two results?
questions.explain: Combining tools and comparing their results lets one tool expose the weakness of another.

questions.stem: In a focus group of eight Sunset cashiers, the head cashier does most of the talking and the others simply agree with her. Which limitation of focus groups is this?
options: One confident member dominating, so quieter views are lost
questions.explain: Focus groups can be dominated by one or two confident members. A skilled facilitator invites each person to speak.

questions.stem: The requirements specification says: "The system must print a reorder list when any item falls below its reorder level." What kind of requirement is this?
questions.explain: It states what the system does, so it is a functional requirement.

questions.stem: The specification also says: "Stock look-ups must return a result in under two seconds at every till." What kind of requirement is this?
questions.explain: It states how well (how fast) the system must work: a non-functional performance requirement.

questions.stem:
You are the systems analyst for the Sunrise Medical Centre in West Bay, which wants a new appointment system. Choose your fact-finding tools well.

The centre has 3 senior doctors, 12 receptionists and nurses, and about 2,000 registered patients. You start with the doctors, who set clinic policy. What do you do?
options: Send the doctors a ten-question tick-box questionnaire.
Interview each of the three doctors, with prepared questions and follow-ups.

questions.stem: Next, you want patients' views on waiting times and preferred booking methods. What do you use?
options: A short anonymous online and paper questionnaire with mostly closed questions.
Interview patients one by one in the waiting room until you have spoken to most of them.

questions.stem: Receptionists say booking is "quick and easy", but patients complain about long queues. How do you find out what really happens?
options: Accept the receptionists' answer; they know the job best.
Observe the front desk over several mornings, timing each booking, and compare with the appointment logs.

questions.stem:
Analysts across the Caribbean are modelling new systems. Read what each one is drawing and sort it by the type of model.

Which type of model is this?

For Belmopan Clinic: rectangles PATIENT and DOCTOR joined by a diamond "is seen by", with M and 1 at the ends.
questions.explain: Entities, a relationship and cardinality: an ER diagram.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For Breadfruit Valley Secondary: STUDENT with StudentID, Name and DateOfBirth, linked to COURSE in a many-to-many (M:N) relationship.
questions.explain: Stored data, attributes and cardinality with no processes: an ER diagram.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For the Island Pizza in Punta Cana: order details flowing from the CUSTOMER into "Process order" and on to the Orders data store.
questions.explain: Data moving from an external entity, through a process, into a data store: a DFD.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For a water utility: meter readings moving from the meter reader, through "Calculate bill", into the Accounts data store.
questions.explain: The focus is how data moves between entities, processes and stores: a DFD.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For Belize City Car Rentals: receive request, check availability, confirm booking, take deposit, issue confirmation, drawn in order to spot slow manual steps.
questions.explain: A sequence of activities used to find bottlenecks: a process model.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For Harbourside Hotel: each check-in activity from guest arrival to key issued, drawn in sequence to find a duplicated step.
questions.explain: Activities and their order: a process model.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

A Booking class listing bookingID and pickupDate, then the method calculateCost(), linked to a Vehicle class.
questions.explain: Attributes plus methods in a class: an object model.

questions.stem:
Which type of model is this?

For a Java ticketing app at Island Link Ferries: classes Passenger and Ticket, each with attributes and operations such as issueTicket().
questions.explain: Classes with data and behaviour for an object-oriented program: an object model.

questions.stem:
Use the Island Link Ferries decision tree from the notes (Under 12? then Return? leading to four leaves), and decide which tool suits each Caribbean situation.

A 9-year-old buys a single (not return) Island Link Ferries ticket to Bequia. Following the tree, which leaf is reached?
questions.explain: Under 12: Y, then Return: N, leads to the Child fare leaf.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old buys a return ticket. Following the tree, what is charged?
questions.explain: Under 12: N, then Return: Y, leads to Adult fare + 10% discount.

questions.stem: The board of Northstar Credit Union, none of whom are technical, must approve the loan rules at a meeting. Which tool should the analyst present?
questions.explain: A tree is visual and easy for non-technical readers to follow branch by branch.

questions.stem: Before coding, a programmer must prove that all 32 combinations of five loan conditions are handled. Which tool should be used?
questions.explain: Completeness is easy to check in a table: count the 2 to the power 5 = 32 columns.

questions.stem: At Wellcare Pharmacy, staff ask questions in a fixed order: prescription first, then insurance, then age. Which tool shows that order?
questions.explain: A tree shows the order of conditions from left to right; a table does not.

questions.stem: A tree for two yes/no conditions has four leaves. How many rules would the equivalent decision table have?
questions.explain: Each leaf matches one rule: 2 to the power 2 = 4.

questions.stem: A customs duty rule at a Kingstown port agent has six conditions. What happens if it is drawn as a tree?
options: It loses the order of conditions
It becomes very wide and cluttered
It can no longer show actions
questions.explain: With many conditions a tree becomes cluttered (64 leaves here); a table stays compact.

questions.stem:
The Island Hardware uses this delivery policy table. C1 Order over $200? C2 Customer in Freeport or Lucaya? Actions: A1 Free delivery; A2 Charge $15 delivery; A3 Add 5% loyalty discount.
R1 (Y,Y): A1, A3 · R2 (Y,N): A1 · R3 (N,Y): A2, A3 · R4 (N,N): A2.

How many rules does a table with these 2 conditions need?
questions.explain: 2 to the power 2 = 4 rules.

questions.stem: A customer in Freeport orders $250 of goods. Which rule applies?
questions.explain: Over $200 (Y) and in Freeport (Y): Rule 1.

questions.stem: A customer in St. George’s orders $120. What happens?
questions.explain: Not over $200 (N), not in Grand Anse/Gouyave (N): Rule 4, $15 delivery only.

questions.stem: Which condition alone decides whether delivery is free?
questions.explain: Free delivery appears in R1 and R2, exactly where C1 is Y, whatever C2 says.

questions.stem: If a third condition (Paid online?) were added, how many rules would be needed?
questions.explain: 2 to the power 3 = 8 rules.

questions.stem:
Designers at the Island Code Studio in Holetown are specifying a booking system for the Harbourside Hotel in Bridgetown. Sort each piece of design work by the tool being used.

Which design tool is this?

GuestID: text, 8 characters, unique, must start with "HH". The same kind of entry is recorded for every field.
questions.explain: Name, type, size and validation for each data item: a data dictionary.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

One shared entry for RoomRate that the form designer and the programmer both check, so the screens and the code agree.
questions.explain: A central record that keeps the team consistent: a data dictionary.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

FOR EACH booking / IF guest is a loyalty member THEN apply member rate OTHERWISE apply standard rate, written for the hotel manager to approve.
questions.explain: Plain English with capitalised keywords and no variables, for users to check: structured English.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

Indented plain-English steps with keywords in capitals and no variables, shown to the front-desk staff so they can confirm the check-out process.
questions.explain: Readable by users, limited keywords, no programming syntax: structured English.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

INPUT nights / IF nights > 7 THEN rate ← weeklyRate ELSE rate ← nightlyRate ENDIF / OUTPUT rate
questions.explain: Variables and assignment arrows written for the programmer: pseudocode.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

total ← 0 / FOR each item on the bill: total ← total + price / OUTPUT total
questions.explain: A loop with variables and assignment: pseudocode.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

A grid with Y/N entries for "Member?" and "Weekend?", four rules, and X marks against the rate to charge.
questions.explain: Conditions, rules and X marks in a grid: a decision table.

questions.stem:
Which design tool is this?

A branching diagram from a root: "Member?" then "Weekend?", with the rate at each leaf, shown to the hotel board.
questions.explain: Conditions at branch points and actions at the leaves: a decision tree.

questions.stem:
The Hilltop Bakery in Paramaribo is developing an online ordering system. Its Gantt chart shows:

TaskWeeks
A Feasibility study1 to 2
B Analysis2 to 5
C Design5 to 7
D Development7 to 12
E Testing11 to 13
F Implementation14 to 15

How long does Analysis (weeks 2 to 5) last?
questions.explain: 5 − 2 + 1 = 4 weeks: weeks 2, 3, 4 and 5.

questions.stem: How long does Development (weeks 7 to 12) last?
Which two tasks overlap in week 5?
questions.explain: Analysis ends in week 5 and Design starts in week 5, so both run that week.

questions.stem: In which weeks do Development and Testing overlap?
questions.explain: Testing starts in week 11 and Development ends in week 12: both bars appear in weeks 11 and 12.

questions.stem: Testing ends in week 13 and Implementation starts in week 14. How are these two tasks scheduled?
questions.explain: There is no shared week, so Implementation follows Testing: sequential tasks.

questions.stem: What is the total length of the project?
questions.explain: Week 1 to week 15 = 15 weeks. The durations add to 20 weeks, but overlaps shorten the project.

questions.stem: Development falls two weeks behind during Carnival. What should the project manager do with the chart?
options: Replace it with a decision table
Update the chart and reschedule the later tasks
Nothing: a Gantt chart is fixed at the feasibility stage
questions.explain: A Gantt chart is a monitoring tool that must be updated whenever the schedule changes.

questions.stem: Every Monday the bakery owner, the programmer and the web designer check the same chart and can all see when each task starts and ends. Which strength of a Gantt chart does this show?
options: It lists every combination of conditions
It removes the need for testing
It keeps everyone on the same page about the schedule
questions.explain: Showing each activity's start and end to the whole team keeps everyone on the same page.

questions.stem: Caribbean Code Works in Barbados later plans a hospital system with 250 tasks. What weakness of a Gantt chart is it likely to meet?
options: The chart grows complex and cluttered on a large project
The chart can show only one task at a time
The chart can only be drawn by hand
The chart cannot show start and end weeks
questions.explain: A Gantt chart grows complex on large projects; hundreds of bars become hard to read.

questions.stem: The project manager for the Harbourside Hotel in St. George's is checking the Gantt chart for its new online booking system. Development runs from week 6 to week 10 and Testing runs from week 9 to week 11. Which statement is correct?
options: Development lasts 5 weeks and does not overlap Testing.
Testing lasts 2 weeks and starts after Development ends.
Development lasts 5 weeks and overlaps Testing for 2 weeks.
Development lasts 4 weeks and overlaps Testing for 1 week.

questions.stem:
The Island Code Studio in Grand Anse is building a guest-booking system for a Gouyave guest house. Sort each tool or feature it uses into upper CASE, lower CASE or integrated CASE.

Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The analysts draw the DFDs and the tool flags a process that has no output.
questions.explain: Drawing and checking DFDs supports analysis: upper CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The data dictionary records that GuestID is 8 characters on every screen.
questions.explain: A data dictionary supports analysis and design: upper CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The designers lay out the check-in screen and the nightly occupancy report in the package.
questions.explain: Screen and report design belong to the design stage: upper CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The ER diagram is drawn and checked for missing relationships before the database is designed.
questions.explain: ER diagramming supports analysis and design: upper CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The tool generates the SQL table definitions and program code from the approved ERD.
questions.explain: A code generator supports development: lower CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

A programmer steps through the code in a debugger to find why the invoice total is wrong.
questions.explain: Debugging belongs to development and testing: lower CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

An automated testing tool runs 200 test bookings overnight and reports failures.
questions.explain: Testing tools are lower CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

After go-live, a documentation generator updates the technical manual whenever the code is changed.
questions.explain: Supporting maintenance with generated documentation is lower CASE.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

The analysts model the system in Visible Analyst, like an architect drawing plans before building starts.
questions.explain: Visible Analyst is an example upper-CASE tool for the early phases.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

Every change to the booking code is saved to Git so the team can roll back a bad change.
questions.explain: Git supports development and maintenance: lower CASE, like the site crew building the walls.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

One package links the planning schedule, the diagrams, the code and the test results, from planning through maintenance.
questions.explain: Covering the whole life cycle with linked tools is integrated CASE, like one project manager overseeing every stage.

questions.stem:
Upper, lower or integrated CASE?

Renaming a field in the ERD automatically updates the data dictionary, the generated code and the manual.
questions.explain: A change flowing through every phase's tools is the mark of integrated CASE.

questions.stem: At the Island Code Studio in St. George's, analysts finish the ER diagram and data dictionary for a Grand Anse hotel's guest-booking system. The team's software then automatically produces the database tables and program code from them. This feature is BEST described as

Scenario: the Island Code Studio in Holetown is building a ticket-booking system for the Oistins Water Taxi. The team needs to draw data flow diagrams, prototype screens and track code changes. For each task, choose the CASE category, then the SDLC phase it supports.

Task 1: the analysts must draw DFDs showing how booking data moves from passengers into the Bookings data store. Which CASE category do they need?
questions.explain: Drawing DFDs and ERDs is diagramming and modelling (Visible Analyst, Visio, Lucidchart, Enterprise Architect).

questions.stem: Task 1 again: in which SDLC phase are these DFDs mainly drawn?
questions.explain: DFDs document how data moves and is stored, which is analysis work.

questions.stem: Task 2: the designers must build clickable ticket-booking screens that captains and passengers can try before any code is written. Which CASE category?
questions.explain: Clickable prototype screens come from UI prototyping tools such as Figma or Balsamiq.

questions.stem: Task 2 again: which SDLC phase does the prototype mainly support?
questions.explain: Users check layouts in the design phase, before development starts.

questions.stem: Task 3: three programmers edit the same booking code and must be able to review, merge and roll back each other's changes. Which CASE category?
questions.explain: Tracking every code change so it can be reviewed, merged and rolled back is code and version control (Visual Studio, Git).

questions.stem: Task 3 again: in which SDLC phase is the code tracked?
questions.explain: Code is written and changed during development.

questions.stem: Which example tools suit tasks 1, 2 and 3, in that order?
questions.explain: Visible Analyst draws the DFDs, Figma builds the prototype screens and Git tracks the code changes.

questions.stem: The tools for tasks 1 and 2 (diagramming and UI prototyping) belong mainly to which type of CASE?
questions.explain: Diagramming and prototyping support the early phases (analysis and design): upper CASE.

questions.stem: Later, the team wants regression tests to rerun automatically after every build. Which category and phase?
options: Version control such as Git, in analysis
Project management such as Jira, in the planning phase
UI prototyping such as Balsamiq, in design
Testing tools such as Selenium, in the testing phase
questions.explain: Automated regression tests after each build belong to testing tools in the testing phase.

questions.stem: The diagramming tool flags a DFD process with no output weeks before any code is written. Which benefit of CASE tools does this show?
questions.explain: Automatic checking finds flaws early, when they are cheap to fix. CASE tools also make work faster, cut errors and keep documentation consistent.

questions.stem:
You are an analyst at Seaview Systems, building a new student portal for Sandbox Tree College. Use prototyping well.

Students cannot say clearly what they want on the timetable and grades pages. "We'll know it when we see it," one tells you. What do you do?
options: Build a clickable prototype of the two pages and let a group of students try it.
Code the full portal from your own best guess, then show students the finished product.

questions.stem: Students like the prototype and ask for a mobile-friendly layout and a hurricane-closure notice banner. The prototype was built quickly in a design tool, with no security or database behind it. How should you treat it?
options: As an evolutionary prototype: put the design-tool mock-up live as the final portal straight away.
As a throwaway prototype: use it to fix the requirements, then build the real portal properly with security.

questions.stem: The registrar sees the prototype at a demonstration and announces that the portal will launch next week. What do you do?
options: Explain that it is only a model: the real portal still has to be built and tested. Agree a realistic schedule.
Say nothing and accept the launch date to keep the registrar happy.

questions.stem:
The Island Code Studio in Montego Bay is developing and testing a ticket-booking system for the Ocho Rios Water Taxi. Choose the right development or testing tool for each situation.

The finished booking program must run fast on the Kingston kiosk, and the source code must not be handed over. Which translator should the team use?
questions.explain: A compiler produces a fast executable file in one go, so the source code need not be shipped.

questions.stem: A trainee programmer wants the program to stop at the first error so she can fix lines one at a time. Which translator suits her?
questions.explain: An interpreter runs one statement at a time and stops at the first error, which helps while testing.

questions.stem: The team must create the bookings tables and list all of Saturday's bookings. Which language is designed for this?
questions.explain: SQL is the database language for creating tables and querying data.

questions.stem: The passenger app must run on many models of Android phone. Which of the named languages suits it best?
questions.explain: Java is object-oriented and runs on many platforms; it is widely used for Android apps.

questions.stem: A tester reads the fare code and designs tests so that both branches of IF age < 12 are run. Which kind of testing is this?
questions.explain: Seeing the code and testing every path is white box testing.

questions.stem: Without seeing any code, a tester books a return ticket for a 30-year-old and checks the fare against the specification. Which kind of testing?
questions.explain: Inputs and outputs checked against the specification, with the code hidden: black box testing.

questions.stem: The fare routine is tested on its own before it is joined to the payment module. Which kind of testing?
questions.explain: Testing one module on its own is unit testing.

questions.stem: The booking module and the payment module are now tested together to check the fare passes correctly. Which kind of testing?
questions.explain: Checking that modules work together is integration testing.

questions.stem: Captains and office staff try the system with a week of real bookings before they sign it off. Which kind of testing?
questions.explain: Users testing with real data before sign-off is acceptance testing.

questions.stem: After a payment bug is fixed, Selenium re-runs every earlier booking test. Which kind of testing?
questions.explain: Re-running earlier tests after a change is regression testing.

questions.stem: Every screen matches the design specification, but pier staff say the system does not fit how they actually sell tickets. Which question has the project failed?
options: Validation: are we building the right product?
Integration: do the modules work together?
Verification: are we building the product right?
questions.explain: The system meets the specification (verification passed) but not users' real needs, so validation failed.

questions.stem:
Sort each tool by the SDLC stage in which it is MAINLY used.

Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Interviews with department managers
questions.explain: Fact-finding about the current system and requirements: analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Review of existing invoices and reports
questions.explain: Investigating printed material is fact-finding: analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Observation of staff at work
questions.explain: Observation gathers facts about the current system: analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Pseudocode for each module
questions.explain: Pseudocode specifies program logic: design.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Flowchart of the login algorithm
questions.explain: A flowchart represents the logic to be programmed: design.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Writing source code in Python
questions.explain: Using a programming language builds the system: development.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Lower-CASE code generator
questions.explain: Generating code supports development.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Debugger in an IDE
questions.explain: Finding and fixing errors in code: development.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Focus group with eight users from different departments
questions.explain: A guided group discussion gathers requirements: analysis.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Structured English for the discount rule
questions.explain: Plain-English logic that specifies the solution: design.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Data dictionary entry for every field
questions.explain: Defining each data item for the new system: design.

questions.stem:
Which stage is this tool mainly used in?

Compiler translating the finished source code
questions.explain: Translating source code into machine code: development.

questions.stem: An analyst for the Northstar Credit Union records the loan policy in a limited-entry decision table. The conditions are: Is the applicant employed? Is the loan under $5,000? Does the applicant have a savings account? Has the applicant missed a payment before? How many rules will the complete table contain?

The Breadfruit Valley Secondary canteen is moving to phone pre-orders, and an analyst is drawing a DFD. For each situation, decide what the DFD can and cannot do for her.

The canteen supervisor wants to know whether the kitchen actually receives the list of orders. Would a DFD show this?
options: Yes: it shows data flowing to Kitchen Staff
No: a DFD only shows hardware
questions.explain: A DFD shows where data goes, so a "preparation list" flow to Kitchen Staff answers her question.

questions.stem: The principal asks what time the order cut-off is each morning. Would the DFD show this?
options: No: a DFD does not show timing or the order of steps
questions.explain: Timing and sequence are not shown on a DFD; it shows only what data moves and where.

questions.stem: The IT technician wants to know whether students order from Android phones or iPhones. Would the DFD show this?
options: No: a DFD does not show hardware, programs or devices
Yes: devices are drawn as entities
questions.explain: DFDs show data, not hardware. The student is the entity, whatever phone she uses.

questions.stem: The analyst draws the current paper system and asks the supervisor, "Is this how orders really move?" Why is she drawing this DFD?
options: To understand the current system and check it with users
questions.explain: Understanding the current system and communicating with users are two key purposes of a DFD.

questions.stem: On the draft, order records are written to the Orders store but no process ever reads them. What is the DFD helping the analyst to do?
options: Show the decisions a student makes
questions.explain: Data that goes nowhere shows up clearly on a DFD; finding problems is one reason analysts draw them.

questions.stem: A student either pays by card or uses lunch credit. Would the DFD show this yes/no choice as a branch?
options: No: a DFD does not show decisions or loops
questions.explain: Decisions belong on a flowchart. The DFD shows only the data that flows, such as "payment details".

questions.stem: For the new system, the analyst wants to plan which files the canteen will need and which reports the bursar will receive. Can a DFD of the proposed system help?
options: No: DFDs only describe old systems
Yes: it shows the data stores and outputs needed
questions.explain: Planning the new system is a key purpose: the DFD shows what data must be captured, stored and output.

questions.stem: In a Gane and Sarson DFD for Island Wheels Car Rentals, the analyst draws an open-ended rectangle labelled "D2 | Rental agreements". What does this symbol represent?
options: A process that produces rental agreements
A data store holding rental agreement records for later use
A data flow carrying rental agreements to the customer
An external entity that receives rental agreements

questions.stem:
An analyst is modelling the Wellcare Pharmacy prescription system in Georgetown. Decide how each item would appear on the DFD.

How should this be drawn?

Doctor: sends a prescription to the pharmacy system
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: The doctor only sends data in, so this external entity is a source.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

Supplier: receives purchase orders from the system
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: The supplier only receives data out, so it is a sink.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

Pharmacy Owner: receives a monthly sales report
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: The owner only receives a report: a sink.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

Patient: hands in a prescription and receives a medicine label and receipt
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: The patient sends data in and receives data out: both a source and a sink.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

Health Insurer: receives claims and sends back claim approvals
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: Data flows both ways, so the insurer is a source and a sink.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

"Record prescription": the work the system does with each prescription
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: This is an action inside the system: a process, not an entity.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

The Prescriptions file on the pharmacy computer
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: Data held inside the system is a data store, not an external entity.

questions.stem:
How should this be drawn?

Mrs Richardson, a regular customer
options: Not drawn as an external entity
questions.explain: Entities are named by role, not by a person's name. Draw the entity "Patient" instead.

questions.stem:
An analyst has listed the parts of the Breadfruit Valley Secondary canteen pre-order system. Sort each one into the correct Gane and Sarson symbol.

Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Student
questions.explain: A student is a person outside the system who sends orders in: an external entity.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Kitchen Staff
questions.explain: Kitchen staff receive the preparation list: an external entity (a sink).

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Record order
questions.explain: Verb + noun, and it transforms order details into a stored record: a process.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Produce preparation list
questions.explain: An action that turns stored orders into a list: a process.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Orders
questions.explain: A plural noun for data held for later: a data store.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

Menu
questions.explain: The menu items and prices are kept for later use: a data store.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

order details
questions.explain: Data moving from the student into the system: a data flow.

questions.stem:
Which DFD symbol should represent this?

sales report
questions.explain: Data moving out of the system to the bursar: a data flow.

questions.stem: A student draws a context level DFD for the Wellcare Pharmacy prescription system. Which feature shows that the diagram is INCORRECT for this level?
options: An external entity "Health Insurer" receiving a "claim" data flow
A single process numbered 0 labelled "Prescription System"
An external entity "Doctor" sending a "prescription" data flow to the process
A data store labelled "D1 | Prescriptions" connected to the central process

questions.stem:
You are reviewing a trainee's level 1 DFD for the Blue Water Marine Services payroll in Kralendijk. Answer each review question.

Process 3.0 "Calculate pay" reads "hours worked" from D1 Timesheets but receives nothing from D2 Employees. What should you ask?
options: Why is the process not numbered 0?
Where does the pay rate come from?
questions.explain: Pay cannot be calculated from hours alone. Add "pay rate" read from D2 Employees.

questions.stem: The context diagram has four external flows. The draft shows timesheet, new employee details and payslip, but not payment details to the Bank. Is the level 1 balanced?
options: No: "payment details" to Bank is missing
questions.explain: Every external flow on the context diagram must appear on level 1, attached to the same entity.

questions.stem: The Supervisor's timesheet goes to process 1.0, which writes "hours worked" to D1 Timesheets. Is this legal?
options: Yes: a process sits between the entity and the store
questions.explain: Correct. The entity never touches the store directly; process 1.0 handles the data.

questions.stem: D2 Employees is written to by process 2.0 but no process ever reads from it. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing: stores are only ever written to
Something is missing: a store should be both written to and read from
questions.explain: A store that is never read is a warning sign. Here, 3.0 should read "pay rate" from D2.

questions.stem: Which is the best name for the process that turns new employee details from the HR Officer into a stored record?
questions.explain: A process takes a verb phrase. "Employee file" sounds like a store and "employee details" like a flow.

questions.stem: Which data store should hold each crew member's pay rate?
questions.explain: Pay rates are standing employee data, so they belong in D2 Employees. The Bank is an external entity, not a store.

questions.stem:
Read each description of a DFD and decide which level it describes.

One process numbered 0 labelled "Ferry Booking System" surrounded by four entities.
questions.explain: A single process for the whole system is the context level.

questions.stem: Processes 1.0 "Check availability", 2.0 "Take payment" and 3.0 "Issue e-ticket" with a store D1 Sailings.
questions.explain: Several numbered processes and a data store: level 1.

questions.stem: Shows the system boundary and nothing inside it.
questions.explain: The context diagram treats the system as one box: it defines the boundary.

questions.stem: Shows data being written to and read from data stores.
questions.explain: Stores first appear at level 1.

questions.stem: Must contain the same external flows as the diagram above it.
questions.explain: Level 1 must balance with the context diagram.

questions.stem: Used early to agree the scope of the project with managers.
questions.explain: The overview of the context diagram suits scope discussions.

questions.stem:
Each card describes part of a faulty DFD for the Saba Dive Centre booking system. Sort it by the type of error.

Which type of error is this?

Process 2.0 "Check equipment" receives a gear request but sends nothing out.
questions.explain: Inputs only: a black hole.

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

Process 4.0 "Print certificate" sends a certificate to Diver but has no input.
questions.explain: Outputs only: a miracle.

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

Diver sends "booking form" straight into D1 Bookings.
questions.explain: Entity to store with no process between them.

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

D1 Bookings sends "dive list" straight to D2 Boats.
questions.explain: Store to store is illegal.

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

Diver sends "medical form" directly to Instructor.
questions.explain: Entity to entity is outside the system.

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

A flow from Diver to process 1.0 is labelled "book dive".
questions.explain: A verb phrase on a flow; rename it "booking request".

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

Process 3.0 is labelled "Payments".
questions.explain: A noun on a process; rename it "Record payment".

questions.stem:
Which type of error is this?

An arrow from process 3.0 to Diver has no label.
questions.explain: Label omitted.

questions.stem: On a level 1 DFD for the Anguilla Water Taxi company, process 3.0 "Calculate fare" receives "trip details" from process 2.0 and "fare rates" from D2 Fares. No arrow leaves process 3.0. Which error is this?
options: An illegal connection, because a process cannot read from a data store
A miracle, because the process produces a fare from nothing
A labelling error, because "Calculate fare" is a noun
A black hole, because the process has inputs but no output

questions.stem:
You are a junior analyst working with Blue Channel Ferries in Grand Anse. Your senior analyst asks you to review a draft level 1 DFD before it goes to the manager.

The draft shows the Passenger sending "booking request" in an arrow that goes straight into D1 Bookings. What do you recommend?
options: Insert process 1.0 "Record booking" between Passenger and D1, so the request is checked and then written to the store.
Leave it. Passengers type their own bookings, so they really do write to the file.

questions.stem: Next you notice process 2.0 is labelled "Payment" and an arrow from 2.0 to Card Payment Provider is labelled "send money". What do you change?
options: Rename the process "Take payment" and the flow "payment request".
Rename the process "Payments" and leave the flow as it is.

questions.stem: Finally, process 3.0 "Produce manifest" sends a "passenger manifest" to the Immigration Officer, but nothing flows into it. The context diagram has exactly six external flows. What do you do?
options: Delete process 3.0 because it has an error.
Call it a miracle and add an input: "passenger list" read from D1 Bookings. Then check that all six context flows still appear.

questions.stem: At City Taxi Dispatch, callers phone in trip requests, a process matches each request to the nearest free driver, and driver details are kept in a store. The analyst is labelling the DFD. Which set of labels follows the Gane and Sarson naming rules?
options: Process: "Driver assignment"; data flow: "request trip"; data store: "Drivers"
Process: "Assign driver"; data flow: "sends request"; data store: "Store drivers"
Process: "Drivers"; data flow: "trip request"; data store: "Assign driver"
Process: "Assign driver"; data flow: "trip request"; data store: "Drivers"

questions.stem:
These examples come from homes, businesses and schools around the Caribbean. Decide whether each one is an algorithm (a plan of finite, clear, ordered steps), a program (a plan already coded so a computer can execute it) or not an algorithm at all.

Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

A numbered recipe card at Warrens Bakery: "1. Weigh 500 g of flour. 2. Add 10 g of baking powder. ... 6. Bake for 20 minutes at 180 °C."
questions.explain: Finite, precise steps in order that produce a result: an algorithm, even though it is not about computers.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

Written directions for a taxi driver: "1. Leave the airport and turn onto the coast road. 2. Cross the harbour bridge. 3. Stop at Lagoon Hotel."
questions.explain: Clear, ordered steps with a definite end: an everyday algorithm.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

Pseudocode on a whiteboard at Flamboyant Heights College: INPUT hours, charge ← hours * 2, OUTPUT charge.
questions.explain: Pseudocode is one way of writing an algorithm. It is not coded in a real language, so a computer cannot run it yet.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

A Python file on the Sea-Almond Secondary School server that calculates each student's average mark when it is run.
questions.explain: It is coded in a programming language and can be executed: a program.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

The app on the Carenage Water Taxi tablet that works out a group's fare when the crew taps "Calculate".
questions.explain: The fare algorithm has been coded and runs on a device: a program.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

Unity Credit Union's withdrawal check, written in Java and running on the credit union's computers.
questions.explain: Coded in Java and executing: a program. Its plan, the steps before coding, was the algorithm.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

A note on a fridge in Georgetown: "Do something nice for dinner."
questions.explain: Vague and not a sequence of steps, so it is not an algorithm.

questions.stem:
Algorithm, program or not an algorithm?

A clean-up volunteer's instruction after Hurricane Irma: "Keep sweeping the street", with no point at which to stop.
questions.explain: It never ends, so it is not finite and does not qualify as an algorithm.

questions.stem:
The StormGuard Shutters is using an algorithm as a problem-solving strategy to quote hurricane shutters at $120 per square metre. For each action, choose the stage of problem solving it belongs to.

The manager asks: "What will customers tell us about their windows, and what result do we need to give them?"
questions.explain: Working out the data given and the result required is understanding the problem.

questions.stem: A clerk writes: "1. Get the width. 2. Get the height. 3. Multiply the width by the height to find the area. 4. Multiply the area by 120 to find the price. 5. Display the price."
questions.explain: Writing the ordered steps is planning the solution: this is the algorithm.

questions.stem: A worker follows the written steps for a 2 m by 1.5 m window in Marsh Harbour and tells the customer the price is $360.
questions.explain: Following the steps with real data to get the result is carrying out the plan (2 × 1.5 = 3 m², × 120 = $360).

questions.stem: Before writing any steps, the team notes that every window has a width and a height in metres and that the rate is fixed per square metre.
questions.explain: Identifying the data available is part of understanding the problem.

questions.stem: The staff check that the area is worked out before the price, and move a step that was in the wrong place.
questions.explain: Putting the steps in the right order is part of planning the solution.

questions.stem: A programmer codes the agreed steps into the shop's quoting app so that the computer produces each quote.
questions.explain: Coding the plan so a computer follows it is one way of carrying out the plan.

questions.stem: Before planning a program that works out each student's average mark, an IT class at Palmetto Point Secondary is asked to agree a definition of "algorithm". Four students offer answers. Which is the BEST definition?
options: A program written in a high-level language such as Python
A diagram that uses standard symbols to show a process
A finite sequence of clear, unambiguous steps that, when followed in order, solves a problem
Any list of instructions given to a computer

questions.stem:
Students at Bayleaf Hill Secondary made these claims about why algorithms matter. Sort each claim.

Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

An algorithm lets the team agree on the logic before anyone writes code.
questions.explain: Valid. It is a shared plan for communication.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

An algorithm only works in one programming language.
questions.explain: Misconception. Algorithms are language-independent.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

Logic errors can be found by working through the steps by hand.
questions.explain: Valid. Early error detection is cheaper than fixing code.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

Once you have an algorithm, the computer can run it immediately without coding.
questions.explain: Misconception. An algorithm must be coded in a programming language before a computer can execute it.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

A written algorithm documents how the solution works for future maintenance.
questions.explain: Valid. It helps other programmers understand and change the solution.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

Algorithms are only needed for very large programs.
questions.explain: Misconception. Every program, however small, needs a clear plan.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

A general algorithm can be reused for similar problems.
questions.explain: Valid. Reuse saves time.

questions.stem:
Is this a valid reason why algorithms are important, or a misconception?

Algorithms make programs slower because of the extra planning.
questions.explain: Misconception. Planning happens before coding and does not slow the program down; it usually saves development time.

questions.stem:
Each algorithm below was written by a student for a Caribbean business. Choose the characteristic of a well-designed algorithm that it BEST fails to show.

Frigate Bay Car Rentals: "1. Multiply 3 days by $45. 2. Display $135."
questions.explain: It works only for a 3-day rental at $45, so it is not a general solution.

questions.stem: Roseau Bakery: "1. Bake the bread until it looks right. 2. Remove from oven."
questions.explain: "Until it looks right" can be read in many ways. It should state a time or temperature.

questions.stem: Montego Bay Gym: "1. Display the member's fee. 2. Get the number of months. 3. Calculate fee as months times 50."
questions.explain: The fee is displayed before it is calculated. The steps are in the wrong order.

questions.stem: Grand Anse Fishing: "1. Cast the net. 2. Go back to step 1."
questions.explain: There is no condition for stopping, so it never ends.

questions.stem: King George V Street Jewellers: "1. Get the price. 2. Apply a reasonable discount. 3. Display the new price."
questions.explain: "A reasonable discount" is vague. A precise rule, such as 10% off, is needed.

questions.stem: Saba Dive Centre: "1. Get the number of divers. 2. If there are more than 6, book two boats. 3. ???"
questions.explain: There is no next step for 6 or fewer divers, so control has nowhere to go: a dead end in the flow of control.

questions.stem: A programmer at the Anguilla Ferry Service writes the step "If the boat is nearly full, stop selling tickets." Which characteristic of a well-designed algorithm does this step violate?

Students at Calabash Point Secondary drew flowcharts for businesses around the Caribbean. Sort each feature: does it follow the rules for a well-formed flowchart, or break one?

Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Jan Thiel Car Wash: one Start at the top, and both branches of the decision rejoin and flow to a single Stop.
questions.explain: One Start, every path reaches Stop: a well-formed, finite flowchart.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Wellcare Pharmacy: the diamond "Prescription?" has two exits labelled Yes and No.
questions.explain: A decision has one line in and two labelled lines out.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Palm Beach Bar: the diamond "Age >= 18?" has two exits, but neither is labelled.
questions.explain: Decision exits must be labelled Yes and No (or True and False); otherwise the reader cannot tell which path is which.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Salem Bakery: the No path from "Enough flour?" ends in an arrow pointing to nothing.
questions.explain: Every path must reach Stop. This is a dead end in the flow of control.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Town Library: two flow lines would cross, so the student uses connector circles labelled A instead.
questions.explain: Connectors avoid crossing or very long lines.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Island Link Ferry: the process box "fare = adults * 10" has two arrows leaving it to different boxes.
questions.explain: A process has one line in and one line out. Only a decision has two exits.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Dickenson Bay Hotel: the flowchart has two Start symbols, one for guests and one for staff.
questions.explain: A flowchart has exactly one Start.

questions.stem:
Does this feature follow the flowchart rules?

Calabash Point Secondary tuck shop: the flow runs top to bottom and each symbol holds short, precise text such as "Input price".
questions.explain: Top-to-bottom flow and precise text keep the flowchart clear and unambiguous.

questions.stem: In a flowchart for Sea Breeze Marina, the step "Display the berth fee" should be drawn in which symbol?

A Montego Bay software team has left notes from a planning meeting. Sort each description or fragment by the representation it belongs to.

Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

"3. Multiply the number of tickets by the price to find the cost."
questions.explain: A full English sentence describing a step: natural language.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

cost ← tickets * price
questions.explain: An assignment statement with a variable and operator: pseudocode.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

A parallelogram containing "Input tickets".
questions.explain: A standard symbol: flowchart.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

IF tickets > 10 THEN discount ← 5 ENDIF
questions.explain: Keywords IF, THEN, ENDIF: pseudocode.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

A diamond with arrows labelled Yes and No.
questions.explain: The decision symbol: flowchart.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

Most easily understood by a client with no technical training.
questions.explain: Everyday sentences need no training to read.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

Converts almost line by line into program code.
questions.explain: Pseudocode is closest to real code.

questions.stem:
Natural language, flowchart or pseudocode?

Shows the flow of control visually with arrows.
questions.explain: Flow lines make flowcharts the most visual.

questions.stem: The Barbados Bus Co-operative wants to show its board of directors, none of whom are programmers, the decision steps for approving a refund. Which representation is MOST suitable?
options: A flowchart, because it shows the decision points and paths visually without needing programming knowledge
Program code, because it is the most precise
Any representation, because they all communicate equally well
Pseudocode, because it converts easily into a program

questions.stem:
You are a student intern with the Kittitian software firm Harbour Code, building a simple app that helps households in Basseterre estimate their electricity bill from meter readings. Make good design decisions.

Your team leader asks how you will begin. A fellow intern says, "Let's just open the editor and start coding." What do you do?
options: Write an algorithm first, so the team agrees on the steps before coding.
Start coding straight away and fix problems as they appear.

questions.stem: Your first draft says: "Get this month's reading. Subtract a reasonable previous reading. Multiply by the rate." What do you change?
options: Replace "a reasonable previous reading" with "the previous month's reading", and state the exact rate per unit.
Nothing. The programmer will know what "reasonable" means.

questions.stem: The client, a manager with no programming background, wants to check the logic before you code. How do you present the algorithm to her?
options: As detailed pseudocode only, since that is what the programmers need.
As a flowchart using standard symbols, with the pseudocode kept for the programmers.

questions.stem:
For each statement, choose the representation it BEST describes.

Its biggest weakness is that the same words can be understood in different ways.
questions.explain: Ambiguity is the classic weakness of natural language.

questions.stem: It is slow to modify because shapes and lines have to be redrawn.
questions.explain: Editing a diagram is harder than editing text.

questions.stem: There is no single universal standard, so styles vary between textbooks.
questions.explain: Pseudocode conventions vary; the key is to be consistent.

questions.stem: Decision points and both of their paths can be seen at a glance.
questions.explain: Diamonds with labelled exits make branches visible.

questions.stem: A programmer can convert it almost line by line into a program.
questions.explain: Pseudocode statements map closely onto program statements.

questions.stem: A student's flowchart for the Statia Dive Shop has a diamond containing "Certified diver?" with only one arrow leaving it. What is wrong?
options: The question should be in a parallelogram
Diamonds may only be used at the start of a flowchart
A diamond should contain a calculation, not a question
The decision needs two labelled exits, Yes and No, so the flow of control is clear for both answers

questions.stem:
The Carenage Water Taxi is writing an algorithm for its new ticket kiosk on the Port of Spain boardwalk. Sort each line of pseudocode by the kind of statement it is.

What kind of statement is this?

INPUT adults (the kiosk asks how many adults are travelling)
questions.explain: INPUT brings data from the user into the variable adults.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

READ children
questions.explain: READ is another input keyword: it stores data in children.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

fare ← adults * 15 + children * 8
questions.explain: A calculation assigned to fare with the arrow: processing.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

OUTPUT "Fare due: US$", fare
questions.explain: OUTPUT sends the result to the screen, even though it names a variable.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

GET paymentMethod (cash or card)
questions.explain: GET accepts data from the customer: input.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

change ← tendered - fare
questions.explain: Working out the change and storing it is an assignment: processing.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

ticketCount ← ticketCount + 1
questions.explain: Updating a variable with the arrow is processing (here, a counter).

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

PRINT "Ticket number ", ticketCount
questions.explain: PRINT produces a result on the receipt: output.

questions.stem:
What kind of statement is this?

DISPLAY "Thank you for sailing with us"
questions.explain: DISPLAY shows a message: output.

questions.stem: Sea Breeze Marina uses an algorithm to charge boats for berthing. Which ONE of these lines is a processing statement?

The FreshMart Supermarket is automating its checkout. Sort each description by the control structure it needs MOST.

Which control structure does this describe?

Scan every item in the customer's basket until there are no more items.
questions.explain: Doing the same steps for each item until none are left is repetition.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Give a 5% discount only if the customer shows a loyalty card.
questions.explain: "Only if" signals a condition: selection.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Input the amount tendered, calculate the change, then print the change.
questions.explain: Three steps, once each, in order: sequence.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

If the change is negative, display "Insufficient payment"; otherwise print the receipt.
questions.explain: Two alternative paths chosen by a condition: IF-THEN-ELSE selection.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Print the store name, the date and the cashier number at the top of the receipt.
questions.explain: Simple statements carried out one after the other: sequence.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Keep asking for the PIN while the PIN entered is wrong and fewer than three attempts have been made.
questions.explain: "Keep asking while" is a WHILE loop: repetition.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Add up the prices of the 12 items in a box of mangoes.
questions.explain: A fixed number of passes (12) suits a FOR loop: repetition with an accumulator.

questions.stem:
Which control structure does this describe?

Charge a bag fee when the customer asks for a plastic bag.
questions.explain: The fee depends on a condition: selection.

questions.stem:
Each condition below comes from a Caribbean system. Do the arithmetic first (precedence), then decide TRUE or FALSE, then choose the result.

An airline at GAIA uses: IF weight > 23 THEN charge an excess fee. A passenger's bag weighs exactly 23 kg. Is a fee charged?
questions.explain: 23 > 23 is FALSE, so no fee. With >= 23 the 23 kg bag would be charged: always check the boundary.

questions.stem: Bright Minds Tutoring Centre grades with: IF mark >= 70 THEN grade ← "A" ELSE IF mark >= 55 THEN grade ← "B" ELSE grade ← "C". A student scores 80. What grade?
questions.explain: 80 >= 70 is TRUE at the first test, so grade is A and the other tests are skipped. This is why the highest boundary is tested first.

questions.stem: A King Street shop algorithm sets a ← 6 and b ← 4, then tests IF a + b * 3 > 20. Is the condition TRUE or FALSE?
questions.explain: Multiply first: 4 * 3 = 12; 6 + 12 = 18; 18 > 20 is FALSE. Adding first, (6 + 4) * 3 = 30, is the classic error.

questions.stem: Sea Breeze Marina gives a discount IF length > 20 OR nights >= 5. A boat is 18 m long and stays 5 nights. Discount given?
questions.explain: length > 20 is FALSE but nights >= 5 is TRUE. OR needs only one TRUE condition, so the discount is given.

questions.stem: FreshMart Supermarket gives a discount IF total > 100 AND card = TRUE. A customer spends US$120 but has no loyalty card. Discount given?
questions.explain: total > 100 is TRUE but card = TRUE is FALSE. AND needs both conditions TRUE, so no discount.

questions.stem: A Bridgetown bus company marks a bus as an express IF busNumber MOD 3 = 0. Is bus 14 an express?
questions.explain: 14 MOD 3 = 2 (14 = 4 × 3 + 2). 2 = 0 is FALSE, so bus 14 is not an express.

questions.stem: A tour bus works out seats ← 20 − 8 / 4 * 2 + 1. What value is stored in seats?
questions.explain: 8 / 4 = 2, then 2 * 2 = 4 (left to right), then 20 − 4 + 1 = 17. Working strictly left to right gives the wrong answer 7.

questions.stem:
A Sixth Form student at Palmetto Point Secondary is desk-checking this loyalty-points rule for the Grand Anse Bakery before coding it.

x ← 5
y ← 3
IF x * 2 - y >= 7 THEN
    z ← x + y * 2
ELSE
    z ← (x + y) * 2
ENDIF
OUTPUT z

What is output?

For each loop, choose how many times its body runs.

FOR k ← 1 TO 12 DO ... ENDFOR
questions.explain: k takes 1 to 12 inclusive: 12 − 1 + 1 = 12 passes.

questions.stem: FOR k ← 10 DOWNTO 3 DO ... ENDFOR
questions.explain: 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3: eight passes. Counting down is allowed with DOWNTO.

questions.stem: FOR k ← 0 TO 20 STEP 5 DO ... ENDFOR
questions.explain: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20: five passes.

questions.stem: n ← 10. WHILE n < 5 DO n ← n + 1 ENDWHILE
questions.explain: 10 < 5 is FALSE at the first test, so a WHILE loop body never runs.

questions.stem: n ← 10. REPEAT n ← n + 1 UNTIL n > 5
questions.explain: REPEAT runs the body once (n becomes 11), then 11 > 5 is TRUE, so it stops.

questions.stem: n ← 1. WHILE n < 50 DO n ← n * 3 ENDWHILE
questions.explain: n goes 1 → 3 → 9 → 27 → 81: four passes. 81 < 50 is FALSE, so it stops.

questions.stem:
A Sixth Form student at Mahoe Grove High School is dry-running algorithms for the Rainwatch Weather Club before they are coded. For each item, choose the value or answer the trace table should show.

total ← 0. FOR k ← 5 DOWNTO 1: total ← total + k * 2. ENDFOR. What is the FIRST value of k in the trace table?
questions.explain: DOWNTO starts at the first number, 5, and counts down to 1.

questions.stem: Same algorithm. What is total after the pass where k = 3?
questions.explain: k = 5 adds 10 (10), k = 4 adds 8 (18), k = 3 adds 6 (24). 30 is the final total after k = 1.

questions.stem: p ← 10. FOR i ← 4 DOWNTO 1: IF p − i * 2 > 4 THEN p ← p − i ELSE p ← p + 2 * i − 1 ENDIF. ENDFOR. On the first pass (i = 4), which branch runs?
questions.explain: i * 2 = 8 first, then 10 − 8 = 2. 2 > 4 is FALSE, so the ELSE branch runs.

questions.stem: Same algorithm. What is p after the first pass?
questions.explain: ELSE: 10 + 2 * 4 − 1 = 10 + 8 − 1 = 17. 16 comes from 2 * (i − 1); 6 comes from wrongly taking the THEN branch.

questions.stem: c ← 0. FOR n ← 1 TO 10: IF n MOD 3 = 0 THEN c ← c + 1 ENDIF. ENDFOR. OUTPUT c. What is output?
questions.explain: n MOD 3 = 0 is TRUE for 3, 6 and 9, so c becomes 3. 18 adds the numbers (accumulator) instead of counting them.

questions.stem: What is the FUNCTION of the algorithm in the previous item?
options: It counts the multiples of 3 from 1 to 10
It adds up the numbers from 1 to 10
It outputs every number from 1 to 10
questions.explain: The function is the purpose in plain words: it counts how many numbers from 1 to 10 are divisible by 3.

questions.stem: Rainfall of 12, 0 and 8 mm is entered into: total ← 0. FOR d ← 1 TO 3: INPUT r; total ← total + r. ENDFOR. OUTPUT total. How many values appear in the Output column?
questions.explain: OUTPUT is after ENDFOR, outside the loop, so it runs once and prints 20.

questions.stem:
Peak Fitness Club's app works out a "workout score" during a short countdown routine. What is output by this algorithm?

s ← 0
FOR j ← 6 DOWNTO 2 STEP -2 DO
    s ← s + j * j
ENDFOR
OUTPUT s

Sort each description or language into its programming paradigm.

Which paradigm does this belong to?

A program written as step-by-step instructions grouped into procedures.
questions.explain: Step-by-step "how" instructions in procedures: procedural.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

A class called Booking has attributes (name, date) and methods (confirm, cancel).
questions.explain: Classes, attributes and methods: object-oriented.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

Facts and rules are stated; the system answers queries such as "Who is the parent of Ana?"
questions.explain: Facts, rules and queries: logic programming (declarative).

questions.stem:
