Which paradigm does this belong to?

Programs are built from functions that return values without changing any variables.
questions.explain: Pure functions and no changing state: functional.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

Pascal
questions.explain: Pascal is a classic procedural (structured) language.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

C++
questions.explain: C++ is classed as object-oriented ("C with classes"), though it can also be used procedurally.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

Prolog
questions.explain: Prolog is the standard example of a logic language.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

Haskell
questions.explain: Haskell is a purely functional language.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

Java
questions.explain: Java is object-oriented: nearly everything is written inside classes.

questions.stem:
Which paradigm does this belong to?

A Sales object inherits features from a Transaction class.
questions.explain: Inheritance is an OOP feature.

questions.stem:
The Seagrape Bay Secondary School canteen wants a small program to total each student's lunch order and count orders during the lunch break. You are the student programmer. Make the best decisions.

The canteen manager is in a hurry: "Just start typing the code now, we need it by Friday." What do you do first?
options: Start coding immediately and fix problems as they appear.
Define and analyse the problem, then write and desk-check an algorithm before coding.

questions.stem: Orders arrive one at a time and nobody knows how many students will buy lunch. The cashier types 0 after the last order. Which loop do you design?
options: A WHILE loop with 0 as a sentinel value, with one INPUT before the loop and another at the end of the loop body.
FOR order ← 1 TO 200, because the school has about 200 students.

questions.stem: You trace your algorithm with the test data 12, 8, 0. The trace table shows a final total of 8 instead of 20. What is the most likely cause?
options: total ← 0 has been placed inside the loop, so the accumulator is reset on every pass.
The trace table must be wrong; the computer will get it right.

questions.stem: The algorithm now traces correctly. The manager asks which language to use; the IT teacher suggests an object-oriented language so that a MenuItem class can be reused later. Which do you choose?
options: HTML, because the menu will appear on a screen.
C++ or Java, both object-oriented languages.

questions.stem: A developer at the Statia Shipping Agency writes: parent(maria, john). parent(john, ana). grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z). She then asks the system who is Ana's grandparent, without writing any steps for how to search. Which paradigm is she using?

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: At the Spanish Town firm TechWave Jamaica, staff set up laptops, run the network, back up customer data and secure email. Which statement best describes the field they work in?
options: The use of computers, software, networks and data to create, store, process, protect and share information.
The repair and servicing of computer hardware, without any concern for data, networks or users.
The mathematical theory of computation, studied separately from any real organisation.
The design of electronic circuits and processor chips for new computer hardware.
questions.explain: TechWave's staff use computers, networks and data to handle information, which is IT. Hardware repair, pure theory and chip design are narrower parts of related fields.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: A Seagrape Bay Secondary School student is choosing between IT, Computer Science and Information Systems degrees at a Caribbean university. Which comparison should her counsellor give?
options: Computer Science stresses deploying technology; IS stresses theory; IT stresses organisational strategy.
Computer Science stresses theory and computation; IS stresses organisational use; IT stresses deploying and supporting technology.
All three study identical content and differ only in the name each university gives them.
IS stresses hardware design; IT stresses pure mathematics; Computer Science stresses management.
questions.explain: The counsellor should explain that CS is the most theoretical, IS focuses on information in organisations, and IT on deploying and supporting technology.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: Bartica firm CodeReef uses formal methods, standards and testing to build and maintain a large booking system for Caribbean hotels. Which discipline is this?
questions.explain: CodeReef treats building its booking system as an engineering process with methods, standards and quality control, which is Software Engineering.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: A graduate designs the circuit boards and embedded processor inside a solar inverter for the Freeport firm SunGrid Bahamas. Which field is this?
questions.explain: Designing SunGrid Bahamas's circuit boards and embedded processor is hardware work, which is Computer Engineering. The other fields focus on software, theory or organisational use.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: A Port of Spain network technician wants chartered status from the UK-based chartered institute for IT professionals. Which organisation should she join?
questions.explain: BCS, the British Computer Society, is the Chartered Institute for IT in the UK, so it suits her goal. ACM and IEEE are US-founded bodies; AIS serves the IS discipline.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: A lecturer in Philipsburg researching how Caribbean businesses use information systems wants a body devoted to IS research and teaching. Which one should he join?
questions.explain: AIS serves academics and practitioners in Information Systems, which matches his research. IEEE, BCS and ACM cover computing more broadly.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: Villa Beach café SeaBreeze buys a Wi-Fi router labelled "IEEE 802.11ac". For which contribution to computing is IEEE best known?
options: Awarding the Turing Award and running the largest society for computer science educators.
Granting chartered status to IT professionals working in the United Kingdom.
Representing only Information Systems researchers in business schools.
Publishing technical standards, such as IEEE 802.11 for Wi-Fi, and supporting electrical and electronics engineers.
questions.explain: The 802.11 label on SeaBreeze's router is an IEEE standard; IEEE publishes such standards. The Turing Award belongs to ACM, chartered status to BCS and IS research to AIS.

questions.topic: SO 1.1 · The Field of Information Technology
questions.stem: A Flamboyant Heights College IT class lists ways in which IT affects daily life on the island. Which item on their list is a LIMITATION of IT rather than a use?
options: IT lets the Simpson Bay Marina take berth bookings online at any hour of the day.
IT depends on electricity and connectivity, so outages such as those after Hurricane Irma in 2017 can halt it.
IT lets teachers at Flamboyant Heights College share notes with students through online classrooms.
IT lets shops on Front Street process card payments quickly and accurately at the till.
questions.explain: The class should flag dependence on power and networks, shown by outages after Hurricane Irma, as a limitation; the other three items are uses.

questions.stem: A Hummingbird Ridge High School display traces computing from bead counters to the first room-sized electronic machines. Which pair belongs to the era before electronic computers?
options: The abacus and Babbage's Difference Engine.
questions.explain: On the display, the abacus and Babbage's mechanical engines come before electronic computing. ENIAC and UNIVAC were first-generation electronic machines.

questions.stem: At the Port-au-Prince library, a student finds a photo of a 1940s computer that filled a room and overheated constantly. Which technology characterised first-generation computers?
options: Integrated circuits, as used in early operating-system computers.
Single-chip microprocessors, as used in home computers.
Transistors, as used in the first minicomputers.
Vacuum tubes, as used in machines such as ENIAC and UNIVAC.
questions.explain: The machine in the photo used thousands of vacuum tubes, which made first-generation computers huge, hot and unreliable.

questions.stem: A retired Belmopan engineer recalls that late-1950s computers became smaller, cooler and more reliable than the valve machines before them. What replaced vacuum tubes?
questions.explain: The change he remembers came from transistors, the hallmark of second-generation computers (late 1950s to mid-1960s).

questions.stem: For a timeline at Calabash Point Secondary, students must label the 1960s-70s computers on which operating systems first became common. Which development marks this generation?
options: Vacuum tubes, which filled whole rooms and produced great heat.
Individual transistors soldered one by one onto circuit boards.
Integrated circuits, which put many transistors on one silicon chip.
Microprocessors, which put an entire CPU on a single chip.
questions.explain: Those machines used integrated circuits, the mark of the third generation. The whole-CPU microprocessor belongs on the timeline's fourth generation.

questions.stem: A Harbour Drive museum shows a 1980s desktop PC once used by a George Town shop, under the label 'fourth generation'. Which statement correctly matches that generation?
options: It is marked by vacuum tubes and room-sized machines, from the 1940s onward.
It is marked by transistors replacing valves, from the late 1950s onward.
It is marked by integrated circuits and the first operating systems in the 1960s.
It is marked by microprocessors and personal computers, from the 1970s onward.
questions.explain: The museum's desktop PC was made possible by the microprocessor, which put a whole CPU on one chip and marks the fourth generation from the 1970s.

questions.stem: A hurricane-forecast model, a regional bank's records, a small firm's server and a student's laptop each run on a different class of computer. Which list runs from MOST to LEAST powerful?
questions.explain: The forecast model needs a supercomputer, the bank a mainframe, the small firm a minicomputer and the student a microcomputer, in that order of power.

questions.stem: Caribbean Union Bank processes thousands of transactions at once for many users on one central computer. Which category is this?
questions.explain: The bank's huge volume of simultaneous transactions for many users is mainframe work. Supercomputers are built for intense scientific calculation instead.

questions.stem: A Frangipani Hill Academy student emailing a friend in Trinidad learns that the Internet began as a late-1960s US network linking research computers. What was it called?
questions.explain: The network behind her email began as ARPANET, which first linked computers in 1969. The Web came later (1989-91) and runs on top of the Internet.

questions.stem: For a St. George's telecoms exhibition, students must arrange the telegraph, telephone, radio, satellites and mobile phones in date order. Which sequence is correct?
options: Telephone, telegraph, satellite communication, radio, mobile phones
Telegraph, telephone, radio, satellite communication, mobile phones
Radio, telegraph, telephone, mobile phones, satellite communication
Telegraph, radio, mobile phones, telephone, satellite communication
questions.explain: The exhibition should run telegraph (1830s-40s), telephone (1876), radio (c.1900), communication satellites (1960s), then mobile phones (1980s onward).

questions.stem: A student writing Python at Breadfruit Valley Secondary asks how people programmed before English-like languages existed. Which sequence correctly shows how programming software developed?
options: Machine code, then assembly language, then high-level languages such as FORTRAN
High-level languages, then assembly language, then machine code
Assembly language, then machine code, then high-level languages
Machine code, then high-level languages, then assembly language
questions.explain: Before languages like Python, programmers used binary machine code, then assembly mnemonics, then high-level languages such as FORTRAN (1957).

questions.stem: A weather sensor near Simpson Bay logs the numbers 31, 29 and 33 every minute, with no labels, units or dates attached. Which description of data in the CXC syllabus fits these readings?
options: Facts that have been processed and placed in a meaningful context.
Information applied by a person to make a decision.
Facts that have been sorted, checked and summarised in a report.
Raw facts that are unprocessed, unorganised and discrete.
questions.explain: The unlabelled sensor readings are raw, unprocessed, unorganised and discrete, so they are data. Processing them in context would produce information.

questions.stem: Nieuw Nickerie Minimart's till lists 400 separate sales, while the manager's chart shows 'Saturday sales up 20%'. How is information, like the chart, different from data?
options: Information is raw data that has not yet been checked for errors.
Information is the hardware on which data files are stored.
Information is data that has been processed and given context, so it has meaning.
There is no difference; the two words mean exactly the same thing.
questions.explain: The chart is the till data processed and given context, so it means something to the manager; that is information.

questions.stem: A St. John's shop owner reads a report showing umbrellas sell out before storms, so she orders extra stock when a storm warning is issued. Knowledge, as in the syllabus, is:
options: A large collection of unprocessed sensor readings.
Information stored on a hard disk for later use.
The use of information, with understanding, to make decisions.
Data typed into a spreadsheet without headings.
questions.explain: The owner applies the report's information with understanding to make a stock decision, which is knowledge. Merely storing the report is not.

questions.stem: Guests at the Turtle Cove Inn describe rooms as "cosy" or "cramped" while staff record room temperatures in degrees Celsius. Which is correct?
options: The comments are quantitative data; the temperatures are qualitative data.
Both are quantitative, because both can be stored on a computer.
Both are qualitative, because both describe the comfort of a room.
The comments are qualitative data; the temperatures are quantitative data.
questions.explain: The guests' comments are opinion-based and subjective (qualitative); the staff's temperature readings are measured and objective (quantitative).

questions.stem: A survey records the views of every tenth passenger at the Santo Domingo cruise pier instead of every passenger. This data is:
questions.explain: Asking only every tenth passenger takes a selection of the population, so the data are sampled; detailed data would record every passenger.

questions.stem: Two staff reports at the Speightstown Hardware store give different stock figures for the same day. Which characteristic of information does this show?
questions.explain: Because the two Speightstown Hardware reports disagree, the information is inconsistent, which makes it unreliable for ordering decisions.

questions.stem: Palm Beach loyalty-card firm IslandPoints sells lists of its customers' shopping habits to advertisers. Which characteristic of information does this illustrate?
questions.explain: IslandPoints is selling information for money, which shows that information has value and can be traded as a commodity.

questions.stem: Kingston Corner Café keeps raw till totals, produces a weekly sales report, and the owner uses it to order extra stock for carnival. Which is correct?
options: The till totals are information, the report is data, and the stock decision is data.
The till totals are data, the report is information, and the stock decision uses knowledge.
The till totals are knowledge, the report is information, and the decision is data.
All three are information, because each one involves the café's money.
questions.explain: The café's raw till totals are data, the weekly report is information, and the owner's carnival stock decision applies that information as knowledge.

questions.stem: You are a Coralstone College student who designs and runs a survey of classmates about campus Wi-Fi speeds. What type of source is your completed survey?
options: A secondary source, because it will later be summarised in your report.
An electronic source, so it cannot be classed as primary or secondary.
A primary source, because it is original evidence you collected yourself.
A traditional source, so it cannot be used in IT research.
questions.explain: Your survey is original, first-hand evidence that you collected yourself, so it is a primary source.

questions.stem: For a research assignment, a Roseau student reads a textbook chapter that explains a researcher's cybersecurity experiment. How should the chapter be classified?
options: Primary, because it is printed and bound as a book.
Primary, because the author is an expert on the topic.
Electronic, because the experiment used computers.
Secondary, because it discusses or interprets original work.
questions.explain: The chapter reports and interprets someone else's experiment rather than being the experiment itself, so it is a secondary source.

questions.stem: A Sea-Almond Secondary School librarian sorts resources into traditional and electronic shelves for a CAPE IT class. Which list contains ONLY electronic information sources?
options: Electronic databases, wikis, blogs and CD-ROMs
questions.explain: The electronic shelf would hold databases, wikis, blogs and CD-ROMs. Books, newspapers, magazines and people belong with traditional sources.

questions.stem: Researching overfishing for a class project, a student interviews a fisherman at Cane Garden Bay. What is a key advantage of using a person as an information source?
options: You can ask follow-up questions and get first-hand, current detail.
Personal accounts are always free from bias and error.
People's information never needs to be checked against other sources.
A person can always be reached instantly at no cost.
questions.explain: The fisherman gives first-hand, current detail and the student can ask follow-up questions, though his account may still be biased or mistaken.

questions.stem: A Cole Bay student copies facts about Caribbean telecoms from a wiki page that an anonymous user edited an hour ago. What is the main disadvantage of a wiki as a source?
options: It cannot be searched, so finding information takes too long.
It is only available in printed form in a library.
It never links to the original sources it summarises.
Anyone can edit it, so content may be inaccurate or changed without expert review.
questions.explain: Because anyone, like that anonymous user, can edit the wiki, its content may be wrong or changed without expert review.

questions.stem: A Mahoe Grove High School student uses a 2015 printed textbook on mobile networks instead of a website updated last week. Compared with the website, the textbook's main disadvantage is that:
options: It is always less accurate than any website on the same topic.
Its content cannot be updated after printing, so it may become out of date.
It can never be used as a source in a research report.
It cannot be read without a computer or electricity.
questions.explain: The 2015 textbook cannot be changed after printing, so its mobile-network content may be out of date, whereas the website was updated last week.

questions.stem: A tropical storm passes over St. Lucia and a reporter at the Island Times must update readers quickly. Why might the reporter use social media as a source?
options: Social media posts are refereed, so they never need to be checked.
It gives fast updates from people on the ground, though claims must be verified.
Social media is a primary source that is always more accurate than official reports.
Social media guarantees the identity of every person who posts.
questions.explain: Social media gives the reporter fast updates from people on the ground in the storm, but claims must be verified before they are published.

questions.stem: A CAPE IT student at Palmetto Point Secondary must compare a library book with a website using SO 1.5. Which list gives the characteristics of information sources named in the CXC syllabus?
options: Currency, relevance, authority, accuracy and purpose
Input, processing, output, storage and feedback
Bias, cultural context, completeness and refereed status
Availability, cost, currency, depth, breadth, reliability, format and medium
questions.explain: For SO 1.5 she should use availability, cost, currency, depth, breadth, reliability, format and medium. Bias and refereeing are SO 1.6 selection criteria.

questions.stem: For a Rincon network project, a student finds a book covering every networking topic briefly and a journal article on Wi-Fi security in great detail. Which is correct?
options: The book has greater breadth; the article has greater depth.
The book has greater depth; the article has greater breadth.
Both have equal breadth because both discuss networking.
The article has greater breadth because it is more recent.
questions.explain: The book covers networking widely (breadth); the article goes into great detail on one topic (depth).

questions.stem: A reference book at the Fort Street Reference Library may only be read on site during opening hours. Which characteristic limits it?
questions.explain: Being readable only on site during opening hours restricts when and how the book can be accessed, which is its availability.

questions.stem: A Sandbox Tree College student finds an online journal charging US$40 per article, while a government report on the same topic is free. Which characteristic differs?
questions.explain: The US$40 charge versus a free report is a difference in cost, which affects whether the student can practically use the journal.

questions.stem: A Willemstad student cites 2009 mobile-phone statistics in a 2026 report, and her teacher questions the currency of the source. Currency of information refers to:
options: The price of the source in local money.
How widely the source covers a topic.
How up to date the information is.
The physical form in which it is stored.
questions.explain: Her teacher means the 2009 figures may be out of date; currency is how up to date information is, not money.

questions.stem: Before hurricane season, the group Montserrat Ready issues the same hurricane guide as a printed booklet, a PDF and a radio broadcast. Which characteristics vary?
questions.explain: Montserrat Ready's guide changes format (text or audio) and medium (paper, digital file or radio) while the content stays the same.

questions.stem: Caribbean Statistics Bureau's reports have been accurate and trustworthy for 20 years, so students cite them with confidence. Which characteristic does this describe?
questions.explain: The Bureau's long record of accurate, trustworthy reports shows reliability, which is how dependable a source is over time.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: A Bayleaf Hill Secondary student must justify her choice of sources for a CAPE IT assignment using SO 1.6. Which set lists the CXC criteria for selecting information sources?
options: Availability, cost, depth, breadth, format and medium
Bias, accuracy, cultural context, completeness, currency and refereed status
Currency, relevance, authority, accuracy and purpose
Define, analyse, evaluate, select, implement and review
questions.explain: To justify her choices under SO 1.6 she should apply bias, accuracy, cultural context, completeness, currency and refereed or un-refereed status.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: A student in The Valley finds a report praising cruise tourism that was written and paid for by the cruise line BlueWave. Which criterion should make her cautious?
questions.explain: BlueWave has a financial interest in the report's conclusion, so it may present only one side; the student should suspect bias.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: Researching phishing in the Caribbean, a Coralstone College student can cite a peer-reviewed journal article or an un-refereed blog. The refereed article is usually preferred because:
options: It is always more current than any blog on the same topic.
It is guaranteed to contain no bias of any kind.
It is always free and easy to obtain online.
Experts checked its methods and claims before it was published.
questions.explain: Experts checked the article's methods and claims before publication, giving the student quality control a blog lacks. It does not guarantee currency, zero bias or free access.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: Writing a field-trip guide for Seagrape Bay Secondary School, a teacher finds a US website advising students to pack winter coats. Why is it a poor source for this guide?
options: It is un-refereed, so every fact on it must be false.
It is a primary source, which cannot be used for guides.
Its cultural context does not match the Caribbean setting of the readers.
It is too complete, so it contains too much detail.
questions.explain: Winter-coat advice suits a US climate, not the Caribbean setting of the school's students, so its cultural context does not match.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: A Spanish Town student finds an unsigned, undated web page claiming one Caribbean island has the world's fastest Internet. Which characteristic of Internet information affects source selection?
options: Every page is checked by a central authority before it goes live.
Information online never changes once it has been published.
Anyone can publish without review, so quality and authorship vary widely.
Web content is always more accurate than printed content.
questions.explain: The page has no author or date because anyone can publish online without review, so the student must check authorship, date and accuracy.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: Before quoting a tourism statistic from a website, a Flamboyant Heights College student checks it against a government report and a journal. Which criterion is she applying?
questions.explain: Checking the website's statistic against other trusted sources tests whether it is correct, which is the accuracy criterion.

questions.topic: SO 1.6 · Criteria for Selecting Information Sources
questions.stem: A student comparing exam results across five Guyanese secondary schools finds a source giving pass rates for only two of them. Which criterion does it fail?
questions.explain: With figures for only two of the five schools, the source does not cover everything the student needs, so it fails on completeness.

questions.stem: Nassau Family Clinic enters patient data, calculates bills, prints receipts, saves records and reviews complaints. Which is the information processing cycle in the CXC syllabus?
options: Input, processing and output, with no other stages
Input, processing, output, storage and feedback
Define, analyse, implement, evaluate and review
questions.explain: The clinic's work maps onto all five stages: input (entering data), processing (bills), output (receipts), storage (records) and feedback (complaints).

questions.stem: At Scarborough Dive Shop, customer ratings are reviewed each month and used to improve the booking form. In the information processing cycle, feedback is:
options: Optional evaluation or updates that loop back to the input stage.
The final printed report given to the customer.
Saving data to a hard disk for later retrieval.
Keying data from paper forms into a computer.
questions.explain: Reviewing ratings and updating the booking form uses results to evaluate the system and loops back to input, which is feedback.

questions.stem: Layou Supermarket's system totals daily sales, sorts items by quantity sold and analyses weekly trends. Which activities belong to the processing stage?
questions.explain: Totalling, sorting and analysing the supermarket's sales turn data into information, so they are processing activities.

questions.stem: A clerk at the Port-au-Prince Family Clinic keys patient details from paper forms into a computer. Which stage is this?
questions.explain: Keying the clinic's paper forms into the computer is data capture and entry, which makes up the input stage.

questions.stem: A CAPE IT class compares how shops on Albert Street in Belize City keep their records. Which of these is an example of an automated information system?
options: A teacher's paper mark book totalled with a pencil and calculator.
A card index of library borrowers kept in wooden drawers.
A handwritten ledger of daily sales at a market stall.
A supermarket checkout that scans barcodes and updates stock levels.
questions.explain: The barcode checkout uses a computer to capture data and update stock automatically; the other three Albert Street examples are manual systems.

questions.stem: The George Town law firm Hodge & Lake is replacing its paper filing cabinets with a computerised records system. Compared with the manual system, its main advantage is that it:
options: Needs no electricity, equipment or trained staff.
Never needs any data to be entered by people.
Sorts and retrieves records much faster and more accurately.
Costs nothing to set up or to maintain.
questions.explain: The firm's new system will sort and retrieve case records far faster and more accurately, though it still needs power, equipment and data entry.

questions.stem: Sunset Beach Hotel emails its monthly occupancy report to the tourism office. Which stage is this?
questions.explain: Emailing the report disseminates the hotel's information to those who need it, which is the output stage.

questions.stem: A Hummingbird Ridge High School student's database stores names, single grade letters, test scores, voice notes and photos. Which list gives the types of DATA representation named in the syllabus?
options: Text, graphics, sound, video and tables
Character, string, numeric, aural and visual
questions.explain: Her database holds string (names), character (grades), numeric (scores), aural (voice notes) and visual (photos) data, the five types in the syllabus.

questions.stem: The courier app IslandDrop stores the town name "Philipsburg" as a sequence of letters in its address field. Which data type is this?
questions.explain: "Philipsburg" is a sequence of characters, so IslandDrop stores it as a string; a character type would hold only one symbol.

questions.stem: A landline call from Grenville travels as a smoothly varying voltage, while a laptop sends its files as pulses for 0 and 1. Which statement correctly contrasts analogue and digital signals?
options: Analogue signals use discrete values; digital signals vary continuously.
Analogue signals vary continuously; digital signals use discrete values such as 0 and 1.
Both use only the values 0 and 1, but at different speeds.
Analogue signals carry only text; digital signals carry only sound.
questions.explain: The landline's smoothly varying voltage is analogue, taking any value in a range; the laptop's 0 and 1 pulses are digital, using discrete values.

questions.stem: A Calabash Point Secondary student types a capital "A" and the computer stores its ASCII code, denary 65. What is this in 7-bit binary?
questions.explain: 65 = 64 + 1, so the computer sets the bits for 64 and 1: 1000001. 1100001 would be 97, lower-case "a".

questions.stem: A sensor at the Commewijne marina SeaDock sends the binary number 1011 to report how many boats are docked. What is the denary value?
questions.explain: 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11, so SeaDock's sensor is reporting 11 boats.

questions.stem: With its radio damaged, a boat crew off St. John's flashes an SOS with a torch in Morse Code to a ship nearby. Morse Code represents letters using:
options: Seven-bit binary numbers stored in memory.
Musical notes written on a five-line stave.
Patterns of short and long signals (dots and dashes).
Graphs and charts that show trends.
questions.explain: The crew's torch flashes are short and long signals (dots and dashes), which is how Morse Code encodes each character.

questions.stem: The agency Turks and Caicos Tourism Watch must show how monthly cruise passenger arrivals at Cockburn Town change over a year. Which representation shows this best?
questions.explain: A line graph lets Turks and Caicos Tourism Watch show the rise and fall in monthly arrivals across the year at a glance.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: A Santiago family, the Peñas, connect their home PC to the Internet over a telephone line using a modem. What does a modem do?
options: Stores web pages so they load faster for every user on a network.
Translates a domain name into an IP address for the browser.
Converts between digital computer signals and analogue signals carried on a phone or cable line.
Scrambles data so only someone with a key can read it.
questions.explain: The Peñas' modem modulates the PC's digital data onto the analogue phone line and demodulates incoming signals back to digital.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: The Bridgetown firm Island Traders calls its suppliers in Miami over its Internet connection rather than a traditional phone line. Which tool is this?
questions.explain: Island Traders is using Voice over Internet Protocol, which carries voice calls as data over the Internet, often at lower cost.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: A Palm Beach web designer must upload the San Nicolas Bakery's new website files to a remote server. Which tool is designed for this?
questions.explain: File Transfer Protocol lets the designer upload the bakery's files from her computer to the remote server.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: An IT technician in Roseau logs in to a remote server with telnet over a café's public Wi-Fi. Which is a valid disadvantage of telnet?
options: It cannot give any form of access to a remote computer.
It sends data, including passwords, unencrypted, so it can be intercepted.
It works only for sending short text messages to phones.
It requires a video camera and microphone on both ends.
questions.explain: Telnet sends the technician's password in plain text, so anyone snooping on the café Wi-Fi could intercept it.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: A Frangipani Hill Academy teacher wants students at home during a storm closure to see and hear her lesson live. Which reason justifies web conferencing rather than a discussion forum?
options: The class needs live audio and video interaction in real time.
Students need to post replies over several days at their own pace.
The teacher wants a permanent threaded record of written posts.
The class has no Internet connection at all.
questions.explain: The teacher needs live audio and video in real time, which web conferencing supports; forums suit asynchronous, threaded discussion.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: SXM Coding Club wants its weekly news to reach members' email inboxes rather than a page they must visit. Which tool should it use?
questions.explain: A mailing list emails each message to every subscribed club member; forums and message boards must be visited online.

questions.topic: SO 1.9 · Tools Used in Information Technology
questions.stem: A Breadfruit Valley Secondary student types "Beef Island airport flight arrivals" into a search box and gets a ranked list of matching web pages. A search engine is best described as:
options: A device that converts digital signals to analogue for phone lines.
A program that uploads files from a PC to a web server.
An online service that indexes web pages and returns results matching a user's keywords.
A website where users post threaded discussions on topics.
questions.explain: The search engine had already crawled and indexed web pages, so it could rank those matching the student's keywords.

questions.stem: At Vieux Fort Supermart, every swipe of a card at the till is recorded the instant the sale is made. Which type of information system is this?
questions.explain: The Vieux Fort Supermart tills capture each sale as it happens, which is the job of a TPS: recording routine, day-to-day transactions.

questions.stem: Each Monday the middle managers of the Lac Bay Resort receive a summary of last week's bookings drawn from the front-desk records. Which type of IS produces this?
questions.explain: The resort's weekly booking summaries are regular reports built from TPS data for middle managers, which is what an MIS provides.

questions.stem: The manager of the Cockleshell Bay Hotel uses "what-if" models to test how a 10% room-rate rise would affect bookings next season. Which type of IS is this?
questions.explain: Testing a rate rise with what-if models is decision support: a DSS lets the Cockleshell Bay manager explore options before deciding.

questions.stem: The CEO of the Caribbean Shipping Group opens a dashboard of key indicators for all its ports and drills down into Willemstad's figures. Which type of IS is this?
questions.explain: A high-level dashboard of key indicators with drill-down for a CEO is an EIS, built for senior executives.

questions.stem: A clinic in Salem installs a program that asks about a patient's symptoms and, using stored rules, suggests a likely cause as a doctor would. An expert system is best described as:
options: A system that uses a knowledge base and rules to give advice like a human specialist.
A system that records routine sales and payments as they occur.
A system that gives senior managers graphical summaries of performance.
A suite of word processing, email and scheduling tools for office staff.
questions.explain: The clinic's program applies a knowledge base and rules to give specialist-style advice, which is exactly what an expert system does.

questions.stem: Every morning The Valley Pharmacy prints a report listing only the medicines whose stock has fallen below the reorder level. What type of report is this?
questions.explain: The pharmacy's report shows only items outside the normal range (below reorder level), so it is an exception report.

questions.stem: The general manager of the Front Street Jewellers asks, just once, for a report on sales during St. Maarten Carnival week. What type of report is this?
questions.explain: A one-off request for Carnival-week sales is not scheduled, so it is an ad hoc report produced on demand.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: A Form 5 student at Coralstone College is listing the parts of the school library's lending system for a CAPE revision chart. Which list gives the six components in the syllabus?
options: Input, processing, output, storage, feedback and users
Hardware, software, data, procedures, users and wisdom
Monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer, CPU and modem
Hardware, software, data, procedures, users and network
questions.explain: The library system, like any IS, is made up of hardware, software, data, procedures, users and network.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: At Montego Bay Marina, a laminated sheet tells staff exactly how to back up the sales database every night at closing. This sheet is which component?
questions.explain: The marina's backup sheet is a set of written instructions for staff, which makes it the procedures component.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: Cole Bay Auto Parts buys new computers but has no software installed, no stock data and no trained staff yet. Why can the hardware not produce useful information on its own?
options: It needs software, data, procedures and users working together with it.
Hardware is only used for storage, never for processing.
Hardware can only work when it is connected to the Internet.
Hardware produces information but cannot display it.
questions.explain: Cole Bay Auto Parts' computers only produce information when software, data, procedures and users work together with the hardware.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: Island Hardware Ltd has branches in Georgetown and Bartica, and both branches check and update one shared stock database. Which component makes this possible?
questions.explain: Linking the Georgetown and Bartica branches to one database depends on the network component.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: Nassau Harbour Guesthouse installs a new booking system, but it fails within a week because no staff were ever trained to use it. Which relationship broke down?
options: Hardware and network: the cables were too short.
Users and procedures: people could not follow the system's procedures.
Software and data: the files used the wrong format.
Data and hardware: the disk was too small.
questions.explain: The guesthouse staff could not follow the system's procedures, so the link between users and procedures failed, not the technology.

questions.topic: SO 2.2 · Components of an Information System
questions.stem: At Store Bay Hotel, guest names, room numbers and payment amounts are stored in the reservation system. These items are which component?
questions.explain: The guest names, room numbers and payments are raw facts held by the Store Bay system, so they are the data component.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A cashier at the Layou Supermart needs a device that reads product codes into the till so prices appear automatically. Which of these is an input device?
questions.explain: A barcode scanner sends product codes into the till, so it is the input device; the others store data or produce output.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A Sea-Almond Secondary School student runs a spreadsheet and the computer carries out each formula instruction in turn. What is the main function of the processor (CPU)?
options: Fetching, decoding and executing program instructions.
Storing files permanently when the power is off.
Displaying output to the user on a screen.
Connecting the computer to the Internet.
questions.explain: Running the student's spreadsheet means the CPU repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes each program instruction.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A teacher in Port-au-Prince needs her lesson files kept on her laptop even after she switches it off overnight. Which of these is a storage device?
questions.explain: A solid-state drive keeps the teacher's files when the power is off; the others are input or output devices.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: The office at the San Pedro Realty plugs a printer and a document scanner into its main desktop PC by USB. A peripheral device is best described as:
options: The main circuit board that holds the processor.
A program that manages the computer's memory.
The part of the CPU that performs calculations.
An external device connected to the computer, such as a printer or scanner.
questions.explain: The realty office's printer and scanner sit outside the main computer and connect to it, so they are peripheral devices.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A cashier at the Harbour Drive Boutique in George Town must hand each customer a paper record of their purchase. Which device is needed?
questions.explain: A paper record is printed output, so the boutique needs a receipt printer at the till.

questions.topic: SO 2.3 · Hardware: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A clerk at the Grenville Insurance loses an unsaved letter when a power cut hits, but saved files are still there. Why does a computer need secondary storage as well as RAM?
options: RAM is much slower than a hard disk, so it is rarely used.
RAM is volatile, so data must be kept on secondary storage when the power is off.
Secondary storage carries out all program instructions.
RAM can only hold data that has been printed.
questions.explain: The unsaved letter was lost because RAM is volatile; the saved files survived because secondary storage keeps data without power.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: The owner of the Commewijne Dive Shop wants a program to work out monthly takings and wages in rows and columns. Which of these is application software?
questions.explain: A spreadsheet program helps the owner do a real-world task (calculating takings), so it is application software.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A Mahoe Grove High School lab PC is running a browser, a word processor and a printer job all at once without them clashing. Which is a function of an operating system?
options: Translating a whole high-level program into machine code.
Managing memory, files, processes and devices.
Creating slides for a business presentation.
Scanning a single file for viruses on request.
questions.explain: Keeping the lab PC's programs, memory, files and printer working together is the operating system's job of managing resources.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A programmer at the Antigua Code Lab finishes a program and converts the whole thing into machine code before anyone runs it. What does a compiler do?
options: Translates a whole high-level program into machine code before it runs.
Translates and runs a program one line at a time.
Converts assembly language mnemonics into machine code.
Compresses files to save storage space.
questions.explain: Translating the whole program into machine code before it runs is what a compiler does, unlike an interpreter's line-by-line approach.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: The IT technician at the Providenciales Medical Centre installs antivirus, backup and file compression programs on every PC. These are examples of:
questions.explain: Antivirus, backup and compression programs maintain and protect the centre's computers, so they are utility software.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: In a classroom at a Santo Domingo school, a chip in the air-conditioner reads the room temperature and switches the compressor on and off. This is an example of:
questions.explain: The air-conditioner chip senses temperature and acts on it by switching the compressor, which makes it an embedded control system.

questions.topic: SO 2.4 · Software: Purpose, Functions and Types
questions.stem: A research team places a buoy in Carlisle Bay whose embedded system only records seawater temperature and changes nothing. It is a:
questions.explain: The Carlisle Bay buoy only reads and records data without acting on it, so it is a monitoring system, not a control system.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: The board of Caribbean Fresh Foods, based in Oranjestad, is reviewing several choices this month. Which decision is strategic?
options: Deciding which staff work tomorrow's morning shift.
Setting next quarter's advertising budget for one store.
Reordering bottled water when stock runs low.
Deciding whether to open a new branch in Curaçao within five years.
questions.explain: Opening a Curaçao branch within five years is long-term and affects the whole company, so it is a strategic decision.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: The duty supervisor at the Portsmouth Supermart is deciding which staff will work tomorrow's morning shift. Which level of decision is this?
questions.explain: Tomorrow's shift rota is a short-term, day-to-day choice made by a supervisor, so it is operational.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: Middle managers at the Cane Garden Bay Resort are setting next quarter's marketing budget for the hotel. Which level of decision are they making?
questions.explain: A quarterly budget set by middle managers is medium-term, so the resort managers are making a tactical decision.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: A shift supervisor at the Castries Bakery checks today's sales and stock figures before ordering flour. Which describes the information needed for operational decisions?
options: Detailed, internal, frequent and highly structured.
Forecast-based, long-term and mainly from outside sources.
Vague, rarely needed and mostly about competitors.
questions.explain: The bakery supervisor needs detailed, internal, frequent and structured figures, which is typical of operational information.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: The directors of the Island Cruises Ltd are deciding whether to add a new route to Antigua within five years. Strategic decisions usually rely on information that is:
options: Detailed, internal, historical and fully structured.
Summarised, often external, future-focused and unstructured.
Produced only by the till system each hour.
questions.explain: A five-year route decision relies on summarised, often external and future-focused information, which is typical of strategic decisions.

questions.topic: SO 2.5 · Importance of Data and Information
questions.stem: A loan officer at the Rincon Credit Union follows set rules on income limits but uses judgement on an applicant's history. A decision like this is:
questions.explain: The loan officer combines fixed rules with personal judgement, so the decision is semi-structured.

questions.stem: A technician in the Palmetto Point Secondary computer lab types "ipconfig /all" at a prompt to see a PC's network settings. Which type of HCI is this?
questions.explain: Typing ipconfig /all at a prompt means the technician gives typed instructions, which is a command line interface.

questions.stem: A bank ATM in Philipsburg shows numbered options: 1 Withdraw, 2 Balance, 3 Deposit, and the customer picks one. Which type of HCI is this?
questions.explain: The ATM offers a list of choices to select from, so it is a menu-driven interface.

questions.stem: A resident of Sandy Point applies for a passport online by filling in labelled boxes for name, date of birth and address. Which type of HCI does this use?
questions.explain: Completing labelled boxes, like a paper form on screen, is a form-based interface.

questions.stem: A traveller types "Show me flights from Curaçao to Aruba next Friday" into the Curaçao Travel app, and it understands. Which type of HCI is this?
questions.explain: The app understands an ordinary everyday sentence, so it uses a natural language interface.

questions.stem: A secretary at the Little Bay Realty drags an old file icon onto the recycle bin to delete it. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Dragging an icon to the bin acts directly on on-screen objects, so it is direct manipulation.

questions.stem: A Form 4 student at Sandbox Tree College opens a laptop and sees windows, icons and menus that she clicks with a pointer. Which features define a graphical user interface (GUI)?
options: Typed commands at a blinking prompt.
Windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP).
Spoken instructions with no screen at all.
Labelled boxes copied from paper forms only.
questions.explain: The student's screen shows windows, icons, menus and a pointer, which are the WIMP features that define a GUI.

questions.stem: Driving along the road to Meads Bay, a driver says "call home" and the car's phone system dials the number. Which type of HCI is this?
questions.explain: The driver controls the system by speaking, so it is a speech (voice) interface.

questions.stem: A Bayleaf Hill Secondary student is asked to evaluate an online timetable app for a CAPE task. Which list gives the CXC principles for evaluating an HCI?
options: Ease of use, ease of learning, ease of navigation, alignment and use of colour
Speed, efficiency, portability, maintainability and storage
Bias, accuracy, currency, completeness and cultural context
Forms, menus, command line, speech and direct manipulation
questions.explain: The student should judge the timetable on ease of use, ease of learning, ease of navigation, alignment and use of colour.

questions.stem: The website of the Spanish Town Car Rentals shows red text on a green background, and many visitors say it is hard to read. Which principle is poorly applied?
questions.explain: Red on green clashes and is hard for many users, including colour-blind users, to read, so use of colour is weak.

questions.stem: On the Parika Tours booking form, the labels and boxes sit at different positions, so the eye jumps around. Which principle is weak?
questions.explain: Labels and boxes that do not line up show poor alignment on the Parika Tours form.

questions.stem: A family in Nassau booking day trips on the Bahamas Ferry website cannot find their way back to the home page from the booking screen. Which principle is weak?
questions.explain: Being unable to get back to the home page shows the ferry site has poor ease of navigation.

questions.stem: A new cashier at the Port of Spain Pharmacy masters the till interface after only ten minutes of training. Which principle does this show?
questions.explain: Mastering the till in ten minutes shows the interface is quick to learn, so ease of learning is strong.

questions.stem: Island Motors is designing a dashboard for its taxis driving the busy Cole Bay roads. Which design choice most improves ease of use in a car dashboard HCI?
options: Large physical controls for frequent tasks that can be used without looking away from the road.
Small touch icons hidden inside several layers of on-screen menus.
Bright flashing colours on every control so all of them stand out.
A command line where the driver types instructions while moving.
questions.explain: Large physical controls let taxi drivers act without looking away from the road, making the dashboard easy and safe to use.

questions.stem: Staff at the Villa Beach Resort include receptionists, a network administrator and guests who book online. Which of these is an IT professional?
questions.explain: The network administrator builds and maintains the resort's IT systems, so he or she is the IT professional.

questions.stem: A cashier at the Cap-Haïtien Supermart uses the till system all day but never builds or repairs it. An end user is best described as:
options: A person who uses a finished system to do tasks, without building or maintaining it.
A person who writes and tests the program code for a system.
A person who designs the network that links the system.
A person who repairs the system's hardware faults.
questions.explain: The cashier uses the finished till system to do tasks without building or maintaining it, which is an end user.

questions.stem: A reservations clerk at the Placencia Hotel has used the booking system daily for six years and works fast with shortcuts. Which describes an expert user?
options: Is using the system for the first time and needs guidance.
Has built the system and maintains its database.
Avoids the system and relies on paper records.
Uses the system often, knows shortcuts and needs little help.
questions.explain: Six years of daily use and confident shortcut use make the clerk an expert user who needs little help.

questions.stem: George Town Library is launching a self-service catalogue for first-time computer users. Which interface feature best supports novice users?
options: Typed commands with many options and no help.
Hidden settings reached only through code.
questions.explain: Menus, prompts and on-screen help guide first-time library users who do not yet know the system.

questions.stem: On her first day at Carriacou Hotel, a receptionist uses the booking system with help from a printed manual. She is a:
questions.explain: The receptionist uses the system but is new to it and needs a manual, so she is a novice end user.

questions.stem: At Commewijne Resort, a database administrator maintains the booking system that the receptionists use. He is classed as:
questions.explain: Maintaining the database behind the receptionists' system makes the administrator an IT professional, not an end user.

questions.stem: A blind student at a St. John's school needs to read the school website's notices on her own. Which adaptation best helps a blind user use a website?
options: A screen reader that reads page content aloud.
A larger, brighter colour scheme on every page.
A faster mouse pointer with animated icons.
More images in place of text descriptions.
questions.explain: A screen reader reads the notices aloud, so the blind student can use the site without seeing the screen.

questions.stem: Statia Care Services is building an app for elderly residents on St. Eustatius to book clinic visits. The app should be adapted mainly by:
options: Using tiny icons so more features fit on one screen.
Using larger text and buttons on simple, uncluttered screens.
Requiring typed commands for every action.
Adding many animations and fast-moving menus.
questions.explain: Elderly users often have weaker eyesight and less IT experience, so larger text and buttons on simple screens suit them best.

questions.stem: Providenciales Health Centre is designing a check-in kiosk for patients who have limited reading skills. For such users, an interface should:
options: Use icons, pictures and audio prompts with simple wording.
Use long technical paragraphs to explain each step.
Rely on a command line with abbreviated keywords.
Remove all help so the screen is less crowded.
questions.explain: Icons, pictures and audio prompts with simple wording let patients with limited reading skills use the kiosk.

questions.stem: Santo Domingo Tourism Kiosk at the cruise pier serves visitors from many countries and backgrounds. Which adaptation addresses cultural differences among users?
options: Increasing the font size on all screens for every user.
Offering Spanish, English, French and German, with local date and currency formats.
Adding a screen reader for blind users.
Fitting motion sensors to the entrance doors.
questions.explain: Offering several languages with local date and currency formats adapts the kiosk to visitors' cultural backgrounds.

questions.stem: At Cole Bay Health Clinic, automatic doors open when a patient in a wheelchair approaches. Which type of adaptation do the doors use?
questions.explain: The clinic doors detect people approaching and open on their own, so they use sensors.

questions.stem: Holetown Resort makes a staff training video, and two new employees are deaf. Which accessibility feature helps deaf users follow it?
questions.explain: Captions or subtitles show the spoken words as text, so the deaf employees can follow the training video.

questions.stem: All the computers in one building of a secondary school in Oranjestad are linked so students can share printers and files. Which best describes a LAN?
options: A network spanning several countries, linked by satellites.
A secure tunnel across the Internet to a private network.
A network covering a small area, such as one school building.
A network covering a whole city's government offices.
questions.explain: A network within one school building covers a small area, which is what defines a LAN.

questions.stem: A network links government offices spread across Philipsburg, Cole Bay and Simpson Bay on the Dutch side of the island. It is best called a:
questions.explain: Offices linked across one town or city-sized area form a MAN, larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN.

questions.stem: A Seagrape Bay Secondary School teacher working from home in Portsmouth connects securely to the school network over the Internet to upload marks. Which technology is this?
questions.explain: A secure, encrypted link to a private network across the Internet is a VPN.

questions.stem: Virgin Gorda Hotel lets trusted food suppliers log in to view its stock orders on its private network. This is:
questions.explain: Giving trusted outside suppliers controlled access to part of a private network is an extranet.

questions.stem: In the Jeremie Street Boutique's office, every PC has its own cable running back to one central switch. In which topology does every device connect to a central switch?
questions.explain: Each PC wired to one central switch is the defining layout of a star topology.

questions.stem: Lifeguards at Mullet Bay use walkie-talkies: both can speak, but only one at a time, saying "over" when done. Which communication mode is this?
questions.explain: Data flows both ways but only one direction at a time, so the walkie-talkies use half duplex.

questions.stem: Lac Bay Café upgrades its Internet plan so more data can flow each second for guests streaming videos. Bandwidth refers to:
options: The amount of data that can be transmitted per second.
The physical length of a network cable.
The number of devices on a network.
The distance a Wi-Fi signal can reach.
questions.explain: The café's upgrade raises bandwidth: the amount of data that can be transmitted per second.

questions.stem: An accountant living on Saba works for the Philipsburg firm Island Accounts from home, sending work over the Internet. This is:
questions.explain: Working for the Philipsburg firm from home using telecommunications is telecommuting.

questions.stem: A CAPE IT class at Flamboyant Heights College draws the OSI model on the board, one layer per row. How many layers does the OSI model have?
questions.explain: The OSI model drawn by the class has seven layers, from Physical up to Application.

questions.stem: An email sent from Philipsburg to Barbados passes through many networks, each choosing the next hop by IP address. Which OSI layer routes packets between networks using IP addresses?
questions.explain: Choosing paths between networks by IP address is the job of the Network layer.

questions.stem: A student at home in Sandy Point opens a web page (HTTP) and uploads a file to a server (FTP). At which layer of the TCP/IP model do these operate?
questions.explain: HTTP and FTP are services used directly by the student's programs, so they work at the Application layer.

questions.stem: Curaçao Bank sends account files to Aruba and needs every packet to arrive, in order, with acknowledgements. Which transport-layer protocol provides this?
questions.explain: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery with acknowledgements, which the bank's file transfers need.

questions.stem: A technician at the Salem ISP tests a damaged cable to check whether electrical signals carrying raw bits get through. Which OSI layer deals with this?
questions.explain: Cables, signals and raw bits are handled by the Physical layer, the lowest OSI layer.

questions.stem: A Hummingbird Ridge High School student is labelling a TCP/IP diagram for a CAPE revision poster, starting from the top. Which correctly lists the TCP/IP layers from top to bottom?
questions.explain: The student's poster should read Application, Transport, Internet, Network access from top to bottom.

questions.stem: In the Meads Bay Realty office, a switch forwards frames to each PC using its MAC address. MAC addresses and switches are associated with which OSI layer?
questions.explain: The office switch forwards frames by MAC address, which is Data link layer work.

questions.stem: A student draws a network diagram for Calabash Point Secondary's computer lab. Which device connects the school LAN to the Internet (WAN)?
questions.explain: In the lab diagram, the router joins the school LAN to the Internet (WAN).

questions.stem: Spanish Town Dental Clinic is designing a new office network and must choose between a hub and a switch. Why is a switch preferred to a hub?
options: It broadcasts every message to all devices, which is more secure.
It connects the LAN directly to the Internet without a router.
It sends data only to the destination device instead of to every port.
It removes the need for any network cables.
questions.explain: A switch sends data only to the destination device, reducing traffic and improving security on the clinic's network.

questions.stem: Guests at the Bartica Café see "BarticaCafe_Guest" in their phone's Wi-Fi list. The SSID in a wireless network design is:
options: The password used to encrypt the wireless network.
The hardware address of each connected device.
The speed of the wireless connection.
The name that identifies the wireless network.
questions.explain: "BarticaCafe_Guest" is the name that identifies the café's wireless network, which is its SSID.

questions.stem: Paradise Island Hotel is planning its guest Wi-Fi for 2026. Which wireless security setting should the design specify for the strongest protection?
options: WPA3 with a strong network key
An open network with MAC filtering only
A hidden SSID with no encryption
questions.explain: WPA3 with a strong network key is the strongest wireless protection for the hotel's 2026 design.

questions.stem: The office router at the Frederick Street Boutique only lets in the shop's three laptops whose hardware addresses it has stored. MAC filtering secures a wireless network by:
options: Encrypting all data sent across the network.
Allowing only devices whose hardware addresses are on an approved list.
Changing the network name every day.
Blocking all websites that are not approved.
questions.explain: The boutique's router admits only devices whose MAC addresses are on its approved list, which is MAC filtering.

questions.stem: The router at the Cole Bay Pharmacy uses WPA2, which protects data with AES so neighbours cannot read it. AES, used in WPA2 and WPA3, is:
options: The encryption standard that scrambles wireless data.
The name broadcast by the wireless router.
A type of Ethernet cable used for LANs.
The password for the router's settings page.
questions.explain: AES is the encryption standard that scrambles the pharmacy's wireless data so outsiders cannot read it.

questions.stem: Villa Beach Realty is drawing a simple network design to protect its office PCs from Internet attacks. Where should a firewall be placed?
options: Between each printer and its power socket.
Between the internal LAN and the Internet connection.
Inside every Ethernet cable on the LAN.
After the Internet, on the remote web server only.
questions.explain: Placing the firewall between the office LAN and the Internet lets it filter all traffic entering and leaving.

questions.stem: An old office at the Port-au-Prince Shipping Co. has all its PCs tapped into one long backbone cable with terminators at each end. Which topology is this?
questions.explain: All devices sharing a single backbone cable with terminators is a bus topology.

questions.stem: Belmopan Mill links its PCs in a closed loop, each passing data on to the next PC until it arrives. In a ring topology, data:
options: Passes through a central switch to reach each device.
Is broadcast along a single backbone with terminators.
Is sent only by wireless signals between devices.
Travels around a closed loop from one device to the next.
questions.explain: In the mill's ring, data travels around the closed loop from one device to the next until it reaches its destination.

questions.stem: A technician is setting up a brand-new router for the Seven Mile Beach Café. What should be done first when configuring it?
options: Turn off all wireless encryption for faster speed.
Share the router password with every customer.
Change the default router admin password.
Remove the firewall so devices connect easily.
questions.explain: Default admin passwords are widely known, so the café's technician should change it first to stop others taking control.

questions.stem: When setting up Wi-Fi for Grand Anse Café, the owner prints a card for guests that says "Wi-Fi code: Sunset2026". The network key is:
options: The password guests enter to join the wireless network.
The name of the network shown in the Wi-Fi list.
The hardware address of the router.
The cable that links the router to the modem.
questions.explain: "Sunset2026" is the password guests enter to join the café's Wi-Fi, which is the network key.

questions.stem: In the Domineestraat Boutique's star network, the cable to the stockroom PC is chewed through by a rat. What happens?
options: The whole network stops working at once.
Data reverses direction around the loop.
All devices switch to wireless automatically.
Only that workstation loses its connection.
questions.explain: In a star, each PC has its own cable to the switch, so only the stockroom PC loses its connection.

questions.stem: At St. John's Shipping Co., a single cut in the main backbone cable stops every PC from communicating. A major disadvantage of a bus topology is that:
options: It needs far more cable than any other topology.
A break in the backbone cable brings down the whole network.
Each device needs its own port on a central switch.
It cannot connect more than two devices.
questions.explain: The shipping office shows the bus weakness: a break in the backbone brings down the whole network.

questions.stem: A technician in the Frangipani Hill Academy lab wants to check whether a web server can be reached and how fast it replies. Which command does this?
questions.explain: ping sends test packets to a host and reports whether it replies and the response time.

questions.stem: The IT helper at the Providenciales Law Office must find a Windows PC's IP address, subnet mask and default gateway. Which command shows these?
questions.explain: ipconfig displays a Windows PC's IP address, subnet mask and default gateway.

questions.stem: At Punta Cana Café, websites fail to open by name but load when the owner types their IP address. Which command helps check the problem?
questions.explain: Sites load by IP but not by name, pointing to DNS, so nslookup is used to test name resolution.

questions.stem: A student's Windows laptop in a Philipsburg classroom shows an IP address beginning 169.254 and cannot get online. This most likely means:
options: It has the fastest possible Internet connection.
Its DNS server is working correctly.
It could not obtain an IP address from the router.
Its firewall has blocked all websites.
questions.explain: A 169.254 address is self-assigned, showing the laptop could not obtain an IP address from the router.

questions.stem: A wired PC at the Speightstown Insurance office suddenly shows no network connection. What is a sensible first step?
options: Replace the router with a new model.
Check the physical cable connection and the port's status lights.
questions.explain: Checking the cable and the port's status lights is a quick physical check that often finds the fault before anything drastic.

questions.stem: A PC at the Eagle Beach Hotel can reach other PCs on the LAN but not the Internet. The most likely fault is:
options: A faulty keyboard on the PC.
A missing HTML tag on the home page.
questions.explain: The default gateway is the route out of the LAN, so a wrong setting lets the hotel PC reach local PCs but not the Internet.

questions.stem: Guests at the Mero Resort complain that the Internet feels slow in the evenings. Which step measures the actual connection performance?
questions.explain: A speed test measures the resort's real upload and download speeds, giving evidence rather than complaints.

questions.stem: East End Design Studio swaps its laptops' hard disk drives for solid-state drives, and programs now open much faster. Why is an SSD faster than an HDD?
options: It has no moving parts, so data is accessed electronically.
It spins its platters faster than any hard disk.
It stores data on optical discs read by a laser.
It uses magnetic tape for random access.
questions.explain: SSDs have no moving parts and access data electronically, so the studio's laptops no longer wait for spinning platters.

questions.stem: A fisheries officer must record catch data on small boats at Simpson Bay and Grand Case. Which feature matters most when choosing a device?
questions.explain: Recording data on boats means the device must be carried easily, so portability matters most.

questions.stem: Gros Islet Hotel needs to store several terabytes of security-camera video cheaply. Which storage medium offers the lowest cost per gigabyte?
questions.explain: A hard disk drive offers large capacity at a low cost per gigabyte, ideal for the hotel's video archive.

questions.stem: Caribbean Link Ltd is laying a cable between Bonaire and Curaçao and needs top speed with no electrical interference. Which transmission medium fits?
questions.explain: Fibre-optic cable carries light, so it gives the highest speed over long distances with no electrical interference.

questions.stem: Programmers at the St. Kitts Code Lab must update a school fee system written by a colleague who has left. The maintainability of software is improved by:
options: Removing all comments to make the code shorter.
Writing the whole program as one long block.
Clear documentation and modular code that is easy to change.
Keeping no record of how the system works.
questions.explain: Clear documentation and modular code let the new programmers understand and change the fee system easily.

questions.stem: Willemstad Builders Ltd replaces its handwritten payroll with a computerised one. Which shows the greater efficiency of the new system?
options: It needs more clerks to check each payslip.
It takes longer but uses more paper.
It processes more payslips in less time with fewer errors.
questions.explain: Processing more payslips in less time with fewer errors shows the computerised payroll is more efficient.

questions.stem: Salem Credit Union is reviewing how it protects member records on its computers. Which is a logical access control measure?
options: A security guard at the door
A swipe card for the main entrance
questions.explain: A user ID and password is controlled by software, so it is a logical access control.

questions.stem: Simpson Bay Bank wants to stop unauthorised people from walking into the room where its servers are kept. Which is a physical access control measure?
options: A locked server room opened with a key card.
Encrypting files stored on the server.
Requiring a password to log on.
questions.explain: A locked server room opened with a key card physically blocks entry, so it is a physical access control.

questions.stem: A new employee at the Sandy Ground Sailing Club must choose a password for the booking system. Which is the most effective password?
questions.explain: Gr8t!Bay#Sail26 is long and mixes upper and lower case, numbers and symbols, so it is the hardest to guess.

questions.stem: Staff at the Negril Hotel unlock the safe-deposit room by placing a finger on a scanner. Biometric authentication uses:
options: Unique physical characteristics such as fingerprints or face shape.
A code sent by text message to a phone.
A plastic card with a magnetic stripe.
A password the user must remember.
questions.explain: The fingerprint scanner checks a unique physical characteristic, which is biometric authentication.

questions.stem: Linden Credit Union is deciding whether to replace staff passwords with fingerprint scanners. Compared with passwords, biometric systems are:
options: Cheaper to install and easier to change if stolen.
Harder to share or forget, but more costly and raise privacy concerns.
Easier to guess because features are public.
Identical in security and cost to passwords.
questions.explain: Fingerprints cannot be forgotten or easily shared, but scanners cost more and storing body data raises privacy concerns.

questions.stem: At Nassau Pharmacy, a patient's prescription record must stay correct and must not be altered by unauthorised staff. Data integrity means that data is:
options: Available on every device at all times.
Encrypted so no one can ever read it.
Accurate, complete and unchanged by unauthorised users.
Stored only on paper in a locked cabinet.
questions.explain: Keeping the prescription record correct and unaltered by unauthorised staff is data integrity.

questions.stem: Scarborough Clinic locks its servers, uses passwords and keeps backups to protect patient records. Data security is best defined as:
options: Making data available to anyone who asks for it.
Converting data into charts and graphs.
Storing data in the cloud for faster access.
Protecting data from unauthorised access, change or loss.
questions.explain: The clinic's locks, passwords and backups all protect data from unauthorised access, change or loss, which is data security.

questions.stem: A Breadfruit Valley Secondary student logs in to Kingstown Study Portal, which checks her user ID and password first. Authentication is:
options: Scrambling data so it cannot be read.
Copying data to a second location.
Verifying that a user is who they claim to be.
Deciding which reports a user may print.
questions.explain: Checking the student's ID and password verifies she is who she claims to be, which is authentication.

questions.stem: After a power surge in Cap-Haïtien, a shop's stock spreadsheet opens with garbled characters and wrong values. This is:
questions.explain: The surge damaged the file so its contents are garbled and wrong, which is data corruption.

questions.stem: A cashier at the Albert Street Boutique types a secret string of characters to log in to the till. Which term describes this?
questions.explain: The secret string the cashier types to prove her identity is a password.

questions.stem: Cayman Bank scrambles customer files into unreadable text before sending them to Curaçao. Ciphertext is produced by:
questions.explain: Scrambling readable data into unreadable ciphertext is encryption, which protects the bank's files in transit.

questions.stem: Island Hardware Ltd in St. George's is investigating several events on its network last month. Which situation shows a breach of data security?
options: A manager prints a report she is authorised to see.
A former employee still logs in and copies customer records.
A backup copy is stored in a locked safe.
A file is encrypted before being emailed.
questions.explain: A former employee logging in and copying customer records is unauthorised access, which breaches data security.

questions.stem: Simpson Bay Tours has one page listing its boat trips, plus other linked pages, all under simpsonbaytours.sx. Which correctly distinguishes a web page from a web site?
options: A web site is a single document; a web page is a collection of sites.
They are the same thing with two different names.
