A web page is stored offline; a web site is stored online.
A web page is a single document; a web site is a collection of linked pages under one domain.
questions.explain: The boat-trip listing is one web page; all the linked pages under the company's domain make up the web site.

questions.stem: Island Tours Suriname advertises its tour page at https://www.example.sr/tours/index.html. Which part of the URL is the domain name?
questions.explain: www.example.sr names the server hosting the tours; https is the protocol and the rest is the path and file name.

questions.stem: A student in All Saints types a school website's name into a browser, and a DNS server looks up the number needed to find it. Domain Name Resolution converts:
options: An IP address into a MAC address.
HTML code into a web page layout.
A domain name into its IP address.
A web page into a PDF file.
questions.explain: DNS converts the website's domain name into its IP address so the browser can locate the server.

questions.stem: When a visitor in Cockburn Town clicks a link, the browser requests the page and the server sends it back using HTTP. HTTP is:
options: The language used to mark up the content of a web page.
The unique numeric address of a computer online.
A program used to view web pages.
The protocol that transfers web pages between servers and browsers.
questions.explain: HTTP is the protocol that transfers the requested page between the server and the visitor's browser.

questions.stem: Santo Domingo Ferry site uses one language to lay out its timetable page and another to store the timetable data with its own tags. Which correctly contrasts HTML and XML?
options: HTML stores data with user-defined tags; XML displays web pages.
Both use only predefined tags for formatting text.
HTML describes how content is displayed; XML describes and stores data with user-defined tags.
XML is a browser; HTML is a protocol.
questions.explain: The ferry site uses HTML to control how the page displays and XML to describe and store the timetable data with user-defined tags.

questions.stem: A Coralstone College student clicks from a news site to a museum site to a blog, following hyperlinks across the Internet. The World Wide Web is best described as:
options: The physical network of cables and routers linking computers.
A system of interconnected hypertext documents accessed over the Internet.
A single computer that stores every web site.
An email service run by Internet providers.
questions.explain: The student is moving through interconnected hypertext documents accessed over the Internet, which is the World Wide Web.

questions.stem: A visitor types simpsonbaytours.sx and lands on the page that welcomes them and links to every section. A web site's home page is:
options: The main entry page, usually the first page visitors see.
Any page saved on the user's own computer.
The last page in a site's navigation.
questions.explain: The page the visitor lands on first, which links to the rest of the site, is the home page.

questions.stem: A Form 5 student is building a web page for Carlisle Bay Beach Bar and wants the menu and photos to show in the browser. Which element contains all the visible content?
questions.explain: Everything visitors see on the beach bar's page, such as the menu and photos, goes inside the <body> element.

questions.stem: A student coding the Palm Beach Café web page wants to leave a note that the menu starts here, without it showing in the browser. Which is a correct HTML comment?
questions.explain: HTML comments are written <!-- ... -->, so the note is hidden from visitors but stays in the code.

questions.stem: A student is adding a photo of Prince Rupert Bay beach to the Island Tours page, with text for visitors who cannot see it. Which correctly displays an image with alternative text?
questions.explain: The tag uses src for the file and alt for the alternative text that screen readers can read aloud.

questions.stem: On the Island Tours home page, a student wants the words "Island tours" to link to tours.html. Which correctly creates a hyperlink?
questions.explain: A hyperlink uses the <a> tag with the href attribute, so <a href="tours.html"> links to the tours page.

questions.stem: A student wants the welcome paragraph on the Cane Garden Bay Café page to appear in blue, using inline styling. Which does this?
questions.explain: Inline styling uses the style attribute with CSS, and CSS spells it color, so style="color:blue;" turns the paragraph blue.

questions.stem: A student lists the steps to book a tour on the St. Lucia Ferry web page and wants them numbered 1, 2, 3. Which tags create a numbered list?
questions.explain: An ordered list <ol> with <li> items numbers the booking steps automatically.

questions.stem: A student builds a ferry timetable table for the SXM Ferry page, with "Departure" and "Arrival" as column headings. Which tag defines a header cell?
questions.explain: The <th> tag defines header cells such as Departure and Arrival, shown bold and centred by default.

questions.stem: A student adds the Kralendijk Beach Bar logo with . What are src and width?
questions.explain: src and width give extra information about the img element, so they are attributes.

questions.stem: At Sea-Almond Secondary School, the IT lab Wi-Fi keeps dropping. Ms. Richardson lists the symptoms, finds the cause and tests a fix. Problem-solving in IT is best described as:
options: A structured process for understanding an issue and finding an effective solution.
Changing settings at random until an error message disappears.
Buying the newest equipment whenever something goes wrong.
Recording a problem without trying to solve it.
questions.explain: Ms. Richardson followed logical stages to understand and fix the Wi-Fi fault, rather than guessing or simply buying new equipment.

questions.stem: Jaden, a student in Sandy Point, fixes his slow laptop by identifying the fault, trying options, applying one and checking it worked. Problem-solving is called a process because it:
options: Happens in a single step as soon as a problem appears.
Follows a series of stages, from understanding the problem to reviewing the solution.
Always produces the same solution for every problem.
Depends only on luck and the right equipment.
questions.explain: Jaden moved through stages, from understanding the slow laptop to reviewing his fix, which is what makes problem-solving a process.

questions.stem: Jan Thiel Dive Shop takes bookings on paper and often double-books, but wants no clashes at all. A problem can be described as:
options: Any computer that is more than five years old.
A solution that has already been implemented.
The gap between the current situation and the desired situation.
Information that has been stored on a disk.
questions.explain: Double-booking is the current situation and clash-free bookings the desired one; the problem is the gap between them.

questions.stem: Marisol, a farmer in Dominica, notices pests spreading through her crops. What is the best first problem-solving action?
options: Spray every chemical available across the whole farm at once.
Replant all crops immediately without investigating.
Wait to see whether the pests leave by themselves.
Find out exactly what the problem is: which pest, which crops and how widespread.
questions.explain: Marisol must first understand which pest, which crops and how far it has spread before she can choose a sensible solution.

questions.stem: A Brades shop owner wants shorter queues, so she first records busy hours and checkout times. Why is it said that nearly every problem has an information component?
options: Every problem can be solved by buying a computer.
Information is only needed after a solution is implemented.
Good solutions depend on gathering and using accurate information about the problem.
Problems disappear once they are written down.
questions.explain: Her queue data shows when and why delays happen, so any solution she chooses is based on accurate information.

questions.stem: Students at Mahoe Grove High School want less litter in the canteen. They suggest extra bins, posters and a clean-up rota, then compare them. Finding solutions to a problem usually involves:
options: Generating several possible solutions and choosing the best one on evidence.
Accepting the first idea anyone suggests.
Choosing the most expensive option available.
Avoiding comparison so the decision is quicker.
questions.explain: Comparing bins, posters and a rota on evidence leads to a better choice than accepting the first idea.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: Blowing Point Pharmacy says its stock 'keeps running out' and asks an analyst for new software. In the CXC syllabus, what is the first stage the analyst should carry out?
options: Select and justify the optimal solution.
questions.explain: Before any software is chosen, the analyst must define the pharmacy's problem clearly; solutions come only after it is understood.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: A Palmetto Point Secondary team is tackling slow lunch queues and must plan its work in the correct order. Which sequence matches the CXC problem-solving stages?
options: Analyse, define, implement, identify solutions, select and justify, evaluate and review
Define, analyse, identify and evaluate solutions, select and justify, implement, evaluate and review
Define, implement, analyse, select and justify, identify solutions, evaluate and review
Identify solutions, define, analyse, implement, select and justify, evaluate and review
questions.explain: The team should define, analyse, identify and evaluate solutions, select and justify, implement, then evaluate and review its queue solution.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: The Kingston firm Island Freight has late deliveries. Staff are interviewed and delivery logs examined for causes. During "analyse the problem", a team mainly:
options: Installs the chosen system and trains staff.
Breaks the problem down, studies its causes and gathers relevant information.
Checks whether the final solution met its goals.
Writes a single-sentence problem statement only.
questions.explain: Interviewing staff and studying delivery logs breaks the late-delivery problem down so suitable solutions can be identified.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: Kayla must recommend one of three booking systems for her family's Bartica guesthouse. To "select and justify the optimal solution", she must:
options: List every possible solution without choosing one.
Choose a solution and give no reasons.
Implement all the solutions at the same time.
Choose one solution and give reasons, such as cost, time and feasibility, why it beats the others.
questions.explain: Kayla should choose one booking system and back it with criteria such as cost, time and feasibility, showing why it beats the other two.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: Sandbox Tree College lists three ways to cut printing costs (duplex printing, print quotas, digital handouts) and compares the pros and cons of each. Which stage is this?
questions.explain: Generating the three options and weighing their strengths and weaknesses is identifying and evaluating possible solutions.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: Freeport Hardware has chosen a new point-of-sale system. Technicians now install it and cashiers attend training. Which problem-solving stage is this?
options: Select and justify the optimal solution
questions.explain: Installing the chosen point-of-sale system and training cashiers puts the solution into practice, which is implementation.

questions.topic: SO 3.2 · Stages of the Problem-Solving Process
questions.stem: Three months after a new library loan system went live at a Port of Spain school, the team checks whether overdue books have fallen. The final stage, evaluate and review, checks:
options: What the problem was before anyone studied it.
Whether the solution solved the problem and what improvements are needed.
questions.explain: Checking overdue-book figures measures the system against the original problem and shows what still needs improving.

questions.stem: A Villa Beach student sorting research for a school problem must label each item by how useful it is. Which four categories does the CXC syllabus use to classify such information?
questions.explain: Each item she found can be essential, desirable, extraneous (irrelevant) or cosmetic (presentation only).

questions.stem: A family in Cap-Haïtien is planning a hurricane evacuation and needs the locations of official shelters. To this family, the shelter locations are:
questions.explain: Without the shelter locations the family cannot plan its evacuation, so this information is essential.

questions.stem: Tia, a Bayleaf Hill Secondary student, is choosing a laptop for school work. A website tells her the year the manufacturer was founded. This information is:
questions.explain: The founding year does not help Tia judge whether the laptop suits school work, so it is extraneous.

questions.stem: Students preparing a report for the Belize City Youth Club add a coloured logo. It improves the look but does not affect the decision. This information is:
questions.explain: The logo only improves how the report looks, so it is cosmetic information.

questions.stem: Bodden Town Bakery is choosing a flour supplier. Customer reviews of each supplier are useful but not strictly required to decide. This information is:
questions.explain: The reviews help the bakery make a better choice, but it could still decide without them, so they are desirable.

questions.stem: Researchers in Guyana collect rainfall and soil data to study why a crop disease is spreading. This information supports which type of problem?
questions.explain: Measured rainfall and soil data used to investigate a disease make this a scientific problem.

questions.stem: A community group in Grenada gathers youth unemployment figures by neighbourhood to plan a job-skills programme. This information supports which type of problem?
questions.explain: The programme tackles a community issue affecting people, so the unemployment figures support a social problem.

questions.stem: Bayside Mart in Paramaribo is deciding whether to stock a new product, using sales forecasts and supplier prices. Which type of problem is this?
questions.explain: Using forecasts and prices to decide what Bayside Mart should stock is a business decision, so it is a commercial problem.

questions.stem: A Seagrape Bay Secondary School team researching ways to reduce street flooding must decide which sources to trust. Which criteria does the CXC syllabus list for accepting or rejecting information?
options: Relevance, reliability, timeliness, cost versus value and ethics
Availability, cost, depth, breadth, format and medium
Bias, accuracy, cultural context, completeness, currency, refereed status and Internet characteristics
questions.explain: The team should judge each source on bias, accuracy, cultural context, completeness, currency, refereed status and Internet characteristics.

questions.stem: Planning a school bus timetable for students from Cole Bay, a team realises it has pick-up times for only half the stops. Completeness, as a criterion for selecting information, asks whether:
options: All the information needed to solve the problem is available.
The document has a colourful, attractive cover.
At least one relevant fact has been found.
The source was published by a primary researcher.
questions.explain: With times for only half the stops, the information is incomplete and must be supplemented before the timetable can be planned.

questions.stem: A Flamboyant Heights College team uses 2012 mobile data prices to plan a 2026 app budget. On which criterion should this information be rejected?
questions.explain: Mobile data prices have changed since 2012, so the team's figures fail the currency criterion.

questions.stem: Jordan in Dickenson Bay is choosing a phone and reads a glowing review written by the seller's own marketing team. He should treat it with caution because of:
questions.explain: The seller's marketing team gains if Jordan buys, so the review is likely to be biased.

questions.stem: A health team is planning a campaign to reduce dengue in the Turks and Caicos Islands and must choose its evidence. Which source is most acceptable?
options: An anonymous social media post about home remedies.
A refereed journal study on mosquito control in the Caribbean.
An un-refereed blog selling insect repellent.
A 1985 leaflet about mosquitoes in Canada.
questions.explain: The refereed Caribbean study is evidence-based and fits local conditions; the others fail on bias, currency or cultural context.

questions.stem: A Hummingbird Ridge High School team copies a solution from a Scandinavian school's report that assumes regular snow days. Why should it be rejected for their school?
options: It is too current to be reliable.
It is refereed, so it must be biased.
Its cultural context does not fit the local situation.
It contains too much complete information.
questions.explain: Snow days do not happen in the Dominican Republic, so the solution's cultural context does not fit the local situation.

questions.stem: Researching hurricane preparedness, a Bridgetown student finds tips on an anonymous website with no date. This information should be:
options: Accepted, because all Internet information is reviewed before posting.
Accepted, because anonymous sources are never biased.
Treated as refereed, because it is publicly available.
Treated with caution or rejected, as its author and currency cannot be checked.
questions.explain: Anyone can publish online, so the student cannot check who wrote the tips or when, and should treat them with caution or reject them.

questions.stem: The firm CaribCode builds a payroll system for an Oranjestad company, finishing and signing off each stage fully before starting the next. Which model is this?
questions.explain: CaribCode's stage-by-stage approach with sign-offs and little going back is the waterfall model.

questions.stem: A Portsmouth accounting firm wants a tax system whose rules are fully known and will not change during the project. The waterfall model is most suitable when:
options: Requirements are clear and fixed from the start.
Users want to see a working version immediately.
The client cannot describe what they need.
questions.explain: Because the firm's tax rules are clear and fixed, the costly backtracking of waterfall is unlikely to be needed.

questions.stem: Developers show Cane Garden Bay restaurant owners a rough working ordering app, gather comments and improve it each week. Evolutionary development (prototyping) builds:
options: The whole system once, with no user feedback until delivery.
Detailed documents only, with no working software.
Hardware prototypes for a factory production line.
An early working version that is refined repeatedly using user feedback.
questions.explain: The owners try an early working version and their feedback shapes each improved version, which is evolutionary prototyping.

questions.stem: A Castries app team delivers working features every two weeks, meets the client often and welcomes changes. Agile software development is characterised by:
options: One long phase per stage with formal sign-off and fixed requirements.
Short iterations delivering working software, with close customer collaboration and welcome change.
No contact with the customer until the system is finished.
Heavy documentation before any code is written.
questions.explain: Two-week deliveries, frequent client meetings and openness to change are the hallmarks of Agile.

questions.stem: Bayside Mart launches its online shop with basic ordering first, then adds payments and delivery tracking in later releases. Which model is this?
questions.explain: Bayside Mart received a working core early, with features added in each release, which is iterative/incremental development.

questions.stem: After seeing a prototype of their booking app, staff at the Lac Bay Marina assume it is finished and keep asking for extras. A disadvantage of prototyping is that:
options: Users never see the system until it is complete.
Requirements must be fully fixed before any work begins.
It cannot involve users in the development.
Users may expect the prototype to be the finished system, and the scope can keep growing.
questions.explain: The marina staff mistook the prototype for the final system and kept adding requests, causing scope creep and delays.

questions.stem: The Anguilla start-up IslandHop is building a ferry-booking app, but its requirements keep changing weekly. Which model suits it best?
questions.explain: IslandHop's weekly changes are best handled by Agile's short iterations and regular feedback.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Cole Bay Clinic is replacing its paper patient records, and an analyst is planning the project. Which is the correct order of the SDLC stages in the syllabus?
options: Analysis, feasibility study, development, design, review, implementation
Design, feasibility study, analysis, implementation, development, review
Feasibility study, analysis, design, development, implementation, review
Feasibility study, design, analysis, implementation, development, review
questions.explain: The clinic project starts with a feasibility study, then analysis, design, development, implementation and finally review.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Basseterre Tours asks whether an online booking system is worthwhile before spending any money. The main deliverable of the feasibility study is:
options: The finished user manual for the new system.
The program code for every module.
A conversion plan for changing over systems.
A system proposal recommending whether the project should go ahead.
questions.explain: The feasibility study ends with a system proposal telling Basseterre Tours whether the booking system should go ahead.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Developers for the Jan Thiel Car Rental produce screen layouts, file designs and system flowcharts for the new rental system. These are deliverables of which stage?
questions.explain: Screen layouts, file designs and flowcharts describe how the rental system will work, so they come from the design stage.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Before a new grade-recording system goes live at a Brades school, the testers write a test plan. A test plan sets out:
options: How users will be trained after the system is installed.
What will be tested, the test data and the expected results.
The budget and timeline for the whole project.
Why the old system should be kept.
questions.explain: The test plan lists what to test, the test data and the expected results, so errors in the grade system are found before it goes live.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Blowing Point Supermarket will switch from its old tills to a new point-of-sale system. A conversion plan, produced for implementation, describes:
options: How the organisation will change over from the old system to the new one.
How data flows between processes in the system.
Which programming language the developers prefer.
How users rated the old system's interface.
questions.explain: The conversion plan sets out how the supermarket changes from the old tills to the new system while trading continues.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: Kingston Hotel's new system comes with two documents: one for front-desk staff and one for IT technicians. Which correctly contrasts a user manual and a technical manual?
options: A user manual contains program code; a technical manual explains basic operation.
A user manual explains how to use the system; a technical manual explains how it was built and is maintained.
Both are for end users and contain the same content.
A technical manual is produced only during the feasibility study.
questions.explain: Front-desk staff use the user manual to operate the system; technicians use the technical manual to understand and maintain it.

questions.topic: SO 3.6 · The SDLC and Software Engineering
questions.stem: The developer IslandSoft follows the SDLC, documents its work and tests carefully when building a system for a Linden business. Software engineering is best described as:
options: A disciplined, engineering approach to developing and maintaining software.
Repairing hardware faults in computer systems.
Writing code without any plan or testing.
Designing the physical layout of an office.
questions.explain: IslandSoft's systematic, documented and tested approach is what software engineering means.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: An analyst at Calabash Point Secondary needs views on a new timetable system from 400 students within one week. Which fact-finding tool should she use?
questions.explain: Questionnaires reach all 400 students quickly and cheaply, although they allow no follow-up questions.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: An analyst studying the Cable Beach Marina's booking system meets the manager to discuss problems in depth. What is the main advantage of interviews as a fact-finding tool?
options: They reach hundreds of people at almost no cost.
People never change their behaviour when interviewed.
They allow in-depth answers and follow-up questions.
They need no planning or preparation.
questions.explain: Meeting the manager gives the analyst detailed answers and the chance to ask follow-up questions, though interviews take time.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: An analyst stands near the checkouts at the Bayside Mart in Port of Spain, watching how cashiers actually process sales. This is which fact-finding tool?
questions.explain: Watching the cashiers at work is observation, which shows what people really do, though they may act differently when watched.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: An analyst at the Layou Hardware studies existing invoices, order forms and sales reports to learn how the current system works. This is:
questions.explain: Examining the store's invoices, forms and reports is a review of printed material, revealing the data the system uses and produces.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: A project manager for a new Frangipani Hill Academy website wants to show each task as a bar against a timeline. Which tool should she use?
questions.explain: A Gantt chart shows the website tasks as bars on a timeline so the schedule can be planned and tracked.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: Jacmel Car Rental sets discounts by age, rental length and membership. Which tool sets out every combination of conditions and the action to take for each?
questions.explain: A decision table lists every combination of age, length and membership with its discount, so no case is missed.

questions.topic: SO 3.7 · Tools Used in the SDLC
questions.stem: Analysts at the CaribCode in Belize City use software to draw DFDs, generate code and produce documentation for client systems. CASE tools are:
options: Software that helps analysts create diagrams, code and documentation.
Paper forms used to interview users.
Cables used to connect development computers.
Reports produced by an executive information system.
questions.explain: The software CaribCode uses to automate diagrams, code and documentation is a set of CASE tools.

questions.stem: A student is drawing a DFD for the Bodden Town Library's book-loan system. Which are the four symbols of a data flow diagram?
options: External entity, process, data store and data flow
questions.explain: The library DFD uses external entities, processes, data stores and data flows; decisions belong to flowcharts.

questions.stem: A student is drawing a DFD for the St. George's Tours booking system, including the process 'Confirm booking'. In Gane and Sarson notation, a process is drawn as:
questions.explain: In Gane and Sarson, 'Confirm booking' is drawn as a rounded rectangle; data stores are open-ended rectangles.

questions.stem: In a DFD for Bayside Mart, the process 'Record sale' has data flowing in but none flowing out. A process with inputs but no outputs is called a:
questions.explain: Sale data goes into 'Record sale' but nothing comes out, so it is a black hole error.

questions.stem: In a DFD for Nieuw Nickerie Clinic, the process 'Print invoice' sends data out but receives none. A process with outputs but no inputs is called a:
questions.explain: 'Print invoice' produces output from nowhere, so it is a miracle error.

questions.stem: An analyst shows managers of the Dickenson Bay Car Rental one diagram of the whole rental system, with customers and suppliers around it. A context-level DFD shows:
options: The whole system as a single process with its external entities and main data flows.
Every sub-process and data store in full detail.
The decisions and loops in a program.
The tables and relationships in a database.
questions.explain: The managers see the whole system as one process with its external entities and main flows; a level 1 DFD adds the detail.

questions.stem: A student's DFD for the Cockburn Town Tours booking system has several data flows. Which of these is a DFD error?
options: A data flow from a process to a data store.
A data flow from an external entity to a process.
A data flow from a data store to a process.
A data flow drawn directly from an external entity to a data store.
questions.explain: In the booking DFD, a customer cannot send data straight to a data store; entities and stores must connect through a process.

questions.stem: A student is labelling the shapes in a DFD for the Santiago Pharmacy's ordering system. Which label is most appropriate for a process?
questions.explain: 'Validate order' is a verb phrase describing an action, so it suits a process; the nouns suit flows, entities and stores.

questions.stem: Before coding a school-fees calculator, Amir, a Breadfruit Valley Secondary student, writes numbered steps that stop once the fee is worked out. An algorithm is best defined as:
options: A program written in a high-level language.
A finite, ordered sequence of clear steps that solves a problem.
A diagram of the network in a building.
A list of possible solutions with no order.
questions.explain: Amir's numbered steps are a finite, ordered plan for the solution; the program comes later when he codes them.

questions.stem: A Bridgetown teacher is checking her students' algorithms for calculating bus fares. Which set lists characteristics of a well-designed algorithm?
options: Infinite steps, flexible wording and a solution for one case only.
Written only in Python, with no fixed order of steps.
Ambiguous steps that the reader may interpret freely.
Finite steps, clear and unambiguous, a general solution and a clear flow of control.
questions.explain: A good bus-fare algorithm has finite steps, is clear and unambiguous, works generally and has a clear flow of control.

questions.stem: A Simpson Bay café writes a recipe algorithm for its guavaberry cake that includes the step "Add some sugar". Which characteristic of a well-designed algorithm does this break?
questions.explain: "Some" can be read in many ways, so the café's step is ambiguous; each step must have one exact meaning.

questions.stem: A student's algorithm for counting passengers arriving at Queen Beatrix airport keeps looping with no stopping condition. Which characteristic of a well-designed algorithm does it break?
options: It must be written in natural language.
It must finish in a finite number of steps.
It must handle only one input.
questions.explain: With no stopping condition, the passenger-counting algorithm never ends, so it is not finite.

questions.stem: A Coralstone College teacher's average-mark algorithm works only for exactly five students, but her class has 28. Which characteristic is missing?
options: It should be written in pseudocode.
It should be a general solution.
questions.explain: The algorithm should work for any class size, such as 28 students, so it is not a general solution.

questions.stem: A developer for the Portsmouth Clinic writes an algorithm for booking appointments before choosing Python or Java. Why is an algorithm important before coding?
options: It replaces the need to test the program.
It is the final program the computer runs.
It plans the solution so it can be checked, then coded in any language.
It can only be used for mathematical problems.
questions.explain: Planning the booking logic first lets it be checked and then coded in any language, whether Python or Java.

questions.stem: Sea-Almond Secondary School students must present an algorithm for calculating a household electricity bill in three accepted forms. Which three ways of representing algorithms are named in the syllabus?
options: DFDs, ER diagrams and Gantt charts
questions.explain: The students can write the bill algorithm in natural language, draw it as a flowchart or write it in pseudocode.

questions.stem: A flowchart for a Cane Garden Bay parking machine must ask "Has the driver paid?" and branch on yes or no. Which flowchart symbol represents a decision?
questions.explain: The "Has the driver paid?" question goes in a diamond, which has two exits for yes and no.

questions.stem: A flowchart for the Bayside Mart till must show 'Enter item price' and 'Display total'. Which flowchart symbol is used for input and output?
questions.explain: Entering prices and displaying the total are input and output, shown in parallelograms; rectangles show processes.

questions.stem: Before coding a grade calculator, a Vieux Fort student writes lines such as IF score >= 50 THEN PRINT "Pass". This representation, pseudocode, is:
options: A structured, English-like description of steps using programming-style keywords.
A diagram of shapes connected by arrows.
Machine code that runs directly on the CPU.
A conversational paragraph with no structure.
questions.explain: The student's lines use keywords such as IF and PRINT in structured English without being tied to one language, which is pseudocode.

questions.stem: A Kralendijk student describes a bus-fare algorithm in one long everyday paragraph, and classmates read it in different ways. What is the main disadvantage of writing an algorithm in natural language?
options: It can only be read by a computer.
It can be wordy and ambiguous.
questions.explain: Classmates interpreted the paragraph differently because everyday language can be wordy and ambiguous.

questions.stem: A Mahoe Grove High School teacher shows a flowchart of a late-arrival procedure instead of a paragraph. What is an advantage of a flowchart over natural language?
options: It is always shorter to draw than any text.
It can be run directly by the computer.
It shows the flow of control visually, so branches and loops are easy to follow.
It never needs updating when the algorithm changes.
questions.explain: The flowchart shows the late-arrival steps, branches and loops visually, so the order is clear at a glance.

questions.stem: A Frigate Bay water park's ride algorithm says: IF height >= 120 THEN allow ride ELSE refuse. Which control structure is shown by IF ... THEN ... ELSE?
questions.explain: The park's algorithm chooses between allowing and refusing based on height, which is selection.

questions.stem: A Palmetto Point Secondary student's program prints ten certificates using FOR count ← 1 TO 10 ... ENDFOR. This is an example of which control structure?
questions.explain: The FOR loop repeats the printing step ten times, which is repetition (iteration).

questions.stem: A check-in kiosk at PJIA runs: scan passport, show booking, print boarding pass, one after another. Steps carried out in the order written use which control structure?
questions.explain: Each kiosk step runs once in the order written, which is sequence.

questions.stem: A Westpunt shop tests part of its pricing code: x ← 4; y ← x * 3; x ← y - 2; PRINT x. What is printed?
questions.explain: y = 4 × 3 = 12, then x = 12 − 2 = 10, so the shop's code prints 10.

questions.stem: A student tests a tally loop for Brades Café: total ← 0; FOR i ← 1 TO 4: total ← total + i; ENDFOR; PRINT total. What is printed?
questions.explain: The loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, so the café tally prints 10.

questions.stem: A Sandbox Tree College teacher tests report code: IF mark >= 50 THEN PRINT "Pass" ELSE PRINT "Fail". What is printed when a student's mark is exactly 50?
questions.explain: 50 >= 50 is true, so the THEN branch runs and the report shows Pass.

questions.stem: A cashier at the Bayside Mart enters prices until she types -1, and every customer buys a different number of items. Which loop suits this?
options: A FOR loop with a fixed count
questions.explain: A WHILE loop keeps reading prices until -1 is entered, so it suits an unknown number of items.

questions.stem: Leah writes pseudocode for a Meads Bay tour-booking tool, then codes it in Python. Which best describes the relationship between an algorithm and a program?
options: The program is written first; the algorithm is produced from it afterwards.
They are unrelated; programs never need algorithms.
An algorithm is a program that has already been compiled.
The algorithm is the plan; the program is that plan coded in a language a computer can run.
questions.explain: Leah's pseudocode is the plan; her Python code is that plan written in a language a computer can run.

questions.stem: A Bayleaf Hill Secondary student is building a program to track overdue library fines. Which is the correct order of stages in program development?
options: Code, define the problem, test, design the algorithm, document
Design the algorithm, code, define the problem, document, test
Define the problem, design the algorithm, code, test and debug, document and maintain
Test, code, document, define the problem, design the algorithm
questions.explain: The student must understand the fines problem and design an algorithm before coding, testing, documenting and maintaining the program.

questions.stem: Developers at the CaribCode create a Booking class whose objects store guest details and have a confirm() method. Which paradigm organises programs around such objects?
questions.explain: Booking objects combine data and methods, which is object-oriented programming, supported by languages such as Java and Python.

questions.stem: A Spanish Town programmer writes a stock program in Pascal and a payroll tool in C, each as a series of procedures. Pascal and C are examples of which programming paradigm?
questions.explain: Both programs are built from sequences of procedures or functions, so Pascal and C are procedural languages.

questions.stem: A Seagrape Bay Secondary School student wants to write a stock program for a Georgetown shop using English-like statements. Which of these is a high-level programming language?
questions.explain: Python's English-like statements make it a high-level language; HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.

questions.stem: A developer enters ages 30, 21 (the minimum) and "abc" into the Cable Beach Car Rental booking program to check its responses. This happens during which stage?
questions.explain: Trying normal, boundary and erroneous ages checks the results and the handling of bad input, which is testing and debugging.

questions.stem: A student writes facts such as parent(ann, joe) and rules in Prolog to find links on a Trinidadian family tree. Prolog is an example of which programming paradigm?
questions.explain: The student states facts and rules and Prolog works out the answers, which is logic (declarative) programming.
